pericopes.text: And now behold, it came to pass in the commencement of the fortieth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, there began to be a serious difficulty among the people of the Nephites.

For behold, Pahoran had died, and gone the way of all the earth; therefore there began to be a serious contention concerning who should have the judgement seat among the brethren, which were the sons of Pahoran.

links.text: I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man;

provenance.other: “the way of all the earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Joshua 23:14 and 1 Kings 2:2, and in both it is first person and spoken by the dying man himself ('I am going', 'I go'). The Book of Mormon has made it a third-person obituary, which no KJV verse does. mediation-check.py returns a DECISIVE verdict for Joshua 23:14 on a one-word backbone; that verdict is an artifact of Joshua's long trailing clause aligning against nothing, and the wording of the borrowed phrase itself is identical in the two verses. Context decides it, not the diff.
provenance.alternative: Joshua 23:14, where Joshua rather than David speaks the sentence.
provenance.significance: This is the fifth appearance of the KJV's dying-ruler sentence in the corpus and the first in Helaman, and the chapter it opens is the reason to prefer David's form of it over Joshua's. In 1 Kings 2 the sentence is the last thing David says before the succession collapses: within the same chapter Adonijah, a son who is not the designated heir, presses a claim and is put to death for it (2:24-25). Helaman 1:2-8 is that sequence — the ruler dies, three of his sons contend for the seat, and the one who tries to take it by force is condemned to death. The KJV supplies the sentence, and the sentence brings the chapter it stands in. Compare Hays on metalepsis: the borrowed clause is short, and what it recovers is the story around it.

links.note: 'Pahoran had died, and gone the way of all the earth; therefore there began to be a serious contention concerning who should have the judgement seat among the brethren, which were the sons of Pahoran.' The phrase entered the corpus at 2 Nephi 1:14 and has been adjudicated three times since, most recently at Alma 1:1 for Mosiah's death; it re-enters here in a new book and a new hand, which is why it is given as a link rather than passed over as a recurrence (ADJUDICATING §4). What is new is the sequel. At Alma 1:1 the formula was negated — Mosiah left 'none to reign in his stead'. Here the succession does happen, and it happens the way 1 Kings 2 says it happens: contested, among brothers, with one of them executed. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: Now these are their names which did contend for the judgement seat, which did also cause the people to contend: Pahoran, Paanchi, and Pacumeni.
Now these are not all the sons of Pahoran, (for he had many,) but these are they which did contend for the judgement seat; therefore they did cause three divisions among the people.
Nevertheless, it came to pass that Pahoran was appointed by the voice of the people to be a Chief Judge and a governor over the people of Nephi.

links.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

provenance.other: “voice of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:7. Every other KJV 'voice of' is the voice of the LORD, of the people's own cry, or of one man; this is the only place the phrase names a constituency whose collective will is to be obeyed.
provenance.significance: The catalogue adjudicated this phrase at Mosiah 7:9 and argued it again at Mosiah 29:2, where Mosiah abolished the kingship the KJV verse instituted. Helaman 1 is the third movement and the darkest: here the voice of the people does not choose a king or refuse one, it convicts a man and sentences him to death (1:8), and the execution is what produces the assassination in 1:9. In 1 Samuel 8:7 the voice of the people is a rejection of God that God tells Samuel to obey anyway. In Helaman 1 it is the only machinery left, and within four verses it has killed a claimant and got a chief judge murdered on his seat. Neither text says the mechanism fails; the borrowing lets the reader hear that it might.

links.note: 'Pahoran was appointed by the voice of the people to be a Chief Judge and a governor.' The phrase carries the whole constitutional argument of Helaman 1-2 and occurs five times in these two chapters (1:5, 1:6, 1:8, 1:13, 2:2) — appointing, uniting, condemning, appointing again. Its KJV home is Samuel's rejection oracle, and Helaman is a new book with a new narrator, so the row is written out rather than left to Mosiah's (ADJUDICATING §4). The 1830 text reads 'a Chief Judge and a governor'; 1920 deletes the article, which does not bear on the source.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Pacumeni, when he saw that he could not obtain the judgement seat, he did unite with the voice of the people.

But behold, Paanchi, and that part of the people that were desirous that he should be their governor, was exceeding wroth; therefore he was about to flatter away those people to rise up in rebellion against their brethren.

links.text: And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come in peaceably, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries.

provenance.other: “obtain the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 11:21. “flatteries” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all of them Daniel 11 (21, 32, 34). The KJV's other flattery vocabulary is devotional and not political: “flatter” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 5:9 and Psalm 78:36, and both are about lying to God with the mouth.
provenance.significance: Daniel 11:21 is the King James Bible's one sentence about a man who is denied the honour of the kingdom and gets it anyway by flattery, and it is the template the Book of Mormon uses for every usurper from here to the end of Helaman. Recovering Daniel's context supplies what Helaman 1:7 does not say: the vile person of Daniel 11 comes in 'peaceably', takes power through corrupted insiders (11:32), and ends by setting himself above every god. Paanchi's rebellion fails in one verse; Gadianton's version of the same manoeuvre at 2:5 succeeds, and by 3:23 his combinations are established in the land and unknown to the government.

links.note: 'He was about to flatter away those people to rise up in rebellion against their brethren.' The Book of Mormon's political flattery — a losing claimant seducing a faction into installing him — has one KJV source and it is Daniel 11:21, where a man to whom 'they shall not give the honour of the kingdom' obtains it by flatteries. The catalogue has read Alma 61:4 in the neighbouring register (Pahoran's own complaint of 'great flattery' against those who took the judgement seat from him), and it is worth noticing that the sons of that Pahoran are the flatterers here. Filed moderate because the shared vocabulary is one word family and the KJV noun ('flatteries') is not the Book of Mormon's verb.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass as he was about to do this, behold, he was taken, and was tried according to the voice of the people, and condemned unto death; for he had raised up in rebellion, and sought to destroy the liberty of the people.

links.text: And king Solomon sent by the hand of Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he fell upon him that he died.

provenance.significance: The verse three lines above this one quotes David's dying sentence (see 1:2), and this is what follows it in the source. Adonijah is the brother who is not given the seat, who gathers a party, and whom the successor executes for reaching after the kingdom; Paanchi is the brother who is not given the seat, who gathers a party, and whom the state executes for the same. The Book of Mormon has not borrowed 1 Kings 2's words here, but it has borrowed 1 Kings 2's shape, and it announced the borrowing four verses earlier with the one clause it did take verbatim.

links.note: 'He was taken, and was tried according to the voice of the people, and condemned unto death; for he had raised up in rebellion, and sought to destroy the liberty of the people.' Read on its own this is a constitutional notice with no biblical wording in it. Read after 1:2 it is the second half of a KJV chapter whose first half the text has already quoted: David goes the way of all the earth, and his sons fight over the throne until the loser is put to death. The differences are the point of the row rather than an objection to it — Adonijah dies at a king's word and by an assassin's hand, Paanchi by trial and 'according to the voice of the people'. The Nephite state does with a court what Solomon did with Benaiah, and the source makes that visible.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact at all: not one distinctive phrase of 1 Kings 2:24-25 appears here, and fratricidal succession disputes are common enough in Kings and Chronicles that Adonijah is not the only candidate. The row stands or falls with the quotation at 1:2; withdraw it if that link is withdrawn.

pericopes.text: Now when those people which were desirous that he should be their governor, saw that he was condemned unto death, therefore they were angry; and behold, they sent forth one Kishkumen, even to the judgement seat of Pahoran, and murdered Pahoran as he sat upon the judgement seat.
And he was pursued by the servants of Pahoran; but behold, so speedy was the flight of Kishkumen, that no man could overtake him.
And he went unto those that sent him, and they all entered into a covenant, yea, swearing by their everlasting Maker, that they would tell no man that Kishkumen had murdered Pahoran;

therefore Kishkumen was not known among the people of Nephi, for he was in disguise at the time that he murdered Pahoran. And Kishkumen, and his band which had covenanted with him, did mingle themselves among the people, in a manner that they all could not be found; but as many as were found, were condemned unto death.

And now behold, Pacumeni was appointed, according to the voice of the people, to be a Chief Judge and a govereor governor over the people, to reign in the stead of his brother Pahoran; and it was according to his right. And all this was done, in the fortieth year of the reign of the Judges; and it had an end.

links.text: And Solomon said unto God, Thou hast shewed great mercy unto David my father, and hast made me to reign in his stead.

provenance.other: “to reign in his stead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 1:8 — Solomon's own account of his accession. The KJV's ordinary regnal formula is the past 'reigned in his stead' (1 Kings 11:43 and dozens more); the infinitive is Solomon's alone. Helaman 1:13 substitutes the possessor: 'to reign in the stead of his brother Pahoran'.
provenance.significance: The corpus has used this infinitive twice before and both times it marked a Solomonic accession: Mosiah 6:4, where Mosiah succeeds Benjamin, and Alma 1:1, where the formula is negated because there is no heir at all. Here it is neither a son nor an absence but a brother, and the text adds 'and it was according to his right' — the one thing Adonijah could not say. Solomon's sentence is a thanksgiving for being given a throne that was contested; Helaman gives it to the third of three contending brothers, the two ahead of him being dead and murdered respectively.

links.note: 'Pacumeni was appointed, according to the voice of the people, to be a Chief Judge and a governor over the people, to reign in the stead of his brother Pahoran; and it was according to his right.' The KJV's one infinitive accession-clause, moved off the son and onto the brother. What makes the row worth writing rather than filing as a recurrence is the collision of two authorities in one sentence: the seat comes 'according to the voice of the people' (1 Samuel 8:7, the demand for a king) and 'according to his right' (dynastic succession), and the borrowed clause belongs to the second. The 1830 printing has the compositor's doubled 'govereor governor' here, corrected out in 1920; it bears on nothing but the press.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass in the forty and first year of the reign of the Judges, that the Lamanites had gathered together an innumerable army of men, and armed them with swords, and with cimeters, and with bows, and with arrows, and with headplates, and with breast-plates, and with all manner of shields of every kind;

links.text: And Uzziah prepared for them throughout all the host shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones.

provenance.other: 2 Chronicles 26:14 is the King James Bible's one full quartermaster's inventory issued to a standing army — 'shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones'. “shields and spears” occurs in exactly two KJV verses. The Book of Mormon's list keeps the shape and changes the contents: swords and cimeters for spears and slings, headplates for helmets, and 'all manner of shields of every kind' for the plain shields.
provenance.significance: Uzziah's armoury is the verse the catalogue adjudicated behind the arming of both Nephite and Lamanite hosts at Alma 43:18-21, where the inventory is split between the two armies. Helaman 1:14 gives the whole of it to the Lamanites and adds the body armour the Nephites had monopolised in Alma 43 — headplates and breastplates. The borrowed KJV list is thereby doing narrative work: the equipment gap that decided Alma's wars has closed, which is exactly what the chapter goes on to show.

links.note: 'Armed them with swords, and with cimeters, and with bows, and with arrows, and with headplates, and with breast-plates, and with all manner of shields of every kind.' A new book and a new war, so the row is written rather than left to Alma 43's (ADJUDICATING §4), and the argument for the source is made there. Filed moderate: the KJV's own words are largely replaced, and what carries the link is the form of the sentence — a named commander equipping a host, item by item, in a single 'and with' chain — rather than its vocabulary. 1830's 'headplates' and 'breast-plates' are respelled in 1920 and nothing turns on it.

pericopes.text: and they came down again, that they might pitch battle against the Nephites. And they were led by a man whose name was Coriantumr; and he was a descendant of Zarahemla; and he was a dissenter from among the Nephites; and he was a large and a mighty man;

therefore the king of the Lamanites, whose name was Tubaloth, who was the son of Ammoron. Now Tubaloth supposing that Coriantumr, he being a mighty man, could stand against the Nephites, insomuch with his strength, and also with his great wisdom, that by sending him forth, he should gain power over the Nephites;

therefore he did stir them up to anger, and he did gather together his armies, and he did appoint Coriantumr to be their leader, and did cause that they should march down to the land of Zarahemla, to battle against the Nephites.

And it came to pass that because of so much contention and so much difficulty in the government, that they had not kept sufficient guards in the land of Zarahemla; for they had supposed that the Lamanites durst not come into the heart of their lands to attack that great city Zarahemla.

But it came to pass that Coriantumr did march forth at the head of his numerous host, and came upon the inhabitants of the city, and their march was with such exceeding great speed, that there was no time for the Nephites to gather together their armies;

therefore Coriantumr did cut down the watch by the entrance of the city, and did march forth with his whole army into the city, and they did slay every one who did oppose them, insomuch that they did take possession of the whole city.

And it came to pass that Pacumeni, which was the Chief Judge, did flee before Coriantumr, even to the walls of the city. And it came to pass that Coriantumr did smite him against the wall, insomuch that he died. And thus ended the days of Pacumeni.

And now when Coriantumr saw that he was in possession of the city of Zarahemla, and saw that the Nephites had fled before them, and were slain, and were taken, and were cast into prison, and that he had obtained the possession of the strongest hold in all the land, his heart took courage, insomuch that he was about to go forth against all the land.

And now he did not tarry in the land of Zarahemla, but he did march forth with a large army, even towards the city of Bountiful; for it was his determination to go forth and cut his way through with the sword, that he might obtain the north parts of the land;

and supposing that their greatest strength was in the centre of the land, therefore he did march forth, giving them no time to assemble themselves together, save it were in small bodies; and in this manner they did fall upon them and cut them down to the earth.
But behold, this march of Coriantumr through the centre of the land, gave Moronihah great advantage over them, notwithstanding the greatness of the number of the Nephites which were slain;

for behold, Moronihah had supposed that the Lamanites durst not come into the centre of the land, but that they would attack the cities round about in the borders, as they had hitherto done; therefore Moronihah had caused that their strong armies should maintain those parts round about by the borders.

But behold, the Lamanites were not frightened according to his desire, but they had come into the centre of the land, and had taken the capital city, which was the city of Zarahemla, and were marching through the most capital parts of the land, slaying the people with a great slaughter, both men, women and children, taking possession of many cities and of many strong holds.
But when Moronihah had discovered this, he immediately sent forth Lehi with an army round about to head them, before they should come to the land Bountiful:
And thus he did; and he did head them, before they came to the land Bountiful, and gave unto them battle, insomuch that they began to retreat back towards the land of Zarahemla.

And it came to pass that Moronihah did head them in their retreat, and did give unto them battle insomuch that it became an exceeding bloody battle; yea, many were slain; and among the number which were slain, Coriantumr was also found.
And now behold the Lamanites could not retreat neither way; neither on the north, nor on the south, nor on the east, nor on the west, for they were surrounded on every hand by the Nephites:

And thus had Coriantumr plunged the Lamanites into the midst of the Nephites, insomuch that they were in the power of the Nephites, and he himself was slain, and the Lamanites did yield themselves into the hands of the Nephites.
And it came to pass that Moronihah took possession of the city of Zarahemla again, and caused that the Lamanites which had been taken prisoners should depart out of the land in peace.
And thus ended the forty and first year of the reign of the Judges.

And it came to pass in the forty and second year of the reign of the Judges, after Moronihah had established again the peace betweem the Nephites and the Lamanites, behold there was no one to fill the judgement seat; therefore there began to be a contention again among the people concerning who should fill the judgement seat.
And it came to pass that Helaman, which was the son of Helaman, was appointed to fill the judgement seat, by the voice of the people;
but behold, Kishkumen, who had murdered Pahoran, did lay wait to destroy Helaman also; and he was upheld by his band, which had entered into a covenant that no one should know his wickedness;

links.text: If they say, Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause:

provenance.other: “let us lay wait” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 1:11. “lay wait” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, two of them Proverbs 1:11 and 1:18. “one purse” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 1:14. “greedy of gain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, one of them Proverbs 1:19.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 1:10-19 is the King James Bible's one sustained portrait of a criminal confederacy: sinners who entice, who say 'let us lay wait for blood', who cast in their lot together and hold one purse, and whose ways are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain. It is the passage the Book of Mormon needed and did not have — a band, a recruiting speech, a common fund, and murder for profit — and the Gadianton robbers are introduced in its vocabulary and its order. Recover the context and the whole trajectory of Helaman is already written into it: 'they lay wait for their own blood; they lurk privily for their own lives' (1:18). Kishkumen lays wait for Helaman in verse 3 and is dead of a stab wound in verse 9, and Proverbs says in advance that this is what laying wait is for. The father in Proverbs 1 is warning a son not to consent; Helaman 2:5 is the consent scene, and 2:8 has the servant refuse it by pretending to give it.

links.note: 'Kishkumen … did lay wait to destroy Helaman also; and he was upheld by his band, which had entered into a covenant that no one should know his wickedness.' Every structural element of Proverbs 1:10-19 is present across Helaman 2:3-11 and mostly in Proverbs' order: the band (1:11), laying wait for blood (1:11), the oath of secrecy that binds them (the Book of Mormon's covenant answering Proverbs' 'cast in thy lot among us'), the promise of shared spoil and power (1:13-14, answered at 2:5), and killing for gain (1:19, answered at 2:8's 'to murder, and to rob, and to gain power'). The verb the Book of Mormon takes is the rarest thing in the passage: the KJV writes 'lay wait' in only four verses and half of them are these.

pericopes.text: for there was one Gadianton, who was exceeding expert in many words, and also in his craft, to carry on the secret work of murder and of robbery; therefore he became the leader of the band of Kishkumen;

links.text: After two days was the feast of the passover, and of unleavened bread: and the chief priests and the scribes sought how they might take him by craft, and put him to death.

provenance.other: “by craft” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 14:1, where the chief priests and scribes seek how they might take Jesus by craft and put him to death. “craft” in the sense of deceit rather than trade occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 14:1 and Daniel 8:25 ('through his policy also he shall cause craft to prosper in his hand … and by peace shall destroy many'); the remaining four are a tentmaker's and a silversmith's occupation. “cause craft to prosper” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The two KJV verses that use 'craft' for deceit are the two the Book of Mormon needs at once, and it takes something from each. Mark 14:1 supplies the thing Gadianton does — a secret deliberation among leaders about how to kill a man without being seen to. Daniel 8:25 supplies the thing he is: a figure whose method is policy, who magnifies himself in his heart, and who 'by peace shall destroy many', which is precisely Helaman 3:23, where the combinations flourish during the years of continual peace and are unknown to those at the head of government.

links.note: 'There was one Gadianton, who was exceeding expert in many words, and also in his craft, to carry on the secret work of murder and of robbery.' The King James Bible has exactly one verse in which 'craft' means the technique of a covert killing, and it is the Sanhedrin's. Filed moderate rather than high because the shared word is one and the Book of Mormon's construction ('in his craft') is not Mark's ('by craft'); what raises it above the vocabulary is that Gadianton is introduced by the two attributes Mark's verse and Daniel's respectively give — expertness in words and expertness in craft — and that the rest of Helaman treats him as the vile person of Daniel 11 whom the catalogue has already met at 1:7.

pericopes.text: therefore he did flatter them, and also Kishkumen, that if they would place him in the judgement seat, he would grant unto those which belonged to his band that they should be placed in power and authority among the people; therefore Kishkumen sought to destroy Helaman.

And it came to pass as he went forth towards the judgement seat, to destroy Helaman, behold one of the servants of Helaman, having been out by night, and having obtained, through disguise, a knowledge of those plans which had been laid by this band to destroy Helaman.

links.text: When they were at the great stone which is in Gibeon, Amasa went before them. And Joab’s garment that he had put on was girded unto him, and upon it a girdle with a sword fastened upon his loins in the sheath thereof; and as he went forth it fell out.

provenance.other: “as he went forth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 20:8, and what goes forth in it is Joab's concealed sword — 'a girdle with a sword fastened upon his loins in the sheath thereof; and as he went forth it fell out'. The Book of Mormon transfers the clause to the walking assassin himself.
provenance.significance: 2 Samuel 20:8-10 is the King James Bible's most exact model for what Helaman 2 does twice: a man walks companionably beside another on a public errand, with a weapon nobody has seen, and kills him mid-conversation. The Book of Mormon has taken the clause that in the source belongs to the hidden weapon and given it to the man carrying it, which is the sentence Helaman 2 needs — Kishkumen goes forth toward the judgement seat and the reader is not told, until 2:9, which of the two walkers is armed.

links.note: 'And it came to pass as he went forth towards the judgement seat, to destroy Helaman, behold one of the servants of Helaman, having been out by night.' The four-word clause is a KJV singleton and its home is the approach to the murder of Amasa. Filed moderate: the words are ordinary and their rarity is partly an accident of the KJV's phrasing habits, and the chapter's dependence on the Joab passage is argued properly at 2:9. Recorded here because the singleton is at this verse and a reader browsing 2:6 should be sent on rather than shown nothing.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he met Kishkumen, and he gave unto him a sign; therefore Kishkumen made known unto him the object of his desire, desiring that he would conduct him to the judgement seat, that he might murder Helaman:

links.text: Now he that betrayed him gave them a sign, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast.

provenance.other: “gave them a sign” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 26:48 — Judas's prearranged kiss. The KJV's other 'signs' given are portents and miracles; this is the only place in the Bible where one conspirator gives another a private signal identifying a man to be seized.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the roles are reversed, which is what makes the borrowing worth having. In Matthew 26:48 the sign is given by the betrayer to the arresting party, and it marks out the innocent man. In Helaman 2:7 the sign is given by the intended victim's servant to the assassin, and it marks out the servant as one of the band — a counterfeit that buys Helaman's life. Both signs work perfectly and both lead directly to a death; the Book of Mormon has taken the mechanism of Gethsemane and put it in the hands of the man protecting the target. The servant's whole tactic in 2:7-8 is to be taken for a conspirator, which is Judas's position exactly.

links.note: 'He met Kishkumen, and he gave unto him a sign; therefore Kishkumen made known unto him the object of his desire, desiring that he would conduct him to the judgement seat, that he might murder Helaman.' The KJV uses the phrase once, of Judas, and it works the same way in both places: the sign is a token of membership that gets the bearer accepted, and acceptance is what makes the killing possible. Helaman 2's whole plot turns on this verse's mechanism and the Book of Mormon gives it in the KJV's own words. Well short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when the servant of Helaman had known all the heart of Kishkumen, and how that it was his object to murder, and also that it was the object of all those which belonged to his band, to murder, and to rob, and to gain power, (and this was their secret plan, and their combination,) the servant of Helaman saith unto Kishkumen, Let us go forth unto the judgement seat.

Now this did please Kishkumen exceedingly, for he did suppose that he should accomplish his design; but behold, the servant of Helaman, as they were going forth unto the judgement seat, did stab Kishkumen, even to the heart, that he fell dead without a groan. And he ran and told Helaman all the things which he had seen, and heard, and done.

links.text: But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab’s hand: so he smote him therewith in the fifth rib, and shed out his bowels to the ground, and struck him not again; and he died. So Joab and Abishai his brother pursued after Sheba the son of Bichri.

provenance.other: “the fifth rib” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all of them in 2 Samuel and all of them single-thrust assassinations (2:23, 3:27, 4:6, 20:10). The Book of Mormon does not use the phrase; it writes 'even to the heart', which is in no KJV verse. What it does take is the sequence and the finality — one blow, no second stroke, instant death — and 2 Samuel 20:10 is the KJV verse that insists on it: 'he smote him therewith in the fifth rib … and struck him not again; and he died.'
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's phrase is 'that he fell dead without a groan', and the silence is the point of the borrowing. Joab's killing of Amasa is the KJV's set piece of an assassination that makes no noise and interrupts nothing — the army marches on past the body. Helaman 2:9 needs the same silence for the same reason: Kishkumen has to die where nobody hears, or Gadianton learns of it before Helaman can move. The catalogue's usual finding is that the Book of Mormon takes the KJV's words; here it has taken the KJV's stagecraft and written its own sentence for it.

links.note: 'The servant of Helaman, as they were going forth unto the judgement seat, did stab Kishkumen, even to the heart, that he fell dead without a groan.' Three elements of 2 Samuel 20:8-10 in the source's order: the walk (2:6, on the singleton 'as he went forth'), the feigned fellowship, and the single unrepeated blow that kills at once. Filed moderate and kjvSpecific 'uncertain' because the wording of the blow itself is not the KJV's — 'even to the heart' and 'without a groan' are the Book of Mormon's own, and 'stab' is a verb the King James translators never use.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact at this verse is nil; the rarity that carries the pair sits at 2:6, and 2 Samuel supplies three other fifth-rib killings that would serve the type equally well. A reader who wants a verbal criterion will decline this row and keep 2:6.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Helaman did send forth to take this band of robbers and secret murderers, that they might be executed according to the law.

But behold, when Gadianton had found that Kishkumen did not return, he feared lest that he should be destroyed; therefore he caused that his band should follow him. And they took their flight out of the land, by a secret way, into the wilderness; and thus when Helaman sent forth to take them, they could no where be found.—
And more of this Gadianton shall be spoken hereafter. And thus ended the forty and second year of the reign of the judges over the people of Nephi.
And behold, in the end of this book, ye shall see that this Gadianton did prove the overthrow, yea, almost the entire destruction of the people of Nephi.—
Behold I do not mean the end of the Book of Helaman, but I mean the end of the Book of Nephi, from which I have taken all the account which I have written.

And now it came to pass in the forty and third year of the reign of the Judges, there was no contention among the people of Nephi, save it were a little pride which was in the church, which did cause some little dissensions among the people, which affairs were settled in the ending of the forty and third year.
And there was no contention among the people in the forty and fourth year; neither was there much contention in the forty and fifth year.

And it came to pass in the forty and sixth, yea, there were much contentions and many dissensions; in the which there were an exceeding great many which departed out of the land of Zarahemla, and went forth unto the land northward, to inherit the land;
and they did travel to an exceeding great distance, insomuch that they came to large bodies of water, and many rivers;

yea, and even they did spread forth into all parts of the land, into whatever parts it had not been rendered desolate, and without timber, because of the many inhabitants which had before inherited the land.
And now no part of the land was desolate, save it were for timber, &c.; but because of the greatness of the destruction of the people which had before inhabited the land, it was called desolate.

And there being but little timber upon the face of the land, nevertheless the people which went forth, became exceeding expert in the working of cement; therefore they did build houses of cement, in the which they did dwell.

And it came to pass that they did multiply and spread, and did go forth from the land southward, to the land northward, and did spread insomuch that they began to cover the face of the whole earth, from the sea south, to the sea north, from the sea west, to the sea east.

And the people which were in the land northward, did dwell in tents, and in houses of cement, and they did suffer whatsoever tree should spring up upon the face of the land, that it should grow up, that in time they might have timber to build their houses, yea, their cities, and their temples, and their synagogues, and their sanctuaries, and all manner of their buildings.
And it came to pass as timber was exceeding scarce in the land northward, they did send forth much by the way of shipping;
and thus they did enable the people in the land northward, that they might build many cities, both of wood and of cement.
And it came to pass that there were many of the people of Ammon, which were Lamanites by birth, did also go forth into this land.
And now there are many records kept of the proceedings of this people, by many of this people, which are particular and very large, concerning them;

but behold a hundredth part of the proceedings of this people, yea, the account of the Lamanites, and of the Nephites, and their wars, and contentions, and dissensions, and their preaching, and their prophecies, and their shipping, and their building of ships, and their building of temples, and of synagogues, and their sanctuaries, and their righteousness, and their wickedness, and their murders, and their robbings, and their plundering, and all manner of abominations and whoredoms, cannot be contained in this work;

links.text: And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.

provenance.other: “could not contain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the world itself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and they are the same verse, John 21:25. The Book of Mormon writes 'cannot be contained in this work', substituting the book for the world as the thing too small to hold the record.
provenance.significance: John 21:25 is the King James Bible's one sentence of editorial apology, and it is the sentence the Book of Mormon's abridgers reach for whenever they have to explain an omission — 1 Nephi 6:3 and Words of Mormon 1:5 before this. What Helaman 3:14 adds is the inventory. John says only 'many other things which Jesus did'; Mormon spends a whole verse listing what will not fit — wars, contentions, dissensions, preaching, prophecies, shipping, temples, synagogues, sanctuaries, righteousness, wickedness, murders, robbings, plundering, abominations, whoredoms. The borrowed excuse is being used to advertise the size of what is withheld, which is the opposite of John's reticence.

links.note: 'A hundredth part of the proceedings of this people … cannot be contained in this work.' The pairing of an impossibly large record with a container too small for it is John 21:25's, and the two rarest strings in that verse are both singletons. A new book and a new stretch of Mormon's own editorial voice, so the row is written rather than left to 1 Nephi 6:3 (ADJUDICATING §4). Note that the Book of Mormon's 'hundredth part' is not from here: “hundredth part” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 5:11, where it is a rate of interest to be restored, and the corpus uses the fraction as its own formula.

pericopes.text: but behold, there are many books and many records of every kind, and they have been kept chiefly by the Nephites;

links.text: And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.

provenance.other: “many books” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ecclesiastes 12:12 — 'of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh'. The rarity is real but the phrase is two ordinary words, which is why the row is filed low.
provenance.significance: Both sentences are a writer's remark about the limits of writing, made at the point where a work is being closed off. Qoheleth's is a warning to a son that book-making has no end; Mormon's is a report that the books already exist in numbers he cannot carry, 'many books and many records of every kind'. If the echo is real, the Book of Mormon has taken the Bible's one weary sentence about too many books and used it to explain an abridgment — which is the same anxiety with the moral removed.

links.note: 'There are many books and many records of every kind, and they have been kept chiefly by the Nephites.' The verse sits immediately after the John 21:25 borrowing at 3:14, and the two together make the closing gesture of the KJV's two most famous remarks about the impossibility of writing everything down. Recorded because the juxtaposition is worth a reader's attention, not because the wording proves anything.
links.whyNot: A two-word singleton where both words are common is nearly worthless as evidence, and nothing else of Ecclesiastes 12 is present — no 'weariness of the flesh', no 'much study', no address to a son. A cautious reader should treat 3:15 as unlinked and keep only 3:14.

pericopes.text: and they have been handed down from one generation to another, by the Nephites, even until they have fallen into transgression, and have been murdered, plundered, and hunted, and driven forth, and slain, and scattered upon the face of the earth, and mixed with the Lamanites until they are no more called the Nephites, becoming wicked, and wild, and ferocious, yea, even becoming Lamanites.
And now I return again to mine account; therefore what I have spoken had passed after there had been great contentions, and disturbances, and wars, and dissensions among the people of Nephi.
The forty and sixth year of the reign of the Judges ended.
And it came to pass that there was still great contentions in the land, yea, even in the forty and seventh year, and also in the forty and eighth year;

nevertheless, Helaman did fill the judgement seat with justice and equity; yea, he did observe to keep the statutes, and the judgements, and the commandments of God; and he did do that which was right in the sight of God, continually; and he did walk after the ways of his father, insomuch that he did prosper in the land.

links.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

provenance.other: “keep his statutes and his commandments” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 26:17 and 1 Kings 2:3, and so does the fuller triad “his statutes and his commandments and his judgments”. mediation-check.py separates them decisively on a six-word backbone: where Deuteronomy 26:17 ends the sentence with 'to hearken unto his voice', 1 Kings 2:3 continues 'that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest' — and Helaman 3:20 ends 'insomuch that he did prosper in the land'. “that thou mayest prosper” occurs in exactly three KJV verses. The evaluation clause is a second source: “walked in the ways of David his father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 34:2 (Josiah), and “ways of his father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 17:3 (Jehoshaphat).
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 2:3 is David's dying charge to Solomon, and it is the verse immediately after the one Helaman 1:2 quoted to bury Pahoran. The book that opened by taking David's death sentence closes its third chapter by taking the charge that follows it, applied to a chief judge rather than a king — statutes, judgments, commandments, walking in his ways, and prospering, in the source's order. The Book of Mormon's promise 'inasmuch as ye will keep my commandments, ye shall prosper in the land' has been running on this verse since 1 Nephi 2:20, but here the whole charge is reassembled at once, and it is reassembled for a man who holds the judgement seat by the voice of the people. The Deuteronomistic evaluation of kings is being used to grade a republic's magistrate.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 26:17, which has the same triad of statutes, commandments and judgments but not the prospering.

links.note: 'He did observe to keep the statutes, and the judgements, and the commandments of God; and he did do that which was right in the sight of God, continually; and he did walk after the ways of his father, insomuch that he did prosper in the land.' Four elements of 1 Kings 2:3 in 1 Kings' order, and the fifth — 'did that which was right in the sight of' — is the regnal-evaluation formula that 2 Chronicles 34:2 joins to 'walked in the ways of David his father'. The mediation is decided rather than defaulted: the only point at which Deuteronomy 26:17 and 1 Kings 2:3 diverge in wording is the ending, and the Book of Mormon has 1 Kings' ending. 1830 spells the plural 'judgements'; 1920 modernizes it, which is the KJV's own spelling being erased rather than restored.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he had two sons. He gave unto the eldest the name of Nephi, and unto the youngest the name of Lehi. And they began to grow up unto the Lord.—

links.text: In those days, and at that time, will I cause the Branch of righteousness to grow up unto David; and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land.

provenance.other: “grow up unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 33:15: 'will I cause the Branch of righteousness to grow up unto David; and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land'. The KJV's ordinary constructions are 'grow up' absolutely (Job 8:11, Malachi 4:2) or 'grow up as' a plant; the dative — growing up *unto* somebody — is Jeremiah's alone, and it is dynastic.
provenance.significance: Recover the source and the verse is a succession oracle. Jeremiah 33:15 promises David a Branch that will grow up to him and execute judgment in the land, in a chapter whose next verses guarantee that David shall never want a man to sit upon the throne. Helaman 3:21 names two sons in the sentence after 3:20 has said their father filled the judgement seat with justice and equity and walked in the ways of *his* father — three generations of the same office — and says they 'began to grow up unto the Lord'. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's one phrase for a dynastic shoot and redirected it: the boys grow up not to their father but to the Lord, which is the point the rest of Helaman will make when Nephi gives up the judgement seat altogether (Helaman 5:1-4).

links.note: 'He gave unto the eldest the name of Nephi, and unto the youngest the name of Lehi. And they began to grow up unto the Lord.' A KJV singleton in a verse that is doing exactly the work the singleton does in Jeremiah — introducing the heirs on whom a line's future rests. Filed moderate because the shared string is three short words and Jeremiah 33 supplies nothing else here; what argues for it is that the redirection ('unto the Lord', not unto their father) is legible only if the KJV's phrase is heard behind it. The names are themselves the argument: the two sons are given the names of the founder and his father, which is the Branch idea in another idiom.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the wars and contentions began to cease, in a small degree, among the people of the Nephites, in the latter end of the forty and eighth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.

And it came to pass in the forty and ninth year of the reign of the Judges, there was continual peace established in the land, all save it were the secret combinations which Gadianton the nobler robber had established, in the more settled parts of the land, which at that time were not known unto those which were at the head of government; therefore they were not destroyed out of the land.

And it came to pass that in this same year, there was exceeding great prosperity in the church, insomuch that there were thousands who did join themselves unto the church, and were baptized unto repentance;
and so great was the prosperity of the church, and so many the blessings which were poured out upon the people, that even the High Priests and the teachers were themselves astonished beyond measure.—

links.text: And were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak.

provenance.other: “beyond measure astonished” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 7:37. Mark's other superlative is 'astonished out of measure' (10:26); the Book of Mormon has the word order of 7:37 with the participle moved — 'astonished beyond measure'.
provenance.significance: In Mark 7:37 the people are beyond measure astonished at deaf ears opened and dumb mouths loosed, and they say 'He hath done all things well'. Helaman 3:25 puts the astonishment in the mouths of the professionals: it is the High Priests and the teachers, the men whose office is to produce exactly this result, who are 'themselves astonished beyond measure' at how many are being baptized. The KJV's crowd is amazed at a miracle done in front of it; the Book of Mormon's clergy are amazed at the success of their own ministry, which the next verse attributes to 'the work of the Lord'.

links.note: 'So great was the prosperity of the church, and so many the blessings which were poured out upon the people, that even the High Priests and the teachers were themselves astonished beyond measure.' The King James Bible reaches for its strongest formula of astonishment once, and the Book of Mormon uses it at the one place in Helaman 3 where the narrative asks for a superlative. Filed as an echo rather than an allusion: the phrase is a stock intensifier as well as a singleton, and nothing else of Mark 7 is in view.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the work of the Lord did prosper, unto the baptizing and uniting to the church of God many souls; yea, even tens of thousands.
Thus we may see that the Lord is merciful unto all who will, in the sincerity of their hearts, call upon his holy name;
yea, thus we see that the gate of Heaven is open unto all, even to those who will believe on the name of Jesus Christ, which is the Son of God;

links.text: And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.

provenance.other: “the gate of heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 28:17 — Jacob at Bethel: 'How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.' The second half of the Book of Mormon's sentence is a New Testament formula: Acts 8:37, 'I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God', is one of the three third-person renditions of the title Frederick collects.
provenance.significance: Recover Genesis 28:17 and the borrowing is an argument, not a decoration. In the KJV the gate of heaven is a *place* — one stone, one night, one man, and the word that goes with it is 'dreadful'. It is the most local sentence in the Bible. Helaman 3:28 takes the phrase off the place and predicates it of a condition: 'the gate of Heaven is open unto all, even to those who will believe on the name of Jesus Christ'. Jacob found the gate of heaven where he happened to be sleeping and was afraid of it; the Book of Mormon says it stands open, has no location, and admits anyone who believes. Compare Hays on metalepsis: what the echo recovers is precisely what the new sentence denies.

links.note: 'Thus we see that the gate of Heaven is open unto all, even to those who will believe on the name of Jesus Christ, which is the Son of God.' The one KJV verse with the phrase is Jacob's at Bethel, and the sentence fuses it with the New Testament's confession formula, giving the verse an Old Testament image and a New Testament condition of entry. Filed moderate: the phrase is short and the theological commonplace could be reached without Genesis 28, but no other English scripture supplies the words. 1830's relative 'which is the Son of God' becomes 'who' in 1920, the ordinary modernization.
bibliography: Frederick 2016: n. 62 — names Helaman 3:28 in his list of Book of Mormon verses carrying the third-person title 'Jesus Christ, Son of God', alongside Mark 1:1, Acts 8:37 and 2 Corinthians 1:19 as the New Testament's third-person renditions of it. He lists the verse in a footnote about the title's distribution; he proposes no source for it, and says nothing about Genesis 28:17.

pericopes.text: yea, we see that whosoever will lay hold upon the word of God, which is quick and powerful, which shall divide asunder all the cunning, and the snares, and the wiles of the Devil, and lead the man of Christ in a straight and narrow course across that everlasting gulf of misery which is prepared to engulf the wicked,

links.text: For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

provenance.other: “quick and powerful” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “dividing asunder” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and they are the same verse, Hebrews 4:12. The Book of Mormon has the adjectives verbatim and turns the participle into a finite verb: 'which shall divide asunder'. “wiles of the devil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 6:11.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has kept Hebrews' two rare words and changed what the sword cuts. In Hebrews 4:12 the word of God divides asunder soul and spirit, joints and marrow: it cuts the hearer open, and the next clause makes it 'a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart'. In Helaman 3:29 it divides asunder 'all the cunning, and the snares, and the wiles of the Devil' — the blade has been turned outward, from the believer's interior onto an external enemy. The Ephesians singleton arrives in the same clause and brings the armour of God with it, so the verse is Hebrews' sword inside Ephesians' battle. The two KJV passages never meet; this verse marries them.

links.note: 'Whosoever will lay hold upon the word of God, which is quick and powerful, which shall divide asunder all the cunning, and the snares, and the wiles of the Devil.' Two KJV singletons from one verse, plus a third from Ephesians 6:11, in eighteen words. The catalogue has adjudicated Hebrews 4:12 three times before, always for the discerning-of-thoughts clause (Mosiah 5:13, Alma 12:7, Alma 31:5); this is the first place in the corpus that takes 'quick and powerful' and the dividing. 1920 inserts 'may' ('whosoever will may lay hold'), which changes the sense of the Book of Mormon's clause and bears on no source. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six.

links.text: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.

provenance.other: “strait is the gate” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:14, where 'strait' is the adjective meaning narrow and governs the gate. The KJV never joins 'straight' to 'narrow'; the Book of Mormon's pair is its own coinage on a homophone, and the 1830 printing spells it 'straight' here, at 1 Nephi 8:20, and at Jacob 6:11's 'straight gate'.
provenance.significance: This is a place where the 1830 running text is evidence and not merely a text choice (CONVENTIONS §8), and where the direction of later correction is the finding. At Jacob 6:11 the 1830 'enter in at the straight gate' was corrected in 1920 to 'strait gate' — back toward the KJV, because the KJV has a gate there to be corrected against. At Helaman 3:29 the noun is 'course', which is nobody's KJV phrase, so there was nothing to correct and 'straight and narrow' has stood in every edition since. The reader of a modern text therefore meets the Book of Mormon's best-known idiom at exactly the verse where the editors could not restore the source's word, and cannot see that the same page of the first edition spelled Matthew's gate the same way.

links.note: 'And lead the man of Christ in a straight and narrow course across that everlasting gulf of misery.' The pairing of straitness with narrowness in a way that leads to life is Matthew 7:14's, adjudicated in the corpus at 1 Nephi 8:20, 2 Nephi 9:41 and Jacob 6:11; a new book and a new hand, so the row is written out (ADJUDICATING §4). What is proper to this verse is the noun: Matthew's is a way and a gate, the Book of Mormon's here is a 'course' across a gulf, which is a navigational image the KJV does not supply. Filed moderate accordingly — the borrowing is of an idiom the corpus already owns rather than of Matthew's sentence.

pericopes.text: and land their souls, yea, their immortal souls, at the right hand of God, in the kingdom of Heaven, to sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and with Jacob, and with all our holy fathers, to go no more out.

links.text: And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.

provenance.other: “sit down with Abraham” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 8:11, and Helaman 3:30 reproduces seven of its words in order: 'in the kingdom of Heaven, to sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and with Jacob'. mediation-check.py returns five decisive points for Matthew over the Lukan parallel on a four-word backbone: Luke 13:28 has 'see' where Matthew has 'sit down with', and 'the kingdom of God' where Matthew and the Book of Mormon have 'the kingdom of heaven'. “go no more out” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Samuel 21:17 and Revelation 3:12.
provenance.alternative: Luke 13:28-29, whose 'and all the prophets' is the one element Matthew lacks and the Book of Mormon appears to have.
provenance.significance: The mediation test is decisive for Matthew and one detail resists it, which is worth stating rather than smoothing: the Book of Mormon adds 'and with all our holy fathers', and the only synoptic form with a comparable addition is Luke's 'and all the prophets'. The tool counts that against Luke, because the Book of Mormon does not have Luke's words; but it has Luke's element. Either the phrase is the Book of Mormon's own expansion of Matthew's patriarchal list, or Matthew's sentence has been supplemented from its Lukan double. The closing clause is a third source: Revelation 3:12's promise to him that overcometh, 'he shall go no more out', which in Revelation is a pillar fixed in the temple and here is a soul landed at the right hand of God.

links.note: 'And land their souls, yea, their immortal souls, at the right hand of God, in the kingdom of Heaven, to sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and with Jacob, and with all our holy fathers, to go no more out.' A seven-word run from Matthew 8:11 with the kingdom-clause moved in front of it, closed by two words of Revelation 3:12. Catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the run and the singleton behind it, though it is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six. The catalogue reached Matthew 8:11 once before, at Alma 7:25, where the same eschatological table appears in Alma's charge to the people of Gideon; this is a different book and a fuller reproduction.

pericopes.text: And in this year there were continual rejoicing in the land of Zarahemla, and in all the regions round about, even in all the land which was possessed by the Nephites.

And it came to pass that there was peace, and exceeding great joy in the remainder of the forty and ninth year; yea, and also there was continual peace and great joy in the fiftieth year of the reign of the Judges.

And in the fifty and first year of the reign of the Judges, there was peace also, save it were the pride which began to enter into the church; not into the church of God, but into the hearts of the people who professed to belong to the church of God;

and they were lifted up in pride, even to the persecution of many of their brethren. Now this was a great evil, which did cause the more humble part of the people to suffer great persecutions, and to wade through much affliction;

nevertheless, they did fast and pray oft, and did wax stronger and stronger in their humility, and firmer and firmer in the faith of Christ, unto the filling their souls with joy and consolation, yea, even to the purifying and the sanctification of their hearts, which sanctification cometh because of their yielding their hearts unto God.

links.text: Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker.

provenance.other: “stronger and stronger” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Samuel 3:1 and Job 17:9. mediation-check.py reports a DECISIVE point for Job on a two-word backbone, on the ground that the Book of Mormon lacks 2 Samuel's answering clause 'and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker' — an absence-artifact rather than a reading, and it is overruled here by the verb. 2 Samuel 3:1 has 'David waxed stronger and stronger'; Job 17:9 has 'shall be stronger and stronger'. Helaman 3:35 has 'did wax stronger and stronger', which is 2 Samuel's verb.
provenance.alternative: Job 17:9, whose 'he that hath clean hands' sits closer to this verse's purifying and sanctification of hearts.
provenance.significance: 2 Samuel 3:1 is a sentence about a long war in which one house grows strong as another grows weak, and the Book of Mormon has taken it for a passage about persecution inside the church — the humble part of the people growing stronger in their humility while the proud part is 'lifted up in pride, even to the persecution of many of their brethren'. The KJV's antithesis is still doing the work even though the answering clause is not quoted: something is waxing weaker in Helaman 3 while the persecuted wax stronger, and by 3:36 the text names it as the pride that grew upon them from day to day.

links.note: 'They did fast and pray oft, and did wax stronger and stronger in their humility, and firmer and firmer in the faith of Christ.' The formula and its verb are 2 Samuel's, and the Book of Mormon extends it by inventing a matching pair ('firmer and firmer') that the KJV does not have. Filed as an echo: the phrase is a stock intensifier in English by 1830 and no other element of 2 Samuel 3 is in view. Recorded here chiefly for the mediation, which the tool decides one way and the verb decides the other.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the fifty and second year ended in peace also, save it were the exceeding great pride which had got into the hearts of the people; and it was because of their exceeding great riches, and their prosperity in the land; and it did grow upon them from day to day.

And it came to pass, in the fifty and third year of the reign of the Judges, Helaman died, and his eldest son Nephi began to reign in his stead. And it came to pass that he did fill the judgement seat with justice and equity; yea, he did keep the commandments of God, and did walk in the ways of his father.

links.text: And Solomon said unto God, Thou hast shewed great mercy unto David my father, and hast made me to reign in his stead.

provenance.route: 2 Chronicles 1:8 + 2 Chronicles 17:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “to reign in his stead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 1:8 — Solomon's own account of his accession; the KJV's ordinary regnal formula is the past 'reigned in his stead'. “ways of his father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 17:3, of Jehoshaphat. mediation-check.py reports divergences pointing both ways and warns that the verse may be a composite; it is, and both halves are Chronicles'.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's regnal notice fuses two formulas the King James Bible never joins — the accession clause and the evaluation clause — and the catalogue has met the fusion before, at Mosiah 11:1, where Noah 'began to reign in his stead' and 'did not walk in the ways of his father'. That was the apostate form, keyed to 2 Chronicles 21:12, the KJV's one negative father-comparison. Helaman 3:37 is its exact positive: the same two-part formula, the same borrowed clauses, and this time the son does walk in the ways of his father. The Deuteronomistic historian's device for grading kings has been made to grade chief judges, and the two halves of the corpus's use of it now stand as a matched pair a hundred and thirty years apart in the narrative.

links.note: 'Helaman died, and his eldest son Nephi began to reign in his stead. And it came to pass that he did fill the judgement seat with justice and equity; yea, he did keep the commandments of God, and did walk in the ways of his father.' Two KJV singletons in one sentence, from two chapters of 2 Chronicles, in the order Chronicles uses them: accession, then evaluation against the father. The verse also closes the chapter by repeating 3:20 almost word for word about the son — 'fill the judgement seat with justice and equity … walk in the ways of his father' — so the 1 Kings 2:3 charge adjudicated at 3:20 is being transmitted, in the source's own language, from Helaman to Nephi.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass in the fifty and fourth year, there were many dissensions in the church, and there was also a contention among the people, insomuch that there was much bloodshed;
and the rebellious part were slain and driven out of the land, and they did go unto the king of the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that they did endeavor to stir up the Lamanites to war against the Nephites; but behold, the Lamanites were exceeding fraid, insomuch that they would not hearken to the words of those dissenters.

But it came to pass in the fifty and sixth year of the reign of the Judges, there were dissenters which went up from the Nephites unto the Lamanites; and they succeeded with those others in stirring them up to anger against the Nephites; and they were all that year preparing for war.

And in the fifty and seventh year, they did come down against the Nephites to battle, and they did commence the work of death; yea, insomuch, that in the fifty and eighth year of the reign of the Judges, they succeeded in obtaining possession of the land of Zarahemla; yea, and also all the lands, even unto the land which was near the land Bountiful;
and the Nephites, and the armies of Moronihah, were driven even into the land of Bountiful;

and there they did fortify against the Lamanites, from the West Sea, even unto the East; it being a day’s journey for a Nephite, on the line which they had fortified and stationed their armies to defend their north country.

And thus those dissenters of the Nephites, with the help of a numerous army of the Lamanites, had obtained all the possession of the Nephites which was in the land southward. And all this was done in the fifty and eighth and ninth years of the reign of the Judges.

And it came to pass in the sixtieth year of the reign of the Judges, Moronihah did succeed with his armies, in obtaining many parts of the land; yea, they retained many cities which had fallen into the hands of the Lamanites.
And it came to pass in the sixty and first year of the reign of the Judges, they succeeded in retaining even the half of all their possessions.

Now this great loss of the Nephites, and the great slaughter which was among them, would not have happened, had it not been for their wickedness and their abomination which was among them; yea, and it was among those also which professed to belong to the church of God;

and it was because of the pride of their hearts, because of their exceeding riches, yea, it was because of their oppression to the poor, withholding their food from the hungry, withholding their clothing from the naked, and smiting their humble brethren upon the cheek, making a mock of that which was sacred, denying the spirit of prophecy and of revelation, murdering, plundering, lying, steeling, committing adultery, raising up in great contentions, and deserting away into the land of Nephi, among the Lamanites;

provenance.other: “Bread to the hungry” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Isaiah 58:7 and Ezekiel 18:7 and 18:16 — and 'covered the naked' in exactly two, both of them Ezekiel 18. 'Hath oppressed the poor' is a KJV singleton at Ezekiel 18:12. The Book of Mormon's three items ('oppression to the poor, withholding their food from the hungry, withholding their clothing from the naked') reproduce Ezekiel's three in Ezekiel's order. Ezekiel 18:16 also supplies the verb: 'hath not withholden the pledge'.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 18 is the KJV's set-piece on whether a generation inherits its fathers' guilt, and it works by two parallel catalogues — what the just man does (18:5-9) and what his wicked son does (18:10-13) — each item of the second answering an item of the first. Helaman 4:12 is that catalogue run once more in a third form: not a list of deeds but a list of gerunds, and not the wicked son's positive crimes but the just man's virtues negated. Feeding the hungry becomes 'withholding their food from the hungry'; covering the naked becomes 'withholding their clothing from the naked'; not oppressing becomes 'oppression to the poor'. Recover Ezekiel and the point of the chapter comes with it, which is exactly the point Mormon is making at 4:11-13 — that the great slaughter 'would not have happened, had it not been for their wickedness'. Ezekiel 18 is the chapter that insists the soul that sinneth, it shall die, and that a people's disaster is its own doing; Mormon has quietly borrowed the KJV's own argument for national desert.

links.note: 'Their oppression to the poor, withholding their food from the hungry, withholding their clothing from the naked.' Three items, three KJV rarities, one chapter. Ezekiel 18's catalogue of the righteous man is here inverted item by item, and the inversion is the argument: what Mormon lists is not a set of crimes but a set of omissions, which is how Ezekiel 18 defines wickedness in the first place. Isaiah 58:7 is the other home of 'bread to the hungry' and is likely fused in — Isaiah 58 is the fast that God chooses, and the naked there are covered too — but Ezekiel supplies the oppression, the withholding, and the sequence.
links.text: And hath not oppressed any, but hath restored to the debtor his pledge, hath spoiled none by violence, hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment;

provenance.other: “committing adultery” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the longer run “stealing, and committing adultery” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Committing adultery' is a KJV singleton at Hosea 4:2, and so is the longer run 'stealing, and committing adultery'. The 1830 spells it 'steeling'; 1920 normalizes to 'stealing'. Jeremiah 7:9's decalogue-list ('Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery') is the only near competitor and uses finite verbs, not participles.
provenance.significance: Hosea 4:2 is the prophet's indictment of a land in which 'there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God', and its next clause is 'they break out, and blood toucheth blood' — which is the chapter's own subject at 4:1, 'insomuch that there was much bloodshed'. What makes the borrowing pointed is Hosea 4:6: 'my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge'. Mormon's verse is the inventory of a nation whose destruction he has just said was self-inflicted, written in the participial form the KJV uses at exactly one place, and that place explains the bloodshed by the sin-list rather than by the enemy.

links.note: 'Murdering, plundering, lying, steeling, committing adultery.' The KJV has one verse that strings sins together as participles and it is Hosea 4:2, whose own string is 'swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery'. Three of the Book of Mormon's five are Hosea's three in Hosea's order, and 'committing adultery' occurs nowhere else in the KJV. That the list is built out of the KJV's one participial sin-catalogue is a stronger fact about it than any single word.
links.text: By swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery, they break out, and blood toucheth blood.

provenance.other: “Make a mock” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Adjudicated at Jacob 6:8, where the object of the mockery is the plan of redemption; the argument is made there and is not restated.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 14:9's mocker is a fool and his object is sin. Jacob 6:8 redirected the idiom at the remedy; Helaman 4:12 redirects it at 'that which was sacred', which is nearer Proverbs' own register and pairs, four clauses later in this chapter, with Matthew 7:6's 'that which is holy' at 4:22. Read with that link, the two verses divide Matthew's sentence between them: the holy thing mocked here, trampled underfoot there.

links.note: 'Making a mock of that which was sacred.' The phrase is a KJV singleton and the link is written rather than filed as a recurrence because Helaman is a new book in a new hand (ADJUDICATING §4). The argument was made at Jacob 6:8; what is new here is the object, 'that which was sacred', which stands in the same relation to Matthew 7:6's 'that which is holy' as 4:22's trampling does to Matthew's.
links.whyNot: Three words, and 'make a mock of' had independent currency in nineteenth-century English; the phrase could arrive without Proverbs.
links.text: Fools make a mock at sin: but among the righteous there is favour.

provenance.route: Micah 5:1 (with Job 16:10 and 2 Chronicles 18:23) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Upon the cheek” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: 2 Chronicles 18:23 (Zedekiah smites Micaiah), Job 16:10 ('they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully'), Psalm 3:7 ('the cheek bone'), and Micah 5:1. No one of the four can be isolated on wording alone.
provenance.significance: What the four verses have in common is the point. In the KJV nobody is ever struck on the cheek except a prophet, a righteous sufferer, or a judge — Micaiah by the court prophet, Job by his mockers, the judge of Israel by the besieger. The gesture is the KJV's emblem of contempt shown to the person who is in the right. Helaman 4:12 gives it to 'their humble brethren', in a chapter whose every date is counted by 'the reign of the Judges', and Micah 5:1 is the KJV's one verse where a judge is smitten on the cheek. That coincidence is not an argument for Micah as the source; it is what the borrowing does once made. The New Testament's 'whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek' (Matthew 5:39) is a different idiom — 'on', not 'upon' — and is not in view.

links.note: 'And smiting their humble brethren upon the cheek.' Proposed under the generative posture (CONVENTIONS §0a). The prepositional phrase is a four-verse KJV rarity with a consistent sense, and the Book of Mormon uses it in that sense: the humiliation of the righteous by those with power over them. Micah 5:1 is named as source because it is the only one in which the person struck holds an office, which is the office this book dates itself by; the other three are recorded as composite rather than excluded, because the wording does not choose between them.
links.whyNot: Four words and one preposition, spread across four possible sources with no verbal test to separate them. If the borrowing is from Job 16:10 the judge reading disappears entirely, and nothing else in Helaman 4 touches Micah.
links.text: Now gather thyself in troops, O daughter of troops: he hath laid siege against us: they shall smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek.

provenance.other: “The spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. This is its first occurrence in Helaman; the phrase returns eleven verses later at 4:23, where it is paired with 'the spirit of revelation' again.
provenance.significance: Revelation 19:10 defines the phrase as it gives it: 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.' Helaman 4:12 lists 'denying the spirit of prophecy and of revelation' among the sins that lost the land, which — with Revelation's gloss recovered — makes the sin a denial of the testimony of Jesus, not merely of an office. The catalogue this sits in is otherwise Ezekiel's and Hosea's, all of it social and none of it christological; the one New Testament item in the list is the one that names what is being refused.

links.note: A KJV singleton, adjudicated repeatedly from Jacob 1:6 onward and written here because Helaman is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4). Recorded at first use in the book; 4:23's repetition is Mormon reusing his own clause and is registered as a recurrence rather than a second link.
links.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

pericopes.text: and because of this their great wickedness, and their boastings in their own strength, they were left in their own strength; therefore they did not prosper, but were afflicted, and smitten, and driven before the Lamanites, until they had lost possession of almost all their lands.

provenance.other: 'Boastings' — the plural noun — occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The singular 'boasting' is commoner (Romans 3:27, 2 Corinthians 7:14 and others), which is what makes the plural worth counting.
provenance.significance: James 4:16 sits inside the KJV's most sustained attack on self-reliance: 'God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble' (4:6), then the merchant who says he will go into such a city and buy and sell and get gain, who does not know what shall be on the morrow, and whose confidence James answers with 'ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil'. Helaman 4:12-13 has run the same sequence in the same order — pride of heart, exceeding riches, contempt for the humble brethren, and then 'their boastings in their own strength'. The sentence that follows is the KJV's verdict carried out: 'they were left in their own strength'.

links.note: 'And their boastings in their own strength, they were left in their own strength.' One word, but a KJV singleton in the plural, arriving at the end of a paragraph that has already worked through James 4's own sequence of pride, riches and the humble. The epigram Mormon builds around it — boasted in their own strength, therefore left in it — is his own and is in no version of the Bible; what is borrowed is the noun and the frame it comes in.
links.whyNot: A single word, and 'boastings' is ordinary nineteenth-century English requiring no KJV source at all. The James context is suggestive but no clause is shared, and nothing else in the chapter touches the epistle.
links.text: But now ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil.

pericopes.text: But behold, Moronihah did preach many things unto the people, because of their iniquity, and also Nephi and Lehi, which were the sons of Helaman, did preach many things unto the people; yea, and did prophesy many things unto them concerning their iniquities, and what should come unto them if they did not repent of their sins.
And it came to pass that they did repent, and inasmuch as they did repent, they did begin to prosper;

for when Moronihah saw that they did repent, he did venture to lead them forth from place to place, and from city to city, even until they had retained the one half of their property, and the one half of all their lands.
And thus ended the sixty and first year of the reign of the Judges.
And it came to pass in the sixty and second year of the reign of the Judges, that Moronihah could obtain no more possessions over the Lamanites;

therefore they did abandon their design to obtain the remainder of their lands, for so numerous was the Lamanites that it became impossible for the Nephites to obtain more power over them; therefore Moronihah did employ all his armies in maintaining those parts which he had taken.
And it came to pass because of the greatness of the number of the Lamanites, the Nephites were in great fear, lest they should be overpowered, and trodden down, and slain, and destroyed;
yea, they began to remember the prophecies of Alma, and also the words of Mosiah; and they saw that they had been a stiffnecked people, and that they had set at nought the commandments of God;

provenance.other: “set at nought” occurs in exactly five KJV verses and “stiffnecked people” occurs in exactly six KJV verses. 'Set at nought' occurs in five KJV verses: Proverbs 1:25, Mark 9:12, Acts 4:11, Acts 19:27 and Romans 14:10. Only Proverbs has divine instruction as the object; the four New Testament occurrences all have a person or a trade set at nought. 'Stiffnecked people' occurs in six, all of them Exodus 32-34 or Deuteronomy 9. The 1830 spells it 'nought'; 1920 modernizes to 'naught', which moves the word away from the KJV's spelling (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: Proverbs 1:24-31 is the KJV's one passage in which wisdom, having been set at nought, refuses to answer when the disaster arrives: 'Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer.' Helaman 4:21 is the verse in which the Nephites, with the Lamanites in Zarahemla, 'began to remember the prophecies of Alma, and also the words of Mosiah' — remembering, that is, precisely the counsel they had set at nought, at precisely the point in Proverbs' sequence where remembering is too late. The chapter then follows Proverbs' outcome to the letter at 4:25: 'they must unavoidably perish.'
