links.note: 'They had been a stiffnecked people, and that they had set at nought the commandments of God.' Two KJV formulas in one clause, and the second is doing more work than its count suggests: of the five verses containing 'set at nought', only Proverbs 1:25 has instruction from God as what is set at nought, and the Proverbs passage is about the moment of belated remembering that this verse describes. The 'stiffnecked people' half is the Exodus 32/Deuteronomy 9 formula and carries no single source; it is recorded as composite rather than argued.
links.whyNot: Three common words. The phrase is available from any of five KJV verses and from ordinary English, and the argument rests on the fit of Proverbs 1's scenario rather than on the wording.
links.text: But ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof:

pericopes.text: and that they had altered and trampled under their feet the laws of Mosiah, or that which the Lord commanded him to give unto the people; and thus seeing that their laws had become corrupted, and that they had become a wicked people, insomuch that they were wicked even like unto the Lamanites.

provenance.other: “under their feet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “trample” occurs in exactly three KJV verses. 'Under their feet' is a KJV singleton at Matthew 7:6, and 'trample' occurs in only three KJV verses (Psalm 91:13 'under feet', Isaiah 63:3, Matthew 7:6). Helaman 4:22 has both halves of the singleton: 'trampled under their feet'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:6 is about entrusting a holy thing to keepers who will not keep it, and its verbs come in that order: give not that which is holy, lest they trample it under their feet, and turn again and rend you. Helaman 4 distributes the sentence across two verses. At 4:12 the people are 'making a mock of that which was sacred'; at 4:22 they have 'trampled under their feet the laws of Mosiah, or that which the Lord commanded him to give unto the people' — and the relative clause names the giving that Matthew forbids. Then the rending: 'they had become weak … driven before the Lamanites.' What the laws of Mosiah are being called, by the borrowing, is the pearl.

links.note: Four words of a KJV singleton, with the pronoun Matthew has. This is the same phrase adjudicated at 1 Nephi 19:7 and Alma 60:33 and it is written again here because Helaman is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4) and because the object is new: not the words of the prophets and not the laws of God in general, but a named legal code, given by a named lawgiver, at the moment the book stops being able to date itself by that code. Read with 4:12's 'that which was sacred', the two verses hold the two halves of Matthew's sentence.
links.text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.

pericopes.text: And because of their iniquity, the church had began to dwindle; and they began to disbelieve in the spirit of prophecy, and in the spirit of revelation; and the judgements of God did stare them in the face.

And they saw that they had become weak, like unto their brethren, the Lamanites, and that the spirit of the Lord did no more preserve them; yea, it had withdrawn from them, because the spirit of the Lord doth not dwell in unholy temples;

provenance.other: “Dwelleth in you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 8:11 and 1 Corinthians 3:16, and only 1 Corinthians has the temple. 'Unholy' occurs in four KJV verses and never of a building; the adjective is the Book of Mormon's own back-formation from 1 Corinthians 3:17's 'the temple of God is holy'. The n-gram stream ranked 1 Corinthians 3:16 in this verse on 'and that the spirit of'.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a question with a threat under it — 'Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you? If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are.' Helaman 4:24 states the same doctrine as a general maxim and then uses it to explain a military defeat: the Spirit withdrew because the temple was defiled, and 'therefore the Lord did cease to preserve them'. Paul's 'him shall God destroy' is not quoted, but it is what the chapter has spent twenty-three verses describing, and the plural 'temples' converts Paul's congregational image into a statement about individual bodies — which is 1 Corinthians 6:19's move, made with 3:16's vocabulary.

links.note: 'Because the spirit of the Lord doth not dwell in unholy temples.' A maxim built from Paul's question, with the affirmation negated and the adjective inverted: the Spirit dwells in you, the temple of God is holy, therefore the Spirit does not dwell in unholy temples. The KJV never calls a temple unholy; the word exists in it only of persons (1 Timothy 1:9, 2 Timothy 3:2), which is exactly the sense the plural requires here.
links.text: Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?

provenance.other: “Become weak” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 16:17 and Isaiah 14:10. But the proximate model here is not the KJV: Mosiah 1:13 reads 'that thereby they become weak, like unto their brethren; and he will no more preserve them, by his matchless and marvellous power', and Helaman 4:24-25 reads 'they had become weak, like unto their brethren, the Lamanites, and that the spirit of the Lord did no more preserve them … therefore the Lord did cease to preserve them by his miraculous and matchless power'. 'Matchless' occurs in no KJV verse at all; it is Benjamin's word, and its reappearance is what fixes the route.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 14:10 — 'Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us?' — has both 'become weak' and 'become like unto', and is thematically apt for a chapter about pride brought low. It is not preferred, because it cannot account for 'preserve' or for 'matchless'.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's conditional at Mosiah 1:13 was Samson's, transposed to a nation: a people set apart, strong only by a kept condition, one transgression away from being indistinguishable from their brethren, with Judges 16:20's 'he wist not that the LORD was departed from him' behind 'he will no more preserve them'. Helaman 4 is that conditional discharged. What Benjamin said would happen has happened, in his words, and Mormon marks it by keeping the one word in the sentence that belongs to no Bible — 'matchless'. The metalepsis therefore runs through two texts, not one: recover Mosiah 1 and the defeat is the fulfilment of a warning; recover Judges behind Mosiah and the nation is Samson waking to find his strength gone.

links.note: This is the clearest OT-via-earlier-BoM case in the chapter and the mediation field carries the finding. The Samson argument was made at Mosiah 1:13 and is not restated; what is claimed here is that Helaman 4:24-25 quotes Benjamin rather than Judges. Three things establish it: 'become weak, like unto their brethren' reproduces Benjamin's clause including the 'brethren' that stands where Judges has 'any other man'; 'did no more preserve them' reproduces his verb; and 'matchless power', in the very next verse, reproduces a word that occurs nowhere in the KJV. Mormon has taken a hundred-and-thirty-year-old royal warning and used it as the caption for a military collapse.
links.text: That he told her all his heart, and said unto her, There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother’s womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man.

pericopes.text: therefore the Lord did cease to preserve them by his miraculous and matchless power, for they had fallen into a state of unbelief and awful wickedness; and they saw that the Lamanites were more exceeding numerous than they, and except they should cleave unto the Lord their God, they must unavoidably perish.

provenance.other: “cleave unto the LORD” occurs in exactly three KJV verses. 'Cleave unto the LORD' occurs in three KJV verses: Deuteronomy 4:4, Joshua 23:8 and Acts 11:23. The first two add 'your God', which the Book of Mormon has as 'their God'. Joshua 23:8 is the imperative form; Deuteronomy 4:4 is the descriptive.
provenance.significance: Joshua 23 is the farewell speech in which Joshua tells Israel that the nations left in the land are left there deliberately, and that if they do not cleave unto the LORD those nations 'shall be snares and traps unto you … until ye perish from off this good land'. Helaman 4:25 reaches the identical conclusion in the identical order: the Lamanites are more numerous, the Nephites hold half their lands, and 'except they should cleave unto the Lord their God, they must unavoidably perish'. Joshua 23:13's 'until ye perish' is the clause Mormon's 'must unavoidably perish' answers to, and the situation — a remnant of the land held, a stronger population beside them — is Joshua 23's exactly.

links.note: 'And except they should cleave unto the Lord their God, they must unavoidably perish.' Three words, available from three KJV verses, but the conditional they sit in belongs to one of them: Joshua 23 is the KJV's one passage that makes cleaving unto the LORD the condition of not perishing before the nations left in the land. That is the chapter's own military situation, described three verses earlier.
links.whyNot: Deuteronomy 4:4 has the same three words and the same 'your God', and 'cleave unto' is a common enough covenant idiom that the choice between the two rests on context alone.
links.text: But cleave unto the LORD your God, as ye have done unto this day.

pericopes.text: For behold, they saw that the strength of the Lamanites was as great as their strength, even man for man. And thus had they fallen into this great transgression; yea, thus had they become weak, because of their transgression, in the space of not many years.
And it came to pass that in this same year, behold, Nephi delivered up the judgement seat, to a man whose name was Cezoram.

For as their laws and their governments were established by the voice of the people, and they which chose evil were more numerous than they which chose good, therefore they were ripening for destruction, for the laws had become corrupted;

provenance.other: “voice of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Adjudicated at Mosiah 7:9 and again at Mosiah 29:2, where the phrase returns to answer the passage it first translated; written here because Helaman is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4).
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 8:7 is God telling Samuel to hearken unto the voice of the people because it is not Samuel they have rejected but God. Mosiah 29 used the phrase to found the reign of the judges on that voice, with the explicit assurance that it is not common for the voice of the people to desire anything contrary to right. Helaman 5:2 is the sentence in which that assurance fails: 'as their laws and their governments were established by the voice of the people, and they which chose evil were more numerous than they which chose good, therefore they were ripening for destruction.' Recover 1 Samuel and the collapse is not a surprise — the KJV's one verse about the voice of the people is a verse in which that voice is a rejection of God, and Mosiah's constitution was built on it.

links.note: The clause names the Mosiah constitution by the phrase Mosiah 29 founded it on, and it names it in the sentence that pronounces its failure. This is the third stage of a single argument the Book of Mormon conducts across three books: 1 Samuel's warning, Mosiah's qualified adoption, Helaman's verdict. The link is written rather than filed as a recurrence because a reader of Helaman meets the phrase in a new hand and a new book, and because what is new is the arithmetic — the voice of the people is here a majority, counted, and wrong.
links.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

pericopes.text: yea, and this was not all; they were a stiffnecked people, insomuch that they could not be governed by the law nor justice, save it were to their destruction.

And it came to pass that Nephi had become weary, because of their iniquity; and he yielded up the judgement seat, and took it upon him to preach the word of God all the remainder of his days, and his brother Lehi also, all the remainder of his days:
for they remembered the words which their father Helaman spake unto them. And these are the words which he spake:

Behold, my sons, I desire that ye should remember to keep the commandments of God; and I would that ye should declare unto the people these words: Behold, I have given unto you the names of our first parents, which came out of the land of Jerusalem; and this I have done, that when you remember your names, that ye may remember them; and when ye remember them, ye may remember their works; and when ye remember their works, ye may know how that it is said, and also written, that they were good;
therefore, my sons, I would that ye should do that which is good, that it may be said of you, and also written, even as it has been said and written of them.

And now my sons, behold, I have somewhat more to desire of you, which desire is, that ye may not do these things that ye may boast, but that ye may do these things to lay up for yourselves a treasure in Heaven, yea, which is eternal, and which fadeth not away; yea, that ye may have that precious gift of eternal life, which we have reason to suppose hath been given to our fathers.

provenance.other: “lay up for yourselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 6:20, whose object is 'treasures in heaven'. Helaman has the singular, 'a treasure in Heaven'. “fadeth not away” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Peter 1:4 (an inheritance 'reserved in heaven for you') and 1 Peter 5:4 (a crown of glory).
provenance.significance: Matthew 6 is the KJV's one sustained argument that a good work done to be seen loses its reward, and the treasure saying is its conclusion. Helaman 5:8 reproduces the argument's structure before it reproduces its words: 'that ye may not do these things that ye may boast, but that ye may do these things to lay up for yourselves a treasure in Heaven'. That is Matthew 6:1's condition ('do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward') attached to Matthew 6:20's clause. The metalepsis is in what Helaman leaves out: Matthew's reason for the heavenly treasure is that moth and rust corrupt the earthly one, and Helaman replaces it with 1 Peter's incorruptible inheritance — the same doctrine, from the epistle that supplies this chapter's other borrowing at 5:44.

links.note: 'To lay up for yourselves a treasure in Heaven, yea, which is eternal, and which fadeth not away.' A KJV singleton in its exact form, with the number of the noun changed, followed immediately by a two-verse Petrine phrase that supplies the reason Matthew gave differently. Helaman's warning against doing good in order to boast is Matthew 6's own frame, and it arrives four verses before 5:12 puts the chapter's other Sermon-on-the-Mount borrowing to work.
links.text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:

pericopes.text: O remember, remember, my sons, the words which king Benjamin spake unto his people; yea, remember that there is no other way nor means whereby man can be saved, only through the atoning blood of Jesus Christ, which shall come; yea, remember that he cometh to redeem the world.

And remember also, the words which Amulek spake unto Zeezrom, in the city of Ammonihah: for he said unto him, That the Lord surely should come to redeem his people; but that he should not come to redeem them in their sins, but to redeem them from their sins.

And he hath power given unto him from the Father, to redeem them from their sins, because of repentance; therefore he hath sent his angels to declare the tidings of the conditions of repentance, which bringeth unto the power of the Redemer, unto the salvation of their souls.—

And now, my sons, remember, remember that it is upon the rock of our Redeemer, which is Christ, the Son of God, that ye must build your foundation, that when the Devil shall send forth his mighty winds; yea, his shafts in the whirlwind; yea, when all his hail and his mighty storm shall beat upon you, it shall have no power over you, to drag you down to the gulf of misery and endless wo, because of the rock upon which ye are built, which is a sure foundation, a foundation whereon if men buildeth, they cannot fall.

provenance.other: “beat upon” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Jonah 4:8, where the sun beats on Jonah's head, and Matthew 7:25 and 7:27, which are the two halves of the house-on-the-rock parable. Luke's version of the parable (6:48) reads 'the stream beat vehemently upon that house' and has 'laid the foundation on a rock', which is nearer Helaman's 'build your foundation' than Matthew's 'founded upon a rock'; but Luke lacks the winds, and Helaman has them.
provenance.significance: Matthew's parable has four elements in a fixed order — the rock, the building, the storm beating upon the house, the not-falling — and Helaman 5:12 has all four in that order with one substitution: the storm has an author. 'When the Devil shall send forth his mighty winds; yea, his shafts in the whirlwind; yea, when all his hail and his mighty storm shall beat upon you.' Matthew's weather is impersonal and is simply what happens to every house; Helaman's is assault by a named adversary, which converts a parable about hearing and doing into a parable about temptation. What survives the change is Matthew's grammar: the storm still beats upon, and the house still does not fall.

links.note: The chapter's best-known verse and a genuine extended allusion rather than a quotation — no clause of Matthew is reproduced whole. What is reproduced is the parable's sequence and its one rare verb. Helaman also inverts the parable's frame: Matthew builds on the rock of hearing Christ's sayings, Helaman on 'the rock of our Redeemer, which is Christ, the Son of God', which makes the rock a person. The 1830's 'a foundation whereon if men buildeth, they cannot fall' keeps the parable's own consequence clause.
links.text: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.

provenance.other: “sure foundation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Isaiah 28:16 is quoted twice in the New Testament, at Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:6, and mediation-check.py run against 1 Peter 2:6 returns one genuinely decisive point: the Book of Mormon has Isaiah's 'a sure foundation', which neither New Testament form contains — 1 Peter reads 'a chief corner stone, elect, precious'. (The tool reports a second decisive point on 'foundation a stone a tried stone a precious'; that one is an artefact of the single shared word 'foundation' and is not counted here.) Against Romans 9:33 the tool finds no decisive divergence at all, which is expected — Romans is the shorter of the two quotations.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 28:16 is the KJV's foundation-stone verse and the New Testament made it a christological proof text, so a nineteenth-century writer reaching for a rock-and-foundation image had two forms available. Helaman took the Old Testament one. That matters because the phrase he took is precisely the phrase the apostles dropped: 'a sure foundation' is the half of Isaiah's oracle that speaks of the building rather than of the stone's preciousness, and it is the half Helaman's argument needs, since his sentence is about whether a structure will stand. The verse fuses it with Matthew 7's parable, so the Old Testament supplies the foundation and the New Testament the storm.

links.note: Two words, but a KJV singleton, and the mediation test makes the finding: 'a sure foundation' survives in neither apostolic quotation of Isaiah 28:16, so the Book of Mormon has the Old Testament form of a verse it would have been far easier to reach through Romans or 1 Peter. Held at high rather than certain because two words is a slender basis for a route claim; what supports it is that the words are the ones the mediators discarded.
links.text: Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that these were the words which Helaman taught to his sons; yea, he did teach them many things which are not written, and also many things which are written.
And they did remember his words; and therefore they went forth, keeping the commandments of God, to teach the word of God among all the people of Nephi, beginning at the city Bountiful;
and from thence forth to the city of Gid; and from the city of Gid to the city of Mulek;
and even from one city to another, until they had gone forth among all the people of Nephi, which were in the land southward; and from thence into the land of Zarahemla, among the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that they did preach with great power, insomuch that they did confound many of those dissenters which had gone over from the Nephites, insomuch that they came forth and did confess their sins, and were baptized unto repentance, and immediately returned to the Nephites, to endeavor to repair unto them the wrongs which they had done.

And it came to pass that Nephi and Lehi did preach unto the Lamanites with such great power and authority: for they had power and authority given unto them that they might speak; and they also had what they should speak, given unto them;

provenance.other: “what ye shall speak” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 10:19 and Mark 13:11, and only Matthew puts the giving and the speaking in one clause: 'it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak'. Mark separates them ('whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye') and Luke 12:12 replaces speaking with 'what ye ought to say'. mediation-check.py run on Matthew against Mark returns a single decisive point, and it is an absence — the Book of Mormon lacks Mark's 'but the Holy Ghost' — which is weak evidence on its own. The construction is the better discriminator: Helaman 5:18's 'they also had what they should speak, given unto them' is Matthew's clause with the participle moved to the end.
provenance.significance: Matthew 10:19 is spoken to disciples about to be delivered up to councils and scourged in synagogues, and its promise is for what to say when arrested. Helaman 5:18 gives the promise three verses before the arrest: 'they had power and authority given unto them that they might speak; and they also had what they should speak, given unto them' — and at 5:21 Nephi and Lehi are taken by an army and cast into prison. The chapter is running Matthew 10's own sequence, and the borrowed clause is the one that tells the reader what the imprisonment is for.

links.note: 'And they also had what they should speak, given unto them.' Matthew's two-verse phrase with Matthew's participle, in an English that reads oddly precisely because it is holding two KJV elements in one clause. Filed as an allusion rather than a quotation because nothing is reproduced whole; the argument rests on the construction and on the arrest that follows it.
links.text: But when they deliver you up, take no thought how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak.

pericopes.text: therefore they did speak unto the great astonishment of the Lamanites, to the convincing them, insomuch that there were eight thousand of the Lamanites which were in the land of Zarahemla and round about, baptized unto repentance, and were convinced of the wickedness of the traditions of their fathers.
And it came to pass that Nephi and Lehi did proceed from thence to go to the land of Nephi.
And it came to pass that they were taken by an army of the Lamanites, and cast into prison; yea, even in that same prison in which Ammon and his brethren were cast by the servants of Limhi.
And after they had been cast into prison many days without food, behold, they went forth into the prison to take them, that they might slay them.

And it came to pass that Nephi and Lehi were encircled about as if by fire, even insomuch that they durst not lay their hands upon them for fear, lest they should be burned. Nevertheless, Nephi and Lehi were not burned; and they were as standing in the midst of fire, and were not burned.

provenance.other: “in the midst of the fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 3:25, but the Book of Mormon reads 'in the midst of fire' without the article, so the singleton is not claimable as verbal contact and the link is filed as figural. Daniel 3:22 has the flame slaying the men who came near; Daniel 3:27 has bodies the fire had no power over, not a hair singed, no smell of fire.
provenance.significance: Daniel 3 is the KJV's only episode in which men stand unharmed inside fire while the people who came to destroy them are the ones endangered by it, and Helaman 5:23-25 reproduces both halves: Nephi and Lehi are not burned, and the Lamanites 'durst not lay their hands upon them for fear, lest they should be burned'. Daniel's fourth figure in the furnace, 'like the Son of God', has a counterpart at 5:36-39, where the prisoners are seen conversing with beings whose faces are not their own. What the Book of Mormon adds is the direction of the fire: in Daniel it is the king's furnace and God protects men from it, here it is God's fire and it is the executioners who are held off by it.

links.note: No clause is shared and the one candidate singleton fails on an article, so this is written as figural under CONVENTIONS §2 and §0a rather than argued as verbal dependence. What justifies it is that the KJV has exactly one fire that does not burn the righteous, and this chapter builds a whole episode on the premise. The pillar of fire at 5:43 is a separate and older image and is excluded rather than fused in.
links.whyNot: Two ordinary words, and the article that would have made the phrase a singleton is absent. A writer describing a miraculous fire in nineteenth-century English would produce this vocabulary with or without Daniel 3, and no distinctive element of Daniel's story — the furnace, the three names, the fourth man, the unsinged hair — appears in the Book of Mormon text.
links.text: He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God.

pericopes.text: And when they saw that they were encircled about with a pillar of fire, and that it burned them not, their hearts did take courage.
For they saw that the Lamanites durst not lay their hands upon them; neither durst they come near unto them, but stood as if they were struck dumb with amazement.

And it came to pass that Nephi and Lehi did stand forth, and began to speak unto them, saying: Fear not, for behold, it is God that hath shewn unto you this marvellous thing, in the which is shewn unto you, that ye cannot lay your hands on us to slay us.

And behold, when they had said these words, the earth shook exceedingly, and the walls of the prison did shake, as if they were about to tumble to the earth; but behold, they did not fall. And behold, they that were in the prison, were Lamanites, and Nephites which were dissenters.

provenance.other: “foundations of the prison” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Acts 16:26 is the KJV's one prison earthquake: 'suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken'. The Book of Mormon has already used it twice, at Mosiah 7:8 and at Alma 14:27, where the prison walls actually fall; Helaman 5:27 is the one place the walls shake and do not fall — 'as if they were about to tumble to the earth; but behold, they did not fall'.
provenance.significance: Acts 16 supplies the whole shape of Helaman 5:21-44: preachers imprisoned, an earthquake at midnight, the jailers in terror, the question 'what must I do to be saved', and a conversion inside the prison. Helaman answers Acts point by point and changes one thing. In Acts the earthquake opens the doors and looses the bands, and the jailer is converted by finding the prisoners still there; in Helaman the walls are explicitly not opened — the fire 'neither did it take hold upon the walls of the prison' (5:44) — and the deliverance is a cloud, a voice and a light rather than an escape. Recover Acts and the refusal is the point: this prison is not being opened, because the people who need delivering are inside it with the preachers.

links.note: The chapter's structural debt is to Acts 16 and 5:27 is where the wording touches it. Written here rather than carried from Alma 14:27 because Helaman is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4) and because the borrowing is inverted: Alma's prison falls, this one shakes and stands. That difference is the argument, and it runs through to 5:40's 'What shall we do'.
links.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one’s bands were loosed.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they were overshadowed with a cloud of darkness, and an awful, solemn fear came upon them.

And it came to pass that there came a voice, as if it were above the cloud of darkness, saying, Repent ye, repent ye, and seek no more to destroy my servants which I have sent unto you to declare good tidings.

And it came to pass when they heard this voice, and beheld that it was not a voice of thunder; neither was it a voice of a great tumultuous noise; but behold, it was a still voice, of perfect mildness, as if it had been a whisper, and it did pierce even to the very soul.

provenance.other: “still small voice” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reads 'a still voice, of perfect mildness, as if it had been a whisper', dropping 'small' and glossing it twice. At 5:46 the formula returns as 'a pleasant voice, as if it were a whisper', and the n-gram stream matched that verse to 1 Kings 19:13, 'there came a voice unto him' — which is the next verse of the same episode.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 19:11-12 is a sequence and Helaman 5:27-33 runs it backwards. Elijah gets wind, then earthquake, then fire, and the LORD is in none of them; then the still small voice, and that is God. Helaman gives the earthquake first (5:27), then the cloud of darkness, then the voice — and the voice is expressly measured against the alternatives Elijah was given: 'it was not a voice of thunder; neither was it a voice of a great tumultuous noise; but behold, it was a still voice'. The negations are the borrowing. Then Helaman does something 1 Kings does not: the earth shakes again while the mild voice is speaking (5:31), so the two are simultaneous rather than sequential, and the point of Elijah's theophany — that God is not in the earthquake — is quietly denied. The voice is mild and the earth shakes anyway.

links.note: A KJV singleton, glossed rather than quoted, inside a theophany that reproduces 1 Kings 19's own list of what the voice is not. Adjudicated at 1 Nephi 17:45; written again here because Helaman is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4) and because this is the passage that argues with its source. 5:46's second 'as if it were a whisper' is Mormon reusing his own gloss and is registered as a recurrence.
links.text: And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.

pericopes.text: And notwithstanding the mildness of the voice, behold, the earth shook exceedingly, and the walls of the prison trembled again, as if it were about to tumble to the earth; and behold, the cloud of darkness which had overshadowed them, did not disperse.

And behold, the voice came again, saying: Repent ye, repent ye, for the kingdom of Heaven is at hand; and seek no more to destroy my servants. And it came to pass that the earth shook again, and the walls trembled;

provenance.other: “Repent ye: for the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “the kingdom of heaven is at hand” occurs in exactly three: Matthew 3:2 (John the Baptist), 4:17 (Jesus, with the singular 'Repent'), and 10:7 (the twelve, without the imperative). Only Matthew 3:2 has the plural imperative the Book of Mormon has.
provenance.significance: The whole of Matthew 3:2 is eight words and Helaman 5:32 reproduces all of them, which puts it well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and above any reasonable doubt about dependence — the verse simply has no more words to reproduce. What the borrowing carries with it is the speaker: Matthew 3:2 is John the Baptist's whole recorded preaching, delivered in a wilderness to a people going out to be baptized. Here it is a disembodied voice above a cloud of darkness in a prison, and it says it three times. The second half of the voice's sentence — 'and seek no more to destroy my servants' — has no Matthean counterpart and is what the borrowing is for: the forerunner's summons is being addressed to men in the act of attempted murder.

links.note: A verbatim eight-word reproduction of a KJV verse, and the highest-scoring machine candidate in the chapter (rarity 2.86, ten-word run) — one of the rare cases where the n-gram stream ranks the true source first. Note that the same clause is already adjudicated at Alma 9:25 and 10:20; it is written again because Helaman is a new book and because the voice, unlike Alma's preachers, is not quoting a prophet but is itself the speaker.
links.text: And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

pericopes.text: and also again the third time the voice came, and did speak unto them marvellous words, which cannot be uttered by man; and the walls did tremble again, and the earth shook as if it were about to divide asunder.

provenance.route: Romans 8:26 + 2 Corinthians 12:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “cannot be uttered” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:26, of the Spirit's 'groanings which cannot be uttered'. “not lawful for a man to utter” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:4, of what Paul heard in paradise. Helaman 5:33's 'marvellous words, which cannot be uttered by man' has the first phrase and the second phrase's agent.
provenance.significance: The KJV has two things that cannot be uttered and they are opposite. Romans 8:26's are groans without words, uttered by the Spirit because the believer does not know what to pray for; 2 Corinthians 12:4's are words too holy to repeat, heard by a man caught up into paradise. Helaman 5:33 fuses them into a third thing — 'marvellous words, which cannot be uttered by man' — which takes Romans' impossibility and applies it to Paul's content. The result is a definition the KJV does not contain: not inarticulate, and not forbidden, but beyond human articulation. That fusion is also what the chapter needs, because twelve verses later the same men 'could speak forth marvellous words' (5:45), so the unutterable becomes utterable once the Holy Spirit has come down.

links.note: Two KJV singletons, from two epistles, joined in one clause. Neither alone would carry the link — 'cannot be uttered' is four common words and Romans' context is prayer, not theophany — but the pairing is the evidence: the Book of Mormon has the phrase from one verse and the agent from the other, and the two verses are the KJV's only statements about speech that cannot be produced.
links.whyNot: Both phrases are short and idiomatic, and 'which cannot be uttered by man' is available to any nineteenth-century writer describing a revelation. If only Romans 8:26 were in view the sense would be wrong, since Paul's groanings are wordless and Helaman's are words.
links.text: Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lamanites could not flee, because of the cloud of darkness which did overshadow them; yea, and also they were immovable, because of the fear which did come upon them.
Now there was one among them who was a Nephite by birth, who had once belonged to the church of God, but had dissented from them.

And it came to pass that he turned him about, and behold, he saw through the cloud of darkness the faces of Nephi and Lehi; and behold, they did shine exceedingly, even as the face of angels. And he beheld that they did lift their eyes to Heaven; and they were in the attitude as if talking or lifting their voices to some being which they beheld.

provenance.other: “the face of an angel” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Helaman 5:36 has the plural, 'even as the face of angels', because there are two prisoners. Matthew 17:2's transfiguration reads 'his face did shine as the sun' and Exodus 34:29 has Moses' skin shining, but neither has the comparison to an angel.
provenance.significance: Acts 6:15 is Stephen before the council, and it is the last thing said about him before the speech that gets him killed; Acts 7:55-56 completes it — he looks up stedfastly into heaven, sees the heavens opened, and says so, and they stone him. Helaman 5:36 gives a dissenter the same sight from the wrong side of it: he 'saw through the cloud of darkness the faces of Nephi and Lehi; and behold, they did shine exceedingly, even as the face of angels. And he beheld that they did lift their eyes to Heaven.' That is Acts 6:15 and Acts 7:55 in Luke's order, seen by a man standing where the council stood. Twelve verses later the borrowing completes itself at 5:48: 'they saw the heavens open'. What Acts makes the prelude to a lynching, Helaman makes the prelude to a mass conversion — the council's own vision, given to the council, and believed.

links.note: A KJV singleton pluralized, in the middle of a sustained reworking of Acts 6-7. Adjudicated at Mosiah 13:5 (Abinadi before Noah's priests) and written again here because Helaman is a new book and because this occurrence is embedded in the Stephen sequence rather than standing alone: the shining face, the lifted eyes, and the opened heaven arrive in Luke's own order across 5:36-48.
links.text: And all that sat in the council, looking stedfastly on him, saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that this man did cry unto the multitude, that they might turn and look. And behold, there was power given unto them, that they did turn and look; and they did behold the faces of Nephi and Lehi.
And they said unto the man, Behold, what doth all these things mean? and who is it with whom these men do converse?
Now the man’s name was Aminadab. And Aminadab saith unto them, They do converse with the angels of God.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites said unto him, What shall we do, that this cloud of darkness may be removed from overshadowing us?

provenance.other: “what shall we do” occurs in exactly twelve KJV verses and is no evidence on its own; “when they heard this” occurs in exactly three, of which Acts 2:37 is one. The n-gram stream ranked John 6:28 here on a seven-word run, 'unto him, What shall we do, that', which is a closer string match than Acts 2:37. It is the wrong verse: John 6:28's question is 'that we might work the works of God', asked of Jesus by a crowd looking for a sign, and nothing else in Helaman 5 touches John 6. Acts 2:37's 'what shall we do' is followed by 'Repent, and be baptized', which is Aminadab's answer at 5:41; and Acts 2:37's opening, 'Now when they heard this', is reproduced word for word at Helaman 5:48, 'And now when they heard this'.
provenance.significance: Helaman 5:38-48 is a Pentecost. The crowd asks what they must do, is told to repent, cries out, and the Holy Spirit comes down from heaven and fills them with fire so that they speak marvellous words (5:45) — which is Acts 2:2-4 in Acts' order. What the borrowing does is relocate Pentecost inside a jail and give it to the wrong audience: Acts' crowd are devout Jews out of every nation, Helaman's are Lamanite soldiers and Nephite dissenters who came to commit a murder. Acts 2:37's crowd are 'pricked in their heart'; Helaman's are held immovable by fear in a cloud of darkness, which is the same conviction rendered as a physical restraint.

links.note: 'What shall we do, that this cloud of darkness may be removed from overshadowing us?' The question is Acts 2:37's, and the answer at 5:41 is Acts 2:38's — 'You must repent'. Written at 5:40 because that is where the wording starts; the Pentecost frame it opens is carried by the separate link at 5:45. The machine's higher-scoring John 6:28 is excluded (see the register).
links.text: Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men and brethren, what shall we do?

pericopes.text: And Aminadab saith unto them, You must repent, and cry unto the voice, even until ye shall have faith in Christ, which was taught unto you by Alma, and Amulek, and by Zeezrom; and when ye shall do this, the cloud of darkness shall be removed from overshadowing you.
And it came to pass that they all did begin to cry unto the voice of him which had shook the earth; yea, they did cry even until the cloud of darkness was dispersed.

And it came to pass that when they cast their eyes about, and saw that the cloud of darkness was dispersed from overshadowing them, and behold, they saw that they were encircled about, yea, every soul, by a pillar of fire.

And Nephi and Lehi was in the midst of them; yea, they were encircled about; yea, they were as if in the midst of a flaming fire, yet it did harm them not, neither did it take hold upon the walls of the prison; and they were filled with that joy which is unspeakable and full of glory.

provenance.other: “unspeakable and full of glory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reads 'that joy which is unspeakable and full of glory' against Peter's 'ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory' — five words verbatim, with the noun moved in front of a relative clause. This is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is catalogued as a quotation on the rarity, per CONVENTIONS §2.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 1:8's joy belongs to people who have not seen Christ: 'whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.' Helaman 5:44 gives it to men who are at that moment inside a pillar of fire, being ministered to by angels, four verses before they see the heavens open. The borrowing therefore says the opposite of its source about sight, and the preceding verse of Peter says why the phrase was reachable at all: 1 Peter 1:7 is about faith 'tried with fire', which is the literal condition of the men in this verse. The fire that tries the faith and the joy that follows are Peter's two images in sequence, and Helaman has put a man inside the first one.

links.note: Five words of a KJV singleton, reproduced exactly. The chapter has already borrowed from 1 Peter at 5:8 ('fadeth not away'), which makes the epistle a live source here rather than a coincidence, and 1 Peter 1:7's trial by fire stands immediately before the borrowed clause in Peter and immediately around the speaker in Helaman.
links.text: Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory:

pericopes.text: And behold, the Holy Spirit of God did come down from Heaven, and did enter into their hearts, and they were filled as if with fire; and they could speak forth marvellous words.

provenance.other: “cloven tongues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and the Book of Mormon does not have it, which is why this is an extended allusion and not a quotation. What it has is Acts' sequence: a coming down from heaven, a filling, fire, and speech. The n-gram stream matched 'the holy Spirit of God' to Ephesians 4:30, which is the KJV's phrasing ('grieve not the holy Spirit of God') and is probably where the exact wording comes from; the scene is Acts'. The 1830 spells 'marvellous', preserving the KJV orthography that 1920 dropped (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: Acts 2:2-4 has a sound from heaven, fire that sits on each of them, all filled with the Holy Ghost, and speech in other tongues 'as the Spirit gave them utterance'. Helaman 5:45 has the Holy Spirit come down from heaven, enter into their hearts, fill them 'as if with fire', and enable them to 'speak forth marvellous words'. Every element is present and every one is softened by an 'as if', which is this chapter's habit — the fire is as if, the whisper is as if, the walls are as if about to tumble. Acts 2:11 calls what the Pentecost crowd heard 'the wonderful works of God'; Helaman calls it marvellous words, and twelve verses earlier (5:33) the same words were the ones that 'cannot be uttered by man'. The Spirit's arrival is what makes them sayable.

links.note: The completion of the Acts 2 frame opened at 5:40. No phrase of Acts is reproduced — the wording of 'the Holy Spirit of God' is Ephesians 4:30's — but the four events of Pentecost arrive in Pentecost's order in a single sentence, and the chapter's own earlier verses supply the two ends of it: the crowd's 'what shall we do' at 5:40 and the unutterable words at 5:33.
links.whyNot: Entirely structural. A writer describing an outpouring of the Spirit in nineteenth-century English would reach for descent from heaven, fire and inspired speech without needing Acts 2 in front of him, and the one KJV singleton in the neighbourhood, 'cloven tongues', is absent.
links.text: And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there came a voice unto them, yea, a pleasant voice, as if it were a whisper, saying,
Peace, peace be unto you, because of your faith in my well beloved, which was from the foundation of the world.

provenance.other: “peace be unto you” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Luke 24:36, John 20:19, 20:21 and 20:26 — and all four are the risen Christ appearing to disciples, twice with the doors expressly shut. The doubling, 'Peace, peace', is Isaiah 26:3's and Jeremiah 6:14's Hebraism and is not from John. “from the foundation of the world” occurs in six KJV verses; the one that joins it to a beloved son is Revelation 13:8's Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.
provenance.significance: The four KJV 'Peace be unto you' verses are the resurrection appearances, and two of them make a point of the shut doors: Jesus is inside a room the disciples had locked for fear. Helaman 5:47 gives the greeting to men inside a prison whose walls have just been described as standing — 'neither did it take hold upon the walls of the prison' (5:44). The salutation therefore arrives exactly where John puts it, in a sealed room, and the speaker is unseen. Jeremiah 6:14's 'Peace, peace; when there is no peace' is the doubling's other home and is the ironic reading the passage does not take.

links.note: 'Peace, peace be unto you, because of your faith in my well beloved, which was from the foundation of the world.' Held at moderate: the greeting is four words available from four verses, and the doubling comes from elsewhere. What argues for John is the setting — the KJV's peace-greeting is spoken to people shut in a room, and this one is spoken to people shut in a prison — and what fills out the sentence is Revelation 13:8's clause, which supplies the two things the KJV never says of anyone else, that he is the beloved and that he was from the foundation of the world.
links.whyNot: 'Peace be unto you' is a formula available from four KJV verses and from ordinary devotional English, and the second half of the sentence is a different source; nothing in the verse is reproduced at more than four consecutive words.
links.text: Then the same day at evening, being the first day of the week, when the doors were shut where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, came Jesus and stood in the midst, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you.

pericopes.text: And now when they heard this, they cast up their eyes as if to behold from whence the voice came; and behold, they saw the heavens open; and angels came down out of heaven, and ministered unto them.—
And there were about three hundred souls which saw and heard these things; and they were bid to go forth and marvel not, neither should they doubt.

And it came to pass that they did go forth, and did minister unto the people, declaring throughout all the regions round about, all the things which they had heard and seen, insomuch that the more part of the Lamanites were convinced of them, because of the greatness of the evidencess which they had received;
and as many as were convinced, did lay down their weapons of war, and also their hatred, and the tradition of their fathers.
And it came to pass that they did yield up unto the Nephites, the lands of their possession.

And it came to pass that when the sixty and second year of the reign of the Judges had ended, all these things had happened, and the Lamanites had become, the more part of them, a righteous people, insomuch that their righteousness did exceed that of the Nephites, because of their firmness, and their steadiness in the faith.

For behold, there were many of the Nephites which had become hardened, and impenitent, and grossly wicked, insomuch that they did reject the word of God, and all the preaching and prophecying which did come among them.

Nevertheless, the people of the church did have great joy, because of the conversion of the Lamanites; yea, because of the church of God, which had been established among them. And they did fellowship one with another, and did rejoice one with another, and did have great joy.

provenance.other: “fellowship one with another” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Helaman 6:3 turns the noun into a verb — 'they did fellowship one with another' — which is a nineteenth-century usage the KJV does not have.
provenance.significance: 1 John 1:7 makes the fellowship conditional and gives it a ground: 'if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.' Helaman 6:3 is the one verse in the chapter where Nephites and Lamanites are one people, and it stands between 6:2, where the Nephites reject the word, and 6:16, where they begin to grow wicked again — so the fellowship lasts exactly as long as the walking in the light does. The whole chapter is then an argument for 1 John's conditional, run in narrative: 6:34's summary, 'the Nephites did begin to dwindle in unbelief … while the Lamanites began to grow exceedingly in the knowledge of their God', is the fellowship dissolving from one side.

links.note: A KJV singleton verbed. Held at moderate because four words and a change of part of speech is thin, and 'fellowship one with another' had independent currency in nineteenth-century church language — but the KJV has it once, and the chapter's structure follows the condition attached to it there.
links.whyNot: Four words, and the phrase was common enough in Protestant devotional English by 1830 that it need not have come from 1 John at all. Nothing else in Helaman 6 touches the epistle.
links.text: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that many of the Lamanites did come down into the land of Zarahemla, and did declare unto the people of the Nephites the manner of their conversion, and did exhort them to faith and repentance;
yea, and many did preach with exceeding great power and authority, unto the bringing down many of them into the depths of humility, to be the humble followers of God and the Lamb.

provenance.route: Ephesians 5:1 + Revelation 14:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “followers of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:1, 'Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children'. “and to the Lamb” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:4, of the firstfruits 'unto God and to the Lamb' — the same verse whose second sentence is 'these are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth'. Helaman 6:5's 'the humble followers of God and the Lamb' joins the two.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:4 is the only KJV verse that both names following the Lamb and pairs God with the Lamb as a single object, and it is about the hundred and forty-four thousand redeemed from among men. Ephesians 5:1 supplies the phrase 'followers of God' and the reason — 'as dear children'. Fusing them produces a title the KJV does not have and the Book of Mormon uses repeatedly, and the fusion is exact: the noun comes from Paul, the compound object from John. What Helaman adds is 'humble', which is the word the chapter will need again at 6:39, where the Gadianton government tramples 'the poor, and the meek, and humble followers of God'. The title is coined in the verse about conversion and spent in the verse about persecution.

links.note: 'To be the humble followers of God and the Lamb.' Two KJV singletons in five words, from two books, joined into a standing Book of Mormon title. Neither phrase is remarkable alone; that both are singletons and that they are adjacent is the evidence.
links.text: Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children;

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that many of the Lamanites did go into the land northward; and also Nephi and Lehi went into the land northward, to preach unto the people. And thus ended the sixty and third year.
And behold, there was peace in all the land, insomuch that the Nephites did go into whatsoever part of the land they would, whether among the Nephites or the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that the Lamanites did also go whithersoever they would, whether it were among the Lamanites or among the Nephites; and thus they did have free intercourse one with another, for to buy and to sell, and to get gain, according to their desire.

provenance.other: “buy and sell, and get gain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “get gain” alone occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Helaman 6:8 reads 'for to buy and to sell, and to get gain, according to their desire' — James's three verbs in James's order, with the infinitive marker repeated.
provenance.significance: James 4:13 is the merchant's sentence — 'To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain' — and James's answer is that he does not know what shall be on the morrow, 'for what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.' Helaman 6:8 gives the merchant's programme to two nations at peace with each other, and the chapter is the answer: by 6:15 the chief judge is murdered, by 6:17 the search for gain has become secret murder, and by 6:40 they are 'ripening for an everlasting destruction'. Helaman 4:13 had already used the other end of the same passage, James 4:16's 'boastings'. That the book returns to James 4 twice in three chapters — once for the boasting and once for the getting of gain — is a fact about this narrator, and it is the passage that supplies both the sin and the sentence on it.

links.note: A KJV singleton reproduced with its three verbs intact. Filed as a quotation on the rarity rather than the length (CONVENTIONS §2); it is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and the whole source clause is only six words long. Its weight comes from the batch: Helaman 4:13 borrowed 'boastings' from James 4:16, and this verse borrows the merchant's programme from James 4:13, so the two links are two halves of the same paragraph of James used eighty verses apart.
links.text: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they became exceeding rich, both the Lamanites and the Nephites; and they did have an exceeding plenty of gold, and of silver, and of all manner of precious metals, both in the land south, and in the land north.
Now the land south was called Lehi, and the land north was called Mulek, which was after the sons of Zedekiah; for the Lord did bring Mulek into the land north, and Lehi into the land south.

And behold, there was all manner of gold in both these lands, and of silver, and of precious ore of every kind; and there was also curious workmen, which did work all kinds of ore, and did refine it; and thus they did become rich.

They did raise grain in abundance, both in the north and in the south; and they did flourish exceedingly, both in the north and in the south. And they did multiply and wax exceeding strong in the land. And they did raise many flocks and herds, yea, many fatlings.

Behold, their women did toil and spin, and did make all manner of cloth, of fine twined linen, and cloth of every kind, to clothe their nakedness. And thus the sixty and fourth year did pass away in peace.

provenance.other: “toil not, neither do they spin” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Toil' occurs in only four KJV verses in all, and 'spin' in two — Matthew 6:28 and its Lukan parallel at 12:27 — so the pairing of the two verbs is effectively Matthew's alone. Helaman 6:13 has them affirmed: 'their women did toil and spin, and did make all manner of cloth'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 6:28's lilies are the argument against taking thought for raiment: they toil not, neither do they spin, and yet Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of them. Helaman 6:13 is a prosperity notice — the women toil and they spin and they make fine twined linen 'to clothe their nakedness' — and it stands in a passage (6:9-13) that is nothing but the taking of thought Matthew forbids: gold, silver, precious ore, grain in abundance, flocks and herds and fatlings. The inversion is exact and the chapter says what comes of it three verses later: 'the people began to grow exceeding wicked again.' Helaman 5:8 had already used Matthew 6, borrowing 'lay up for yourselves' from 6:20 for a warning against boasting; here the same sermon returns as the description of what the warning did not prevent.

links.note: A KJV singleton negated into its opposite. The two verbs are individually rare in the KJV and occur together in one verse; that Helaman puts them together in a catalogue of accumulated wealth, in a book that has already borrowed from the same chapter of Matthew at 5:8, is the argument. The phrase 'to clothe their nakedness' is the Book of Mormon's own and has no KJV source.
links.whyNot: Toiling and spinning are what women did, and a writer describing cloth-making would reach for both verbs without Matthew. The link rests on the KJV's own rarity for the pair and on the chapter's setting, not on any shared clause.
links.text: And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:

pericopes.text: And in the sixty and fifth year, they did also have great joy and peace; yea, much preaching, and many prophecies concerning that which was to come. And thus passed away the sixty and fifth year.

And it came to pass that in the sixty and sixth year of the reign of the Judges, behold, Cezoram was murdered by an unknown hand, as he sat upon the judgement seat. And it came to pass that in the same year, that his son, which had been appointed by the people in his stead, was also murdered. And thus ended the sixty and sixth year.
And in the commencement of the sixty and seventh year, the people began to grow exceeding wicked again.

For behold, the Lord had blessed them so long with the riches of the world, that they had not been stirred up to anger, to wars, nor to bloodsheds; therefore they began to set their hearts upon their riches; yea, they began to seek to get gain, that they might be lifted up one above another; therefore they began to commit secret murders, and to rob, and to plunder, that they might get gain.—

provenance.other: “set not your heart upon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 62:10: 'Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.' Helaman 6:17 has the prohibition performed: 'they began to set their hearts upon their riches'.
provenance.significance: Psalm 62:10 names three things in one verse — oppression, robbery, and riches increased — and forbids the heart's attachment to the third. Helaman 6:17 supplies all three in the same order and in the affirmative: the Lord had blessed them with the riches of the world, they set their hearts upon their riches, and they began 'to commit secret murders, and to rob, and to plunder, that they might get gain'. The Psalm's 'become not vain in robbery' is the verse's other half and it is the whole subject of the chapter from here to the end. What makes the borrowing pointed rather than decorative is the causal chain Helaman builds out of the Psalm's list: the Psalm merely juxtaposes robbery and riches, and Helaman makes the second produce the first.

links.note: A KJV singleton in the affirmative, in the verse that turns the chapter from prosperity to the Gadianton band. The 1 Timothy 6:9-10 passage ('they that will be rich fall into temptation … the love of money is the root of all evil') is the New Testament's version of the same doctrine and may be fused in, but it supplies no wording; the Psalm supplies the clause and the sequence.
links.text: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.

pericopes.text: And now behold, those murderers and plunderers were a band which had been formed by Kishkumen and Gadianton. And now it had come to pass that there were many, even among the Nephites, of Gadianton’s band. But behold, they were more numerous among the more wicked part of the Lamanites. And they were called Gadianton’s robbers and murderers;
and it was they which did murder the Chief Judge Cezoram, and his son, while in the judgement seat; and behold, they were not found.

And now it came to pass that when the Lamanites found that there were robbers among them, they were exceeding sorrowful; and they did use every means whatsoever was in their power, to destroy them off the face of the earth.

But behold, satan did stir up the hearts of the more parts of the Nephites, insomuch that they did unite with those bands of robbers, and did enter into their covenants, and their oaths, that they would protect and preserve one another, in whatsoever difficult circumstances they should be placed in, that they should not suffer for their murders, and their plunderings, and their stealings.

And it came to pass that they did have their signs, yea, their secret signs, and their secret words; and this that they might distinguish a brother who had entered into the covenant, that whatsoever wickedness his brother should do, he should not be injured by his brother, nor by those who did belong to his band, who had taken this covenant;
and thus they might murder, and plunder, and steal, and commit whoredoms, and all manner of wickedness, contrary to the laws of their country, and also the laws of their God;

and whosoever of those which belonged to their band, should reveal unto the world of their wickedness and their abominations, should be tried, not according to the laws of their country, but according to the laws of their wickedness, which had been given by Gadianton and Kishkumen.
Now behold, it is these secret oaths and covenants, which Alma commanded his son should not go forth unto the world, lest they should be a means of bringing down the people unto destruction.

Now behold, those secret oaths and covenants did not come forth unto Gadianton from the records which were delivered unto Helaman; but behold, they were put into the heart of Gadianton, by that same being who did entice our first parents to partake of the forbidden fruit;

provenance.route: Genesis 3:1-6 → Book of Mormon (by reference, not by wording)
provenance.other: No wording is shared. 'Forbidden fruit' is not a KJV phrase — Genesis 3 has 'the tree which is in the midst of the garden' — and 'entice' occurs in Genesis 3 not at all. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 3:1-5 at this verse; the reference is right and it is a reference to an episode, not to a form of words. Revelation 12:9 is the KJV verse that identifies the serpent with the Devil, which is the identification Helaman 6:26 presupposes.
provenance.significance: Helaman 6:26-29 is a genealogy of one agent through four episodes — Eden, Cain, Babel, Gadianton — held together by the repeated formula 'that same being'. Genesis 3 is the first term and the only one the Book of Mormon does not name outright; it says 'our first parents' and 'the forbidden fruit' rather than Adam, Eve or the serpent, which is what makes the reference allusive rather than expository. The point of putting Eden at the head of the list is what the list is for: secret oaths. The chapter's claim is that a conspiracy of silence is the oldest of temptations, and that its first instance was a promise about knowledge — 'God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened' — which is the same structure as Gadianton's secret words at 6:22.

links.note: Hardy cross-references Genesis 3:1-5 here and this catalogue agrees with him about the passage while disagreeing about its type: there is no verbal contact whatever, so the row is discharged as a figural link rather than an allusion (CONVENTIONS §6a, third bullet). What is borrowed is an episode and an identification — that the tempter of Eden and the tempter of Gadianton are one being — and the identification itself is Revelation 12:9's, not Genesis's.
links.whyNot: Not one word is shared with Genesis 3. If the verse's phrase 'that same being who did entice our first parents to partake of the forbidden fruit' were removed, nothing in the chapter would point to Eden at all; the link exists because the verse makes the reference, not because the text carries it.
links.text: Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?

provenance.other: “put into the heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 13:2: 'the devil having now put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him'. The KJV's other formulas are 'put in my heart' (Nehemiah 2:12, 7:5, of God) and 'put in their hearts' (Revelation 17:17, also of God). Helaman 6:26 has 'they were put into the heart of Gadianton, by that same being', and the formula then repeats at 6:28 ('who put it into the hearts of the people') and 6:29 ('who put it into the heart of Gadianton'), three times in four verses. The n-gram stream ranked John 13:2 at 6:26.
provenance.significance: John 13:2 is the KJV's one sentence in which the devil puts something into a man's heart, and what he puts there is a betrayal to be carried out in secret by a member of the inner group. Helaman 6:26 uses the construction to explain the origin of the Gadianton oaths, and 6:22 has already described what those oaths are for: secret signs and secret words by which a brother knows a brother, so that 'whatsoever wickedness his brother should do, he should not be injured by his brother'. That is a covenant of mutual non-betrayal, founded — the verse says — by the agency that produced the KJV's one act of betrayal. The metalepsis runs the other way too: Judas is the brother who did tell.

links.note: A KJV singleton, used three times in four verses, and used each time to name the agency behind a conspiracy. The formula is what holds 6:26-29 together, and it is the only phrase in that passage with a demonstrable KJV source — the Eden, Cain and Babel references around it are episodic, not verbal. Filed at 6:26 as the first occurrence; 6:28 and 6:29 are registered as recurrences.
links.text: And supper being ended, the devil having now put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him;

pericopes.text: yea, that same being who did plot with Cain, that if he would murder his brother Abel, it should not be known unto the world. And he did plot with Cain and his followers, from that time forth.

provenance.other: “of that wicked one” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “slew his brother” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse, 1 John 3:12. Genesis 4:8 narrates the murder — 'Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him' — and says nothing about who prompted it. 1 John 3:12 is the KJV's one verse that assigns it an author: 'Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother.' Helaman 6:27's claim, 'that same being who did plot with Cain, that if he would murder his brother Abel, it should not be known unto the world', is 1 John's, not Genesis's; the Book of Mormon keeps Genesis's 'his brother' and takes the wicked one from the epistle.
provenance.significance: 1 John 3:12 sits inside an argument about brotherhood — 'we should love one another. Not as Cain' — and the Gadianton covenant at Helaman 6:22 is a parody of exactly that: a band whose members call each other brother and whose oath is that a brother shall not be injured by a brother. Helaman 6:27 adds to 1 John one element the KJV does not have anywhere: secrecy. Cain's murder is to be a thing 'not known unto the world', which turns the first fratricide into the first secret combination and makes the chapter's whole thesis genealogical. John 8:44's 'he was a murderer from the beginning' stands behind 6:29's 'he hath brought it forth from the beginning of man'.

links.note: The verse makes a claim about Cain that Genesis does not make and that one KJV verse does. The wording contact is short — 'his brother', the wicked one as agent — but the proposition is 1 John 3:12's proposition, and the chapter's formula 'that same being' is doing the work of John's 'that wicked one'.
links.text: Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.

pericopes.text: And also it is that same being who put it into the hearts of the people, to build a tower sufficiently high that they might get to Heaven. And it was that same being which led on the people which came from that tower, into this land; which spread the works of darkness and abominations over all the face of the land, until he dragged the people down to an entire destruction, and to an everlasting hell;

provenance.other: Genesis 11:4 reads 'let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven'; Helaman 6:28 reads 'to build a tower sufficiently high that they might get to Heaven'. The shared words are 'build', 'tower' and 'heaven' — the irreducible minimum for naming the episode at all — so the paraphrase is deliberate and no version-specific wording is in view. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 11:4 at this verse. Genesis 11:8-9's scattering abroad 'upon the face of all the earth' stands behind 'led on the people which came from that tower, into this land'.
provenance.significance: Genesis 11 gives the tower no author but the builders themselves, and no motive but a name and a fear of being scattered. Helaman 6:28 supplies an author — 'that same being' — and thereby folds Babel into the chapter's genealogy of secret works, between Cain and Gadianton. The consequence Helaman draws is the one Genesis leaves implicit: the scattering that Genesis records as punishment becomes, here, the means of transmission, since the being who prompted the tower 'led on the people which came from that tower, into this land'. Babel is how the conspiracy crossed the ocean. That is also the Book of Mormon's own account of the Jaredites, so the verse is at once a biblical allusion and an internal cross-reference.

links.note: A paraphrase, not a quotation: the Book of Mormon reproduces the episode and drops Genesis's phrasing entirely, which is why kjvSpecific is 'uncertain' — 'build a tower … get to Heaven' would read the same in any English Bible. Hardy cross-references Genesis 11:4 here and the reference is exact.
links.text: And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.

pericopes.text: yea, it is that same being who put it into the heart of Gadianton, to still carry on the work of darkness, and of secret murder; and he hath brought it forth from the beginning of man, even down to this time.

provenance.other: “works of darkness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 13:12 ('cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light') and Ephesians 5:11 ('have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them'). The phrase runs three times through this passage — 6:28 'the works of darkness and abominations', 6:29 'the work of darkness, and of secret murder', 6:30 'his works of darkness and secret murder' — and each time it is paired with secrecy.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:11's clause is the more apt of the two, since it commands that the works of darkness be reproved and brought to light, and the whole Gadianton apparatus exists to prevent exactly that — 6:24 makes revealing the band's wickedness 'unto the world' a capital offence under 'the laws of their wickedness'. Romans 13:12 supplies the antithesis Helaman does not state: darkness cast off and armour of light put on, at a night far spent. Neither verse can be isolated on the wording, which is why this is filed as an echo; what is worth recording is that the KJV's two-verse phrase becomes this passage's refrain, and that both KJV verses attach the phrase to concealment rather than to sin in general.

links.note: Two words with a two-verse KJV home, repeated three times in three verses. Not enough to name a source with confidence, and enough to say that the passage's governing phrase is a KJV phrase used in the KJV's own sense.
links.whyNot: 'Works of darkness' is available from either of two verses and had wide currency in nineteenth-century preaching; neither Romans 13 nor Ephesians 5 shares anything else with the chapter.
links.text: The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light.

pericopes.text: And behold, it is he which is the author of all sin. And behold, he doth carry on his works of darkness and secret murder, and doth hand down their plots, and their oaths, and their covenants, and their plans of awful wickedness, from generation to generation, according as he can get hold upon the hearts of the children of men.

And now behold, he had got great hold upon the hearts of the Nephites; yea, insomuch that they had become exceeding wicked; yea, the more part of them had turned out of the way of righteousness, and did trample under their feet the commandments of God, and did turn unto their own ways, and did build up unto themselves idols of their gold and their silver.

provenance.other: “turn from the holy commandment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 2:21, whose first clause is 'it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness'. “the way of righteousness” occurs in five KJV verses and is not decisive alone; the n-gram stream ranked Matthew 21:32 here on it. What settles the source is the sequence: 2 Peter 2:21 has the way of righteousness known and then the commandment turned from, and Helaman 6:31 has 'turned out of the way of righteousness, and did trample under their feet the commandments of God'. “to his own way” is a KJV singleton at Isaiah 53:6, behind 'did turn unto their own ways'.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 2:22 completes the sentence with the KJV's two proverbs of relapse — the dog returned to his own vomit and the sow to her wallowing in the mire — which are the same two animals as Matthew 7:6's dogs and swine, and Matthew 7:6 is the verse this chapter borrows twice, at 6:31 and at 6:39. So the two New Testament passages standing behind Helaman 6:31 share their bestiary, and both are about holy things given to those who will not keep them. What Helaman adds is the golden calf: 'did build up unto themselves idols of their gold and their silver' recalls Exodus 32:8, where Israel 'turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them: they have made them a molten calf' — the same two motions, out of the way and into an idol, in the same order. Helaman 4:21 had already taken 'stiffnecked people' from the next verse of Exodus 32.

links.note: 'Turned out of the way of righteousness … and did turn unto their own ways, and did build up unto themselves idols of their gold and their silver.' A KJV singleton ('turn from the holy commandment') recast as 'trample under their feet the commandments of God', in 2 Peter's own order, with Isaiah 53:6's singleton supplying the middle clause and Exodus 32:8 the shape of the whole. The trampling itself belongs to Matthew 7:6 and is adjudicated at 6:39, where both halves of that verse appear together.
links.text: For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that all these iniquities did come unto them, in the space of not many years, insomuch that a more part of it had come unto them in the sixty and seventh year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.
And they did grow in their iniquities, in the sixty and eighth year also, to the great sorrow and lamentation of the righteous.

And thus we see that the Nephites did begin to dwindle in unbelief, and grow in wickedness and abominations, while the Lamanites began to grow exceedingly in the knowledge of their God; yea, they did begin to keep his statutes and commandments, and to walk in truth and uprightness before him.
And thus we see that the spirit of the Lord began to withdraw from the Nephites, because of the wickedness and the hardness of their hearts.

provenance.other: “hardness of their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5; Matthew 19:8 has 'hardness of your hearts' and Mark 16:14 'hardness of heart'. The Book of Mormon uses each in its correct grammatical setting throughout, and Helaman 6:35 — a narrator's third-person report — takes the third-person form. The n-gram stream ranked Mark 3:5 first in this verse.
provenance.significance: Mark 3:5 is Jesus in the synagogue looking round on the Pharisees 'with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts', immediately before the healing that makes them plot to destroy him. The grief is the point: the KJV's one use of this exact phrase attaches it to a divine reaction, not to a human condition.
