Helaman 6:35 does the same — 'the spirit of the Lord began to withdraw from the Nephites, because of the wickedness and the hardness of their hearts' — and the withdrawal is the narrator's version of Mark's grief. The verse also completes an arc begun at Helaman 4:24, where the Spirit withdrew for the first time in this book; there the reason was an unholy temple, here it is a hard heart, and 6:36 answers both by pouring the same Spirit out on the Lamanites.

links.note: A KJV singleton with the pronoun the setting requires (ADJUDICATING §4). Adjudicated many times from 1 Nephi 2:18 onward and written here because Helaman is a new book and because this occurrence is one half of a matched pair with 6:36 — the Spirit withdrawn from one people in Mark's words and poured out on the other in Joel's, in consecutive verses.
links.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

pericopes.text: And thus we see that the Lord began to pour out his spirit upon the Lamanites, because of their easiness and willingness to believe in his word.

provenance.other: “pour out my spirit upon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joel 2:28. Acts 2:17 quotes the same oracle with a partitive — 'I will pour out OF my Spirit upon all flesh' — and Helaman 6:36 has no partitive: 'the Lord began to pour out his spirit upon the Lamanites'. tools/mediation-check.py run on Joel 2:28 against Acts 2:17 reports no decisive divergence, exactly as it did at Mosiah 25:24 and Alma 16:16, because the divergence is a single common word and the tool suppresses those by design (ADJUDICATING §4). The argument was made in full at Mosiah 25:24 and is not repeated here.
provenance.significance: What makes this occurrence worth a row of its own is the chapter before it. Helaman 5:40-48 is a Pentecost — the crowd's 'what shall we do', the answer 'repent', the Spirit coming down from heaven, fire, and marvellous words — built on Acts 2. Acts 2:16-18 is Peter identifying that event as Joel's oracle, in the partitive form. So when Helaman 6:36 reports the outcome of the prison Pentecost, the natural quotation is Peter's, and the text gives Joel's instead: the same oracle, in the Old Testament's own words, with the whole Spirit rather than a portion of it. The two chapters therefore take opposite routes to one prophecy, and the mediation is the finding.

links.note: Joel's clause in the third person and without Peter's partitive, which is what settles the mediation as direct-OT. Paired with 6:35's Mark 3:5 in consecutive verses: withdrawn from the Nephites in the Gospel's words, poured out on the Lamanites in the prophet's.
links.text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lamanites did hunt the band of robbers of Gadianton; and they did preach the word of God among the more wicked part of them, insomuch that this band of robbers was utterly destroyed from among the Lamanites.

And it came to pass on the other hand, that the Nephites did build them up and support them, beginning at the more wicked part of them, until they had overspread all the land of the Nephites, and had seduced the more part of the righteous, until they had come down to believe in their works, and partake of their spoils, and to join with them in their secret murders and combinations.

And thus they did obtain the sole management of the government, insomuch that they did trample under their feet, and smite, and rend, and turn their backs upon the poor, and the meek, and humble followers of God.

provenance.other: “under their feet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “turn again and rend” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse, Matthew 7:6: 'lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you'. Helaman 6:39 has both halves in one sentence: 'they did trample under their feet, and smite, and rend, and turn their backs upon the poor, and the meek, and humble followers of God.'
provenance.significance: This is the fullest use of Matthew 7:6 in the Book of Mormon and the only one that reproduces both of its verbs. Matthew's sentence is about giving a holy thing into the keeping of animals that will destroy it and then turn on the giver; its subject is the swine, and its object in the second clause is you. Helaman 6:39 collapses the two clauses onto a single object — the poor and the meek are both what is trampled and what is rent — which converts a warning about misplaced trust into a description of class violence. The verse's own governing word makes the substitution explicit: what is trampled is 'humble followers of God and the Lamb', the title coined at 6:5 out of Ephesians 5:1 and Revelation 14:4. So the holy thing in this version of Matthew 7:6 is a group of people. Helaman 4:22 had trampled the laws of Mosiah and Helaman 6:31 the commandments of God; by 6:39 the object is human.

links.note: Both halves of a verse each of whose halves is a KJV singleton, in one sentence, with Matthew's own sequence. This is the third and last use of Matthew 7:6 in this batch of chapters — 4:22 (the laws), 6:31 (the commandments), 6:39 (the poor) — and the progression from text to person is the argument. Written as a link rather than a recurrence because the second half of Matthew's verse appears here and nowhere else in the book.
links.text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.

pericopes.text: And thus we see that they were in an awful state, and ripening for an everlasting destruction.
And it came to pass that thus ended the sixty and eighth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.

Behold, now it came to pass in the sixty and ninth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of the Nephites, that Nephi, the son of Helaman, returned to the land of Zarahemla, from the land northward:
for he had been forth among the people which was in the land northward, and did preach the word of God unto them, and did prophesy many things unto them;
and they did reject all his words, insomuch that he could not stay among them, but returned again unto the land of his nativity;

links.text: And Haran died before his father Terah in the land of his nativity, in Ur of the Chaldees.

provenance.other: “land of his nativity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The plural and second-person forms are elsewhere — Ruth 2:11, Jeremiah 46:16, Ezekiel 23:15 — but the third-person masculine singular is Genesis 11:28's alone.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one ‘land of his nativity’ is a death-notice: Haran dies at home, in Ur, before the family leaves it, and his death is the last thing recorded before Terah takes Abram out. Nephi comes back to the land of his nativity because the land northward would not have him, and the chapter that follows is a lament that he was born into the wrong days (7:7–9). The one verse the phrase comes from says that the land of your nativity is where you die if you stay.

links.note: ‘Returned again unto the land of his nativity.’ A four-word run on a KJV singleton, and the only KJV occurrence of the phrase in this exact form is Genesis 11:28. The narrative shape is inverted — Genesis has a man who never leaves Ur, Helaman a man who leaves, is rejected, and comes back — which is why this is catalogued as an allusion rather than a quotation, and why the confidence is moderate: a writer could reach ‘land of his nativity’ from the KJV's stock of nativity phrases without having Haran in mind. What makes it worth recording is that the phrase sits at the head of a chapter about a prophet who wishes he had lived in his ancestor's generation instead of his own.

pericopes.text: and seeing the people in a state of such awful wickedness, and those Gadianton robbers filling the judgement seats; having usurped the power and authority of the land; laying aside the commandments of God, and not in the least aright before him; doing no justice unto the children of men;

links.text: And they watched him, and sent forth spies, which should feign themselves just men, that they might take hold of his words, that so they might deliver him unto the power and authority of the governor.

provenance.other: “power and authority” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 9:1 and Luke 20:20, both Luke's. Luke 9:1 gives the phrase to the twelve over devils; Luke 20:20 gives it to a Roman governor. Helaman's is the political sense.
provenance.significance: Recover Luke 20:20 and the borrowed phrase turns out to name what the Gadianton judges are about to do rather than what they have already done. Luke's ‘power and authority of the governor’ is the destination of a plot: spies feign themselves just men and try to take hold of a preacher's words so as to deliver him to it. Two chapters later that is exactly the scene — judges questioning Nephi ‘in divers ways, that they might cross him, that they might accuse him to death’ (9:19). The narrator uses the phrase at 7:4 to describe the office; the plot supplies the rest of Luke's verse at 9:19.

links.note: ‘Those Gadianton robbers filling the judgement seats; having usurped the power and authority of the land.’ Six consecutive words of Luke 20:20, and the collocation is confined to Luke in the KJV. The n-gram stream ranked this first in the verse and was right for once. The substitution is ‘of the land’ for ‘of the governor’, which is the one change a text with no Roman governor has to make; everything else stands. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: condemning the righteous because of their righteousness; letting the guilty and the wicked go unpunished, bacause of their money; and moreover, to be held in office at the head of government, to rule and do according to their wills, that they might get gain and glory of the world; and moreover that they might the more easy commit adultery, and steal, and kill, and do according to their own wills.

Now this great iniquity had come upon the Nephites, in the space of not many years; and when Nephi saw it, his heart was swollen with sorrow within his breast; and he did exclaim in the agony of his soul,

O that I could have had my days, in the days when my father Nephi first came out of the land of Jerusalem, that I could have joyed with him in the promised land; then were his people easy to be entreated, firm to keep the commandments of God, and slow to be led to do iniquity; and they were quick to hearken unto the words of the Lord;
yea, if my days could have been in them days, then would my soul have had joy in the righteousness of my brethren.
But behold, I am consigned that these are my days, and that my soul shall be filled with sorrow, because of this the wickedness of my brethren.

And behold, now it came to pass that it was upon a tower, which was in the garden of Nephi, which was by the highway which led to the chief market, which was in the city of Zarahemla; therefore, Nephi had bowed himself upon the tower which was in his garden, which tower was also near unto the garden gate which led by the highway.

links.text: I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved.

provenance.other: “upon the tower” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Towers are common in the KJV; a prophet on one is not.
provenance.significance: The tower is the whole of Habakkuk's second chapter opening, and Habakkuk's first chapter is the complaint Nephi has just made. Habakkuk 1:4 — ‘the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth’ — is Helaman 7:4–5 in summary: judges laying aside the commandments, doing no justice, condemning the righteous and letting the wicked go unpunished. Habakkuk 1:13 asks why God holds his tongue ‘when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he’, and Helaman 7:24 tells the Nephites the Lamanites are more righteous than they. Then Habakkuk climbs the tower to wait for an answer, and gets one: write the vision, it will surely come. So Nephi's garden tower is the KJV's one prophetic tower, and what he receives on it — the vision of the murdered chief judge, announced in chapter 8 and verified in chapter 9 — is Habakkuk's answer in Nephite form. Neither text says this; the placement does.

links.note: ‘It was upon a tower, which was in the garden of Nephi … Nephi had bowed himself upon the tower which was in his garden.’ The verse is unusually insistent about the tower, naming it three times in one sentence, and ‘upon the tower’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse: Habakkuk 2:1, where a prophet sets himself on one to wait for an answer to a complaint about corrupt judgment. Confidence is held at moderate because the verbal contact is three words and the tower has an obvious narrative job to do — Nephi has to be visible to passers-by for 7:11 to work. But the surrounding chapter reads Habakkuk 1 point for point, and the machine ranked Habakkuk 2:1 in the verse below without seeing why.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there was certain men passing by, and saw Nephi as he was pouring out his soul unto God upon the tower, and they ran and told the people what they had seen; and the people came together in multitudes that they might know the cause of so great mourning for the wickedness of the people.

links.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

provenance.alternative: Psalm 42:4's ‘I pour out my soul in me’ is the other candidate and is also a KJV singleton in that form; but its preposition is ‘in’, and Helaman has ‘unto’ at both 7:11 and 7:14. Hannah's ‘poured out my soul before the LORD’ (1 Samuel 1:15) has a third preposition.
provenance.other: “poured out his soul unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The tell is the preposition: three different KJV verses pour out a soul, and only Isaiah 53:12 does it ‘unto’ something.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 53:12 pours out a soul unto death, and it is the Servant's, poured out in intercession for transgressors. Helaman redirects the preposition's object to God — ‘pouring out his soul unto God upon the tower’ — while keeping the construction. What the borrowing does is make Nephi's grief intercessory rather than merely private: he is not mourning his own days but bearing the wickedness of his brethren, which is what 7:9 says outright and what the Servant song says of its subject. The metalepsis is exact and almost certainly unintended by any reader who does not check the preposition.

links.note: ‘As he was pouring out his soul unto God upon the tower.’ The n-gram stream proposed Isaiah 53:12 on a four-word run and the run is the argument: ‘poured out his soul unto’ occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Helaman uses the construction twice in four verses (7:11, 7:14). Moderate rather than high because ‘pour out the soul’ is a KJV idiom with three attested prepositions and a writer steeped in the Psalter could reach it without Isaiah 53; but the one that got used is the Servant's.

pericopes.text: And now when Nephi arose he beheld the multitudes of people which had gathered together.
And it came to pass that he opened his mouth and said unto them, Behold, why have ye gathered yourselves together? That I may tell you of your iniquities?

links.text: And Jacob called unto his sons, and said, Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which shall befall you in the last days.

provenance.other: “that I may tell you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. ‘Gather yourselves together’ on its own is in five, two of them Genesis 49:1–2; the seven-word run ‘yourselves together that I may tell you’ is Genesis 49:1's alone.
provenance.significance: Genesis 49:1 is the last thing a patriarch says before he blesses his twelve sons and dies: gather, and I will tell you what shall befall you in the last days. Helaman 7:13 turns the sentence into a question and swaps its object — not what shall befall you, but your iniquities — and the swap is the point. Nephi has just spent six verses wishing he had lived in his father Nephi's generation (7:7–9); he then addresses a crowd in the formula of the patriarch whose gathered sons became the tribes. The blessing form arrives with its content replaced by an indictment. Chapters 8 and 9 then supply the missing half: he does tell them what shall befall them, and it befalls.

links.note: ‘Behold, why have ye gathered yourselves together? That I may tell you of your iniquities?’ A seven-word run on the KJV's one occurrence of ‘that I may tell you’, and the highest-scoring machine candidate in the chapter. Two things make it a link rather than a coincidence of common words: the run crosses a clause boundary intact, and the Book of Mormon reproduces Genesis's sequence (gather → that I may tell you → what is coming) in order. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: Yea, because I have got upon my tower, that I might pour out my soul unto my God, because of the exceeding sorrow of my heart, which is because of your iniquities?

And because of my mourning and lamentation, ye have gathered yourselves together, and do marvel; yea, and ye have great need to marvel; yea, ye had ought to marvel, because ye are given away, that the Devil hath got so great hold upon your hearts;
yea, how could ye have given away to the enticing of him who art seeking to hurl away your souls down to everlasting misery and endless wo?
O repent ye, repent ye! why will ye die? Turn ye, turn ye, unto the Lord your God. Why hath he forsaken you?

links.text: Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?

provenance.other: “turn ye turn ye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. ‘Why will ye die’ is in three — Jeremiah 27:13, Ezekiel 18:31 and Ezekiel 33:11 — and only Ezekiel 33:11 has both.
provenance.alternative: The destination clause, ‘unto the Lord your God’, is not Ezekiel's; Ezekiel turns people from their evil ways. It is Joel 2:13's ‘turn unto the LORD your God’, which is the KJV's standing formula for the positive direction of repentance.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 33 is the watchman chapter: the prophet set over the house of Israel who must warn or bear the blood himself. Helaman 7 has just put its prophet on a tower (7:10, and see the Habakkuk 2:1 link there), and 7:29 has him insist the warning is not of himself. So the doubled imperative arrives from the one KJV chapter where the whole question is a watchman's liability for an unwarned city — and chapter 8 opens with the city trying to seize him for giving the warning.

links.note: ‘O repent ye, repent ye! why will ye die? Turn ye, turn ye, unto the Lord your God.’ Two of Ezekiel 33:11's clauses in Ezekiel's order, one of them a KJV singleton. Catalogued as a quotation on the strength of ‘turn ye, turn ye … why will ye die’, which is reproduced as a unit and belongs to one verse; the Book of Mormon substitutes Joel 2:13's destination for Ezekiel's point of departure and prefixes a doubled ‘repent ye’ of its own, so the confidence is high rather than certain. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; this is not one of his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: It is because you have hardened your hearts; yea, ye will not hearken unto the voice of the good shepherd; yea, ye have provoked him to anger against you.

links.text: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.

provenance.other: “good shepherd” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 10:11 and John 10:14, and nowhere in the Old Testament. The adjective is John's.
provenance.significance: Read with the Ezekiel 34:5 link at the next verse, this pair reproduces John 10's own dependence on Ezekiel 34 and keeps the two halves in their biblical order. John 10 is the New Testament's rewriting of Ezekiel's shepherd oracle — the hireling who flees, the sheep scattered, the shepherd who gathers — and Helaman 7:18–19 takes John's adjective for the shepherd and Ezekiel's fate for the flock, in two consecutive sentences. Refusing to hear the shepherd's voice is John 10:3–5 and 10:16, where hearing the voice is what makes a sheep his.

links.note: ‘Ye will not hearken unto the voice of the good shepherd.’ ‘Good shepherd’ is not an Old Testament phrase; it occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both in John 10, and it is joined here to hearing the shepherd's voice, which is the same discourse's test of belonging. The Old Testament shepherd chapters have the flock and the scattering but never the adjective — which is what makes this a New Testament link at a verse whose sequel (7:19) is straight Ezekiel.

pericopes.text: And behold, instead of gathering you, except ye will repent, behold he shall scatter you forth that ye shall become meat for dogs and wild beasts.

links.text: And they were scattered, because there is no shepherd: and they became meat to all the beasts of the field, when they were scattered.

provenance.other: “became meat to” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ezekiel 34:5 and Ezekiel 34:8, and both are in the shepherd oracle. ‘Meat for’ in the sense of carrion is spread across seventeen verses, mostly Jeremiah's fowls-and-beasts formula, but only Ezekiel 34 makes the flock's becoming meat the consequence of having no shepherd.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 34 is the chapter where God takes the flock away from the shepherds who fed themselves, and its structure is exactly Helaman's: because there is no shepherd the sheep are scattered and eaten (34:5), and therefore ‘I will seek out my sheep … and will gather them’ (34:11–13). Helaman 7:19 states the alternative as a threat rather than a promise — ‘instead of gathering you … he shall scatter you forth’ — which is Ezekiel 34 read backwards, with the gathering withheld. The judges of 7:4–5, who feed on office and money, are Ezekiel's shepherds who feed themselves.

links.note: ‘Instead of gathering you, except ye will repent, behold he shall scatter you forth that ye shall become meat for dogs and wild beasts.’ The three terms — not gathered, scattered, become meat for beasts — are Ezekiel 34:5's three terms in Ezekiel's order, and the collocation of scattering with becoming meat belongs to that chapter alone; ‘meat’ in the carrion sense is common in the KJV, and ‘wild beasts’ is in ten verses, so the case rests on the sequence rather than on any one string. The addition is ‘dogs’, which Ezekiel does not have and which the KJV reserves for the deaths of Jezebel and Ahab's house. This was invisible to the n-gram stream, which proposed nothing at all for the verse.

pericopes.text: O how could you have forgotten your God in the very day that he hath delivered you?

links.text: Then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage;

provenance.other: “thine heart be lifted up” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “thy silver and thy gold is multiplied” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the two halves of Deuteronomy 8:13–14. ‘Forget the LORD thy God’ is in two verses, both in Deuteronomy 8.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 8:12–14 is the KJV's one sustained account of how prosperity produces apostasy, and it names the steps in an order Helaman 7 follows across three verses: gold and silver multiplied (8:13 → 7:21), the heart lifted up (8:14 → 7:26), forgetting the God who brought you out (8:14 → 7:20). Helaman inverts the sequence — the forgetting is charged first and the causes given after — which is what a prosecutor does and not what a lawgiver does. Deuteronomy's clause for what is forgotten is ‘which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage’; Helaman's is ‘in the very day that he hath delivered you’, which relocates the deliverance from an ancient exodus to a living memory and makes the ingratitude sharper.

links.note: ‘O how could you have forgotten your God in the very day that he hath delivered you?’ The verbal contact at this verse alone is modest — forgetting God who delivered — but Deuteronomy 8:13–14's other two clauses are both KJV singletons and both turn up within six verses, at 7:21 (gold and silver) and 7:26 (lifted up because of riches). A source that accounts for a passage is preferred to one that accounts for a phrase in it (CONVENTIONS §6a), and no other KJV passage supplies all three. The link is filed here, at the forgetting, because that is where Deuteronomy 8:14 puts the weight.

pericopes.text: But behold, it is to get gain, to be praised of men; yea, and that ye might get gold and silver. And ye have set your hearts upon the riches and the vain things of this world, for the which ye do murder, and plunder, and steal, and bear false witness against your neighbor, and do all manner of iniquity;

links.text: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.

provenance.route: Exodus 20:16 → Matthew 19:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “bear false witness against thy neighbour” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:16 and Deuteronomy 5:20 — the two Decalogues. No New Testament recitation keeps the neighbour clause: Matthew 19:18, Mark 10:19, Luke 18:20 and Romans 13:9 all stop at ‘bear false witness’.
provenance.significance: The mediation runs both ways at once, and that is the finding. The order of the list is Matthew's — Matthew 19:18 is the only Gospel recitation that leads with murder, and Helaman leads with murder — while the clause that closes it, ‘against your neighbor’, survives only in the Decalogue itself. So a Nephite indictment of judges who take money reproduces Jesus's abbreviated commandment list and then restores from Exodus the words the Gospels dropped. ‘Plunder’ stands where every biblical list has adultery, which is what an indictment about riches needs and what no source supplies.

links.note: ‘For the which ye do murder, and plunder, and steal, and bear false witness against your neighbor.’ Two sources fused. mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Matthew 19:18, but the second of them is an artifact of spelling: the tool compares ‘against thy neighbour’ as a unit and Helaman reads ‘against your neighbor’, so it scores a clause the Book of Mormon plainly has as absent. Adjudicated by hand: the sequence is Matthew's, the neighbour clause is Exodus's, and the row is filed at Exodus 20:16 with Matthew 19:18 as composite because the clause that is unique to one verse-pair is the Decalogue's, not the Gospel's.

pericopes.text: and for this cause wo shall come unto you except ye shall repent. For if ye will not repent, behold this great city, and also all those great citties which are round about, which are in the land of our possession, shall be taken away, that ye shall have no place in them: For behold, the Lord will not grant unto you strength, as he hath hitherto done, to withstand against your enemies.

links.text: And they shall fall one upon another, as it were before a sword, when none pursueth: and ye shall have no power to stand before your enemies.

provenance.other: “power to stand before your enemies” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Helaman substitutes ‘strength … to withstand against your enemies’, keeping the syntax and changing both nouns, which is why kjvSpecific is held at uncertain.
provenance.significance: Leviticus 26 is the covenant-curse chapter, and 26:37's withdrawal of the power to stand is the point at which the curses become military. Helaman 7:22 makes the same move and adds the covenantal premise Leviticus leaves implicit — ‘as he hath hitherto done’ — so the threat is not that the enemy grows stronger but that a support is removed. The clause about the cities being taken away, and having no place in them, is answered by the judges at 8:5 and is adjudicated there, where John 11:48 supplies it.

links.note: ‘The Lord will not grant unto you strength, as he hath hitherto done, to withstand against your enemies.’ A paraphrase rather than a run: the one KJV verse with this thought in this syntax is Leviticus 26:37, and every content word has been changed — strength for power, withstand against for stand before. Moderate, and kjvSpecific uncertain, because a paraphrase cannot show which English version it paraphrases. Recorded because the covenant-curse logic is the chapter's, and because the second half of the verse has a much harder-edged source that belongs at 8:5.

pericopes.text: For behold, thus saith the Lord: I will not shew unto the wicked of my strength, to one more than the other, save it be unto those who repenteth of their sins, and hearken unto my words; now therefore I would that ye should behold, my brethren, that it shall be better for the Lamanites than for you, except ye shall repent;

links.text: But I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you.

provenance.other: “than for you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 11:22 and Luke 10:14, which are the same saying. Matthew's is preferred only because Matthew 11:21's ground — mighty works done in you — is the ground Helaman 7:24 gives.
provenance.significance: Matthew 11:21–24 is the KJV's one comparative-judgment oracle: the pagan cities would have repented if they had seen what you saw, therefore their case is better than yours. Helaman 7:23–24 runs the argument on the Lamanites, who occupy the place of Tyre and Sidon exactly — the outsiders who never had the knowledge and are therefore not answerable for it. The uncomfortable half of Matthew's saying is that the compliment to the outsider is not a compliment; it is a way of saying the insider is worse. Helaman keeps that.

links.note: ‘It shall be better for the Lamanites than for you, except ye shall repent.’ The verbal contact is three words, and ‘than for you’ is not a distinctive string on its own; the case is that Helaman 7:23–24 reproduces the whole shape of Matthew 11:21–24 — comparative verdict, named outsider people, and the ground stated as knowledge received rather than deeds done (7:24, ‘they have not sinned against that great knowledge which ye have received’). Moderate because a reader could decline it as a common enough rhetorical move, and because the very next verse has a much stronger Old Testament source for the same argument.

pericopes.text: for behold they are more righteous than you; for they have not sinned against that great knowledge which ye have received; therefore the Lord will be merciful unto them; yea, he will lengthen out their days and increase their seed, even when thou shalt be utterly destroyed, except thou shalt repent;

links.text: Thou also, which hast judged thy sisters, bear thine own shame for thy sins that thou hast committed more abominable than they: they are more righteous than thou: yea, be thou confounded also, and bear thy shame, in that thou hast justified thy sisters.

provenance.other: “they are more righteous than” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Habakkuk 1:13 has ‘the man that is more righteous than he’, which is the same comparison in a different grammar and belongs to the chapter's Habakkuk frame (see 7:10). The promise clause draws on 1 Kings 3:14's ‘I will lengthen thy days’ — ‘lengthen’ occurs in only two KJV verses.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 16 is the KJV's most sustained use of the comparative verdict, and its sting is that the sisters who come off better are Sodom and Samaria. Helaman puts the Lamanites in that position and adds the reason Ezekiel leaves to the chapter as a whole: greater knowledge, greater liability. What the borrowing carries with it is Ezekiel 16:53–55's sequel, in which the sisters are restored first and the accused city last — which is the Book of Mormon's long-range claim about the Lamanites, made here in Ezekiel's words and without argument.

links.note: ‘For behold they are more righteous than you.’ Five consecutive words on a KJV singleton, and the surrounding argument is Ezekiel 16:51–52's: you have sinned worse than the people you despise, therefore they are more righteous than you and you bear your own shame. The one change is the pronoun — Ezekiel's ‘than thou’ for a personified city, Helaman's ‘than you’ for a crowd — which the KJV's own grammar requires once the addressee is plural. Verses 23 and 24 give the same verdict twice, once in Matthew's form and once in Ezekiel's; this is the stronger of the two.

pericopes.text: yea, wo be unto you because of that great abomination which hath come among you; and ye have united yourselves unto it, yea, to that secret band which was established by Gadianton;
yea, wo shall come unto you because of that pride which ye have suffered to enter your hearts, which hath lifted you up beyond that which is good because of your exceeding great riches;
yea, wo be unto you because of your wickedness and abominations.
And except ye repent, ye shall perish; yea, even your lands shall be taken from you, and ye shall be destroyed from off the face of the earth.

links.text: I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.

provenance.other: “except ye repent ye shall” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 13:3 and Luke 13:5, which are the same sentence said twice. “shall be taken from you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 21:43.
provenance.significance: Luke 13:1–5 is the passage where Jesus refuses to read a massacre and a collapsed tower as a verdict on the people they killed, and turns the question back on the hearers: except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. Helaman 7 has been arguing from a tower and about a coming massacre, and 7:28 answers with Luke's refrain. Matthew 21:43's clause then supplies what is taken and from whom — in Matthew a kingdom given to another nation, in Helaman lands — and Matthew 21 is the vineyard parable told against the chief priests, who two chapters later try to seize the teller and dare not because they fear the people. That is Helaman 8:4.

links.note: ‘And except ye repent, ye shall perish; yea, even your lands shall be taken from you.’ Two New Testament sources in one sentence, each a near-singleton: Luke's doubled ‘except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish’ with ‘all likewise’ dropped, and Matthew 21:43's ‘shall be taken from you’, which is the only KJV occurrence of that string. The closing clause, ‘destroyed from off the face of the earth’, is a Book of Mormon formula rather than a fresh borrowing and is not adjudicated here.

pericopes.text: Behold now I do not say that these things shall be, of myself, because it is not of myself that I know these things; but behold, I know that these things are true, because the Lord God hath made them known unto me; therefore I testify that they shall be.

And now it came to pass that when Nephi had said these words, behold there were men which were Judges, which also belonged to the secret band of Gadianton, and they were angry, and they cried out against him, saying unto the people, why do ye not seize upon this man and bring him forth, that he may be condemned according to the crime which he hath done?
Why seest thou this man, and hearest him revile against this people, and against our law?

For behold, Nephi had spoken unto them concerning the corruptness of their law; yea, many things did Nephi speak which cannot be written; and nothing did he speak which were contrary to the commandments of God.

And those Judges were angry with him because he spake plain unto them concerning their secret works of darkness; nevertheless they durst not lay their own hands upon him; for they feared the people, lest they should cry out against them;

links.text: Then went the captain with the officers, and brought them without violence: for they feared the people, lest they should have been stoned.

provenance.other: “for they feared the people lest they should” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — nine consecutive words, Acts 5:26. The half of the sentence before it, 'sought to lay hands on him', matches Matthew 21:46 and Luke 20:19; Matthew reads 'they feared the multitude' and Luke 'they feared the people', so Matthew is ruled out by the noun.
provenance.significance: Acts 5:26 is the officers fetching the apostles from the temple without violence because a stoning was likelier than an arrest. It sits inside the chapter this whole passage runs on: a council enraged by preaching (5:17, 5:33), unable to act for fear of the crowd, and told by one of its own to leave the men alone (5:38-39), after which the prisoners are released. Helaman 8:1-10 is that sequence in Nephite dress, and 9:5's 'fear came upon them' completes it with Acts 5:11's phrase. The metalepsis is in what Acts fears: not that the people will defend the preacher, but that they will stone the officers. Helaman keeps the fear and supplies its object from its own scene — 'lest they should cry out against them'.

links.note: 'Nevertheless they durst not lay their own hands upon him; for they feared the people, lest they should cry out against them.' Nine consecutive words reproduced from a single KJV verse, which is as strong as the verbal evidence in this catalogue gets, and the noun that discriminates comes out right: 'people', not Matthew's 'multitude'. The first half of the Book of Mormon sentence is the Synoptic formula for the same predicament, closest to Luke 20:19 — whose next verse supplies the 'power and authority' of Helaman 7:4, so two consecutive verses of Luke 20 stand behind two chapters of Helaman. Catalogued as a quotation on the nine-word run, though still below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six.

links.text: And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.

provenance.other: “works of darkness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 13:12 and Ephesians 5:11. Ephesians is preferred because its verb is 'reprove' and Helaman's clause is about a prophet speaking plainly against them; Romans 13:12's is 'cast off', which is what the sinner does, not what the witness does.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:11-13 is the KJV's one passage that makes reproof the appropriate response to works of darkness, on the ground that reproof is what makes them visible: 'all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light.' The Book of Mormon adds 'secret' to the phrase — the Gadianton band's defining adjective throughout Helaman — and then spends chapter 9 doing precisely what Ephesians says reproof does, dragging a concealed murder into the open until the murderer confesses.

links.note: 'He spake plain unto them concerning their secret works of darkness.' A three-word phrase confined to two KJV verses and joined here to the verb Ephesians attaches to it. Moderate rather than high: 'works of darkness' is short, and the Book of Mormon's 'secret combinations' vocabulary could reach 'works of darkness' independently. The reason for recording it is the pairing with plain speech, which is Ephesians 5:11's own logic and not Romans 13:12's.

pericopes.text: therefore they did cry unto the people, saying, Why do ye suffer this man to revile against us? For behold, he doth condemn all this people, even unto destruction; yea, and also that these our great cities shall be taken from us, that we shall have no place in them.

links.text: If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation.

provenance.other: “take away both our place and nation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Place' in the sense of a nation's standing ground, coupled with its loss to an invader, is John 11:48's alone in the KJV.
provenance.significance: John 11:47-53 is the council that decides Jesus must die, and 11:48 is the argument that persuades it: if we leave him alone, everyone will believe him, and we will lose our place and our nation. Helaman 8:5-7 is the same deliberation with the same two moves in the same order — the alarm that the preacher's success means the loss of our place (8:5), and the countervailing voice that says let this man alone (8:7, which is John 11:48's own opening clause given to the other side). The verse this council reaches next is John 11:50, Caiaphas on one man dying for the people, which the catalogue adjudicates at 1 Nephi 4:13. So the Book of Mormon's first killing and its last great prophetic trial are argued out of the same three verses of John, at opposite ends of the book.

links.note: 'These our great cities shall be taken from us, that we shall have no place in them.' The KJV has exactly one verse in which a threatened ruling class complains that it will lose its place, and its wording — 'take away both our place and nation' — is reproduced here with 'cities' supplied for 'nation', which is the substitution a text without a nation-state has to make. What raises this above a resemblance is that the objectors' own words at 8:7, 'let this man alone', are the first clause of the same verse; John 11:48 has been split across the two sides of the Nephite argument. Nephi anticipated the threat at 7:22 in different words, and the reader is sent here from the register at that verse.

pericopes.text: And now we know that this is impossible; for behold we are powerful, and our cities great; therefore our enemies can have no power over us.

links.text: The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us.

provenance.other: No wording is shared. The KJV's 'none evil can come upon us' and Helaman's 'our enemies can have no power over us' are the same claim in entirely different words, and the rarity score records the rarity of the CLAIM, not of any string.
provenance.significance: Micah 3:9-12 puts four things in one order: rulers who abhor judgment and judge for reward, priests and prophets who work for money, the ruling class's answer that no evil can come upon them because the LORD is among them, and the prophet's verdict that the city will be plowed as a field. Helaman 7:5, 8:5-6 and 7:22 have the same four in the same order — venal judges, the invulnerability of great cities, and a prophet announcing that the great city will be taken away. What Micah supplies and Helaman keeps is the specific psychology: the invulnerability claim is made BY the corrupt bench, as its answer to the prophecy, and is grounded in privilege rather than in force. The Nephite judges secularize the ground — 'we are powerful, and our cities great' where Micah's say 'Is not the LORD among us?' — which is the one change, and it is a telling one in a book about a people who believe themselves covenanted.

links.note: 'And now we know that this is impossible; for behold we are powerful, and our cities great; therefore our enemies can have no power over us.' A structural link with no verbal contact at all, offered under CONVENTIONS §0a as a proposal rather than a demonstration. The case is that Micah 3 is the KJV's only passage in which corrupt judges answer a prophecy of the city's destruction with a claim of immunity, and that Helaman reproduces the whole four-part sequence across 7:5, 7:22 and 8:5-6.
links.whyNot: Not one word is shared, and the claim 'our enemies cannot touch us' is a commonplace of prophetic literature; Isaiah 47:8, Obadiah 3 and Revelation 18:7 all voice a version of it, and Obadiah's 'who shall bring me down to the ground?' is arguably closer in tone. Nothing here would survive a demand for verbal evidence, and a reader who requires one should decline the row.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that thus they did stir up the people to anger against Nephi, and raised contentions among them; for there were some which did cry out, Let this man alone, for he is a good man, and those things which he saith will surely come to pass except we repent;

links.text: And there was much murmuring among the people concerning him: for some said, He is a good man: others said, Nay; but he deceiveth the people.

provenance.other: “he is a good man” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Samuel 18:27 and John 7:12. 2 Samuel's is David identifying a runner by his gait and expecting good tidings; John's is a crowd divided over a preacher. 'Let this man alone' is in no KJV verse, but 'let him thus alone' is John 11:48's opening clause. The crowd's second clause rests on another singleton: “surely come to pass” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 13:32, where an old prophet at Bethel vouches that the rejected man of God's cry against the altar will stand.
provenance.significance: John 7:12 is the KJV's one instance of a crowd splitting over a teacher in exactly these terms — some say he is a good man, others say he deceives the people — and John 7:40-43 repeats the division at greater length, ending 'so there was a division among the people because of him'. Helaman 8:7 has the identical split and the identical formula, and the objectors at 9:16 will supply John's other half, that the man is manufacturing belief to make himself great. The composite with John 11:48 is what makes the verse remarkable: the crowd's defence of Nephi, 'let this man alone', is verbatim the council's fear about Jesus, 'if we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him.' The same clause is a plea on one side of John and a danger on the other, and Helaman gives it to the plea.

links.note: 'There were some which did cry out, Let this man alone, for he is a good man.' Two Johannine crowd scenes fused into one sentence. 'He is a good man' belongs to two KJV verses and only John 7:12 is a crowd's verdict on a preacher; 'let this man alone' is not KJV wording but 'let him thus alone' is, from John 11:48, whose other clause is adjudicated two verses earlier at 8:5. The Book of Mormon's crowd then adds the clause John's does not have — 'those things which he saith will surely come to pass except we repent' — which is where the third source enters: 1 Kings 13:32 is the KJV's one 'surely come to pass', and it is spoken by a bystander vouching for a prophet the king had tried to seize. That is precisely the function of the speakers here, and it is the reason the division goes the other way in Helaman and not in John.

pericopes.text: yea, behold all the judgements will come upon us which he hath testified unto us; for we know that he hath testified aright unto us concerning our iniquities. And behold they are many; and he knoweth as well all things which shall befal us as he knoweth of our iniquities;
yea, and behold if he had not been a prophet he could not have testified concerning those things.

And it came to pass that those people which sought to destroy Nephi, were compelled because of their fear, that they did not lay their hands on him. Therefore he began again to speak unto them, seeing that he had gained favor in the eyes of some, insomuch that the remainder of them did fear.

Therefore he was constrained to speak more unto them, saying: Behold my brethren, have ye not read that God gave power unto one man, even Moses, to smite upon the waters of the Red Sea, and they parted hither and thither, insomuch that the Israelites, which were our fathers, came through upon dry ground, and the waters closed upon the armies of the Egyptians, and swallowed them up?

links.text: And he took the mantle of Elijah that fell from him, and smote the waters, and said, Where is the LORD God of Elijah? and when he also had smitten the waters, they parted hither and thither: and Elisha went over.

provenance.other: “parted hither and thither” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the adverbial pair is in only two, 2 Kings 2:8 and 2:14, both of the Jordan. Exodus 14 never says Moses smote the sea — he stretches out his hand and lifts up his rod — and never uses 'hither and thither'. 'Upon the dry ground' is Exodus 14:22's, against Hebrews 11:29's 'as by dry land', and 'swallowed them up' is not in the Exodus narrative at all; it belongs to Korah, at Numbers 16:32, 26:10 and Deuteronomy 11:6.
provenance.significance: Nephi is arguing that God gave power to one man, and the sentence he uses to prove it is assembled from three separate KJV miracles. The verb and adverb are Elisha's at the Jordan, where the whole point of the episode is that the power has passed from one man to another and the watching prophets say 'the spirit of Elijah doth rest on Elisha' — which is exactly the inference Nephi wants his hearers to draw about himself in 8:12. The drowning clause comes from Korah, where the earth swallows men who denied that Moses's authority was from God; Nephi is answering men who deny that his is. So the Red Sea proof-text has been written in the words of a succession story and a rebellion story, which are the two things the argument is actually about.
provenance.alternative: Hebrews 11:29 is the New Testament's version of the crossing and is ruled out at the one point that discriminates: it reads 'as by dry land' and the Book of Mormon reads 'upon dry ground', with Exodus 14:22.

links.note: 'To smite upon the waters of the Red Sea, and they parted hither and thither … came through upon dry ground, and the waters closed upon the armies of the Egyptians, and swallowed them up.' Three sources in one sentence, and the tell is that the most distinctive string in it does not come from the Red Sea at all: 'parted hither and thither' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and that verse is Elisha at the Jordan. mediation-check.py reports two decisive points for Hebrews 11:29 over Exodus 14:22, and both are artifacts — the tool has a backbone of zero shared words at each and is matching 'through' against 'passed through'. The word that actually discriminates is ground against land, and the Book of Mormon has the Old Testament's. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Exodus 14:21-29 at this verse.

pericopes.text: And now behold, if God gave unto this man such power, then why should ye dispute among yourselves, and say that he hath given unto me no power whereby I may know concerning the judgements that shall come upon you except ye repent?

But behold, ye not only deny my words, but ye also deny all the words which hath been spoken by our fathers, and also the words which was spoken by this man, Moses, which had such great power given unto him; yea, the words which he hath spoken concerning the coming of the Messiah.
Yea, did he not bear record, that the Son of God should come?— And as he lifted up the brazen serpent in the wilderness, even so shall he be lifted up which should come.

links.text: And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up:

provenance.route: Numbers 21:8-9 → John 3:14 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “lifted up the serpent in the wilderness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “even so must the son of man be lifted up” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the two halves of John 3:14. Numbers 21 has no lifting: Moses makes a serpent of brass and sets it upon a pole. The 1830 reads 'brazen serpent', which is not the KJV's spelling; 2 Kings 18:4 has 'brasen serpent', and that is the only KJV verse with the phrase in any spelling.
provenance.significance: The mediation is not in doubt and the interest lies elsewhere. What Helaman does that John does not is put the typology in a prophet's mouth six hundred years early and make it an argument about the reliability of prophecy rather than about belief — 8:13 has just complained that these people deny 'the words which he hath spoken concerning the coming of the Messiah'. So John 3:14's reading of Numbers 21 is presented as Moses's own intention, which is the strongest possible form of the chapter's thesis that all the prophets testified of Christ.

links.note: 'And as he lifted up the brazen serpent in the wilderness, even so shall he be lifted up which should come.' John 3:14 with two substitutions: 'shall' for 'must', and 'which should come' for 'the Son of man', both of which the Nephite setting requires, since the title is introduced in the previous clause and the event is future. mediation-check.py returns points both ways, but the one it scores for Numbers 21:9 is an artifact — it reports the Book of Mormon as lacking 'in the wilderness even so', which the verse plainly has. On the words that discriminate, the lifting and the even-so construction, John wins outright; Numbers supplies the next verse. Hardy's apparatus cross-references both Numbers 21:4-9 and John 3:14-15 here.

pericopes.text: And as many as should look upon that serpent should live, even so as many as should look upon the Son of God, with faith, having a contrite spirit, might live, even unto that life which is eternal.—

links.text: And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.

provenance.other: “when he looketh upon it shall live” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Have eternal life' is in four, of which John 3:15 is the one that continues John 3:14. 'Contrite spirit' is in exactly two, Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 66:2.
provenance.significance: The two verses divide the sources cleanly: 8:14 takes the lifting from John and 8:15 takes the looking from Numbers, so the Book of Mormon has reassembled John 3:14-15's argument with the Old Testament half restored to its own wording. The addition is the condition. Numbers requires only that the bitten man look, and that literalness is the point of the story; John requires belief. Helaman requires looking 'with faith, having a contrite spirit', which imports Isaiah 66:2's test — the man God will look to is the poor and contrite — and so answers the question Numbers raises and John changes the subject on.

links.note: 'And as many as should look upon that serpent should live, even so as many as should look upon the Son of God, with faith, having a contrite spirit, might live, even unto that life which is eternal.' Numbers 21:8's condition, John 3:15's outcome, and a third clause from neither. The look-and-live construction is a KJV singleton in Numbers 21:8 and its 21:9 variant reads 'when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived'; Helaman has the 21:8 form. The qualifying phrase 'having a contrite spirit' is not in either chapter and belongs to Isaiah 66:2, which is where the KJV puts the condition God attaches to being looked upon in return.

pericopes.text: And now behold, Moses did not only testify of these things, but also all the holy prophets, from his day even to the days of Abraham.
Yea, and behold, Abraham saw of his coming, and was filled with gladness, and did rejoice.

links.text: Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad.

provenance.other: “Abraham rejoiced to see my day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. It is the only place in the Bible where Abraham is said to have foreseen Christ, and the only warrant anywhere for Helaman 8:17's claim.
provenance.significance: John 8:56 is said in a quarrel about whether Abraham's children are behaving like Abraham, and it provokes the crowd to take up stones (8:59). Helaman 8:17 is said in a quarrel about whether the prophets testified of Christ, to men who have just tried to seize the speaker and could not for fear of the people. The borrowing carries the shape of its source: an appeal to Abraham that raises the temperature rather than settling it. Five verses later, 8:22, Helaman applies the same formula to the Nephite fathers — 'have looked forward, and have rejoiced in his day which is to come' — so John 8:56 supplies the template for the whole chapter's argument from the prophets.

links.note: 'Yea, and behold, Abraham saw of his coming, and was filled with gladness, and did rejoice.' John 8:56's three verbs — rejoiced, saw, was glad — in reversed order, with 'was glad' expanded to 'filled with gladness'. The reordering is why this is an allusion and not a quotation. What settles the source is that no other KJV verse makes the claim at all: outside John 8:56 the Bible nowhere says Abraham saw Christ's day, so the sentence has one possible parent.

pericopes.text: Yea, and behold I say unto you, That Abraham not only knew of these things, but there were many before the days of Abraham which were called by the order of God; yea, even after the order of his Son; and this that it should be shewn unto the people a great many thousand years before his coming, that even redemption should come unto them.

And now I would that ye should know, that even since the days of Abraham, there hath been many prophets that hath testified these things; yea, behold, the prophet Zenas did testify boldly; for the which he was slain.

And behold, also Zenoch, and also Ezias, and also Isaiah, and Jeremiah, (Jeremiah being that same prophet which testified of the destruction of Jerusalem.) And now we know that Jerusalem was destroyed, according to the words of Jeremiah. O then why not the Son of God come, according to his prophecy?

And now will ye dispute that Jerusalem was destroyed? Will ye say that the sons of Zedekiah were not slain, all except it were Mulek? Yea, and do ye not behold that the seed of Zedekiah are with us, and they were driven out of the land of Jerusalem? But behold, this is not all.

links.text: Then the king of Babylon slew the sons of Zedekiah in Riblah before his eyes: also the king of Babylon slew all the nobles of Judah.

provenance.other: “the sons of Zedekiah” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — 2 Kings 25:7, Jeremiah 39:6 and Jeremiah 52:10 — and all three say they were slain. Jeremiah 39:6 is preferred over 2 Kings 25:7 only because the surrounding argument at 8:20 is explicitly about Jeremiah and about the destruction of Jerusalem coming to pass according to his words.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's argument here depends on the KJV being complete: it says the sons of Zedekiah were slain 'all except it were Mulek', and no biblical verse leaves an exception open. All three witnesses say the sons were slain without qualification. So the claim is not an inference from scripture but a correction of it, offered as evidence — the seed of Zedekiah are with us — and offered in the same breath as an appeal to Jeremiah's reliability. That is the interesting thing about the row and the reason it is worth cataloguing: the borrowing is used to license a departure from its source.

links.note: 'Will ye say that the sons of Zedekiah were not slain, all except it were Mulek?' A four-word run on a phrase confined to three KJV verses, all of them the same event, and the verse names Jeremiah two lines earlier. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is a proper name plus a kinship term and cannot by itself pick out which of the three witnesses is in view; what raises it above bare coincidence is the argumentative context, which is Jeremiah's fulfilled prophecy. Hardy's apparatus cross-references 2 Kings 25:7 and Jeremiah 39:6 here.

pericopes.text: Our father Lehi was driven out of Jerusalem, because he testified of these things. Nephi also testified of these things, and also almost all of our fathers, even down to this time; yea, they have testified of the coming of Christ, and have looked forward, and have rejoiced in his day which is to come.
And behold, he is God, and he is with them, and he did manifest himself unto them, that they were redeemed by him; and they gave unto him glory, because of that which is to come.

And now seeing ye know these things, and cannot deny them, except ye shall lie. therefore in this ye have sinned, for ye have rejected all these things, notwithstanding so many evidences which ye have received; yea, even ye have received all things, both things in Heaven, and all things which are in the earth, as a witness that they are true.

links.text: Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know these things before, beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness.

provenance.other: “seeing ye know these things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 3 is an argument against scoffers who say the promise of his coming has failed because nothing has changed since the fathers fell asleep, and 3:17 is its conclusion: you already know this, so you have no excuse for being led away. Helaman 8 has spent twenty verses arguing that the promise of his coming did not fail — Jerusalem was destroyed as Jeremiah said, therefore the Son of God will come as prophesied (8:20) — and reaches the same conclusion in the same words. The borrowing brings the shape of Peter's argument with it: knowledge already possessed converts unbelief from an error into a fault, which is what 8:24 says next, 'therefore in this ye have sinned'.

links.note: 'And now seeing ye know these things, and cannot deny them, except ye shall lie.' Five consecutive words on a KJV singleton, with Peter's 'before' dropped. Moderate rather than high because the words are all common ones and the run could be assembled without a source; what makes it worth keeping is that the two passages are doing the same work at the same point in the same kind of argument, and that Helaman's next clause supplies the culpability Peter's 'beware' only implies.

pericopes.text: But behold, ye have rejected the truth, and rebelled against your holy God; and even at this time, instead of laying up for yourselves treusures in Heaven, where nothing doth corrupt, and where nothing can come which is unclean, ye are heaping up for yourselves wrath against the day of judgement;

links.text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:

provenance.other: “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Doth corrupt' is in exactly two, Matthew 6:19 and 6:20, the same antithesis.
provenance.significance: Matthew 6:19-21 ends 'for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also', which is the sentence Helaman has already used at 7:21 — 'ye have set your hearts upon the riches and the vain things of this world'. So the chapter's indictment and its remedy come from the same six verses of the Sermon on the Mount, a chapter apart, and the reader who recovers the context gets the missing middle term: the reason treasure in heaven matters is that the heart follows it.

links.note: 'Instead of laying up for yourselves treusures in Heaven, where nothing doth corrupt, and where nothing can come which is unclean.' The 1830's misspelling of treasures is the compositor's, not evidence. Matthew 6:20's clause is reproduced almost entire, with the participle adjusted; the relative clause is then generalized twice — 'nothing doth corrupt' for the moth and rust, 'nothing can come which is unclean' for the thieves — which replaces Matthew's two concrete threats with a purity criterion Matthew does not have. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six.

links.text: But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God;

provenance.other: “wrath against the day of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The n-gram stream found it on a five-word run.
provenance.significance: Romans 2:5 is already a treasure metaphor — 'treasurest up unto thyself wrath' — which is why it can be set against Matthew 6:20 in a single sentence without a seam. Paul's point is that the impenitent are accumulating something, and the accumulation is invisible until the day it is disclosed. Helaman's judges have just been told their cities will be taken and have answered that this is impossible; the borrowed verse says the account is already running. Recovering Romans 2 supplies the argument's next move, that God will render to every man according to his deeds and that there is no respect of persons with him — which is what a bench that lets the guilty go for money (7:5) has most reason to fear.

links.note: 'Ye are heaping up for yourselves wrath against the day of judgement.' Romans 2:5's clause with 'heaping up' for 'treasurest up' and 'the day of judgement' for 'the day of wrath', and the substitution is what makes the sentence work: the same verse contains both halves of Helaman's antithesis, because Paul's wrath is also something laid up. Two links stand at this verse and they are one sentence — treasures in heaven from Matthew 6:20, wrath laid up from Romans 2:5 — which is a composition, not a coincidence.

pericopes.text: yea, even at this time ye are ripening, because of your murders, and your fornication and wickedness, for everlasting destruction; yea, and except ye repent, it will come unto you soon;

links.text: Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;

provenance.other: “everlasting destruction” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9 is a judgment at the revelation of Christ in flaming fire, and its 'everlasting destruction' is exclusion from a presence rather than an annihilation. Helaman 8:26 attaches the phrase to ripening, which is a harvest figure the KJV uses for judgment at Joel 3:13 and Revelation 14:18, so the verse fuses a Pauline verdict with a prophetic image. The chapter's 'endless wo' at 7:16 and 'everlasting destruction' here mark the two poles the Book of Mormon's punishment vocabulary moves between, and both are New Testament.

links.note: 'Ye are ripening, because of your murders, and your fornication and wickedness, for everlasting destruction.' A two-word borrowing, and it is recorded because those two words occur together in exactly one KJV verse. Moderate: the phrase is short enough that a preacher's ear could produce it, and the surrounding sentence shares nothing else with 2 Thessalonians 1. Filed as an echo rather than an allusion for that reason.

pericopes.text: yea, behold it is now even at your doors; yea, go ye in unto the judgement seat, and search; and behold, your Judge is murdered, and he lieth in his blood; and he hath been murdered by his brother, who seeketh to sit in the judgement seat.

links.text: Grudge not one against another, brethren, lest ye be condemned: behold, the judge standeth before the door.

provenance.other: “the judge standeth before the door” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Even at the doors' occurs in exactly two, Matthew 24:33 and Mark 13:29, which are the same saying; both attach it to the nearness of the end, and Helaman's 'it is now even at your doors' has Matthew's plural.
provenance.significance: This is the batch's clearest metalepsis. James 5:9 is a figure of speech: the judge is at the door, so stop quarrelling. Matthew 24:33 is another: the end is at the doors. Helaman 8:27 says both — 'it is now even at your doors' — and then, in the same breath, tells the hearers to walk through an actual door and look: 'go ye in unto the judgement seat, and search; and behold, your Judge is murdered, and he lieth in his blood.' The metaphor is cashed as a corpse. James's standing judge becomes a judge lying in his blood, and the proof of the prophecy is that the figure has stopped being a figure. Nothing in the KJV does this; the reading exists only when both texts are held together.

links.note: 'Yea, behold it is now even at your doors; yea, go ye in unto the judgement seat, and search; and behold, your Judge is murdered.' Two New Testament door sayings, one of them a KJV singleton, and the Book of Mormon literalizes both in the next clause. The argument for dependence is not length — 'at your doors' is three words — but the coincidence of the two elements James's verse uniquely joins, a judge and a door, in a sentence whose subject is a judge found dead at the door of his court. James 5 supplies this chapter's neighbouring verse too: 9:22's 'begin to howl and mourn' is James 5:1's 'weep and howl'.

pericopes.text: And behold, they both belong to your secret band, whose author is Gadianton, and the evil one which seeketh to destroy the souls of men.

Behold now it came to pass that when Nephi had spoken these words, certain men which were among them ran to the judgement seat; yea, even there were five which went; and they said among themselves, as they went,

Behold, now we will know of a surety, whether this man be a prophet, and God hath commanded him to prophesy such marvellous things unto us. Behold we do not believe that he hath; yea, we do not believe that he is a prophet; nevertheless, if this thing which he hath said concerning the Chief Judge be true, that he be dead, then will we believe that the other words which he hath spoken is true.
And it came to pass that they ran in their might, and came in unto the judgement seat; and behold the Chief Judge had fallen to the earth, and did lie in his blood.
And now behold, when they saw this, they were astonished exceedingly, insomuch that they fell to the earth; for they had not believed the words which Nephi had spoken concerning the Chief Judge;
but now when they saw they believed, and fear came upon them, lest all the judgements which Nephi had spoken should come upon the people; therefore they did quake, and had fallen to the earth.

links.text: And great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things.

provenance.other: “fear came upon” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Job 4:14, Acts 2:43 and Acts 5:11. Acts 5:11 is preferred on context, not on wording, which is why kjvSpecific is uncertain.
provenance.significance: Acts 5 has already supplied this passage's strongest verbal link, at 8:4, and the sequence it supplies here is the rest of the same chapter: a man is found dead where authority sits, those who come in fall down, great fear comes upon all who hear, and the body is carried out and buried the next day (Acts 5:5-11 against Helaman 9:3-10). What the Book of Mormon reverses is the agency. In Acts the fear is of a power that killed; in Helaman the fear is of a prophecy that knew, and 9:5 says so exactly — 'fear came upon them, lest all the judgements which Nephi had spoken should come upon the people'.

links.note: 'And fear came upon them, lest all the judgements which Nephi had spoken should come upon the people; therefore they did quake, and had fallen to the earth.' Three words, and on its own the phrase would not be worth a row. It is recorded because Acts 5 stands behind the preceding chapter on a nine-word singleton (8:4), because the Acts 5 sequence — sudden death at a seat of authority, bystanders falling, great fear on all who hear, burial the following day — runs through Helaman 9:3-10 in order, and because 'lest' recurs in both. Filed as an echo, at moderate, so that the register shows a proposal rather than a demonstration.

pericopes.text: Now immediately when the Judge had been murdered: he being stabbed by his brother, by a garb of secrecy; and he fled, and the servants ran and told the people, raising the cry of murder among them.
And behold the people did gather themselves together unto the place of the judgement seat; and behold, to their astonishment, they saw those five men which had fallen to the earth.

And now behold, the people knew nothing concerning the multitude which had gathered together at the garden of Nephi; therefore they said among themselves, These men are they which have murdered the Judge, and God hath smitten them that they could not flee from us.

And it came to pass that they laid hold on them, and bound them, and cast them into prison. And there was a proclamation sent abroad that the Judge was slain, and that the murderers had been taken, and was cast into prison.

links.text: And when they had laid many stripes upon them, they cast them into prison, charging the jailor to keep them safely:

provenance.other: “cast them into prison” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The three-verb sequence around it — laid hold on, bound, put in prison — is Matthew 14:3's, of Herod and John the Baptist; 'laid hold on' by itself is in six verses.
provenance.significance: The borrowing predicts the end of the chapter. Acts 16:23-34 is the KJV's one prison scene that turns into a conversion: Paul and Silas are cast into prison, the doors are opened, and the jailor and his house believe. Helaman 9:39 closes with the five men believed 'because of the testimony of the five, for they had been converted while they were in prison' — the same movement, with the converts inside rather than outside the cell. Read together, 9:9 and 9:39 bracket the chapter with Acts 16's two halves, and 9:38's 'set at liberty' completes it. Matthew 14:3's contribution is darker and is the sentence's opening: the arrest formula belongs to the imprisonment of a prophet by a court that will kill him.

links.note: 'And it came to pass that they laid hold on them, and bound them, and cast them into prison.' Two sources in one sentence. Matthew 14:3 supplies the sequence — 'laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison' — with the third verb changed, and the verb it is changed to makes 'cast them into prison', which occurs in exactly one KJV verse. That the substitution lands on the KJV's one Philippian-jail phrase, in a chapter whose prisoners are converted in prison and then set at liberty, is what lifts this above the ordinary arrest formula.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that on the morrow, the people did assemble themselves together to mourn and to fast, at the burial of the great and Chief Judge, which had been slain.
And thus were also those Judges which were at the garden of Nephi, and heard his words, were also gathered together at the burial.

And it came to pass that they inquired among the people, saying, Where are the five which was sent to inquire concerning the Chief Judge whether he was dead? And they answered and said, Concerning this five which ye say ye have sent, we know not; but there are five, which are the murderers, whom we have cast into prison.

And it came to pass that the Judges desired that they should be brought; and they were brought, and behold they were the five which were sent; and behold the Judges inquired of them to know concerning the matter, and they told them all that they had done, saying,

We ran and came to the place of the judgement, and when we saw all things, even as Nephi had testified, we were astonished, insomuch that we fell to the earth; and when we were recovered from our astonishment, behold they cast us into prison.
Now as for the murder of this man, we know not who hath done it, and only this much we know, we ran and came according as ye desired, and behold he was dead according to the words of Nephi.

And now it came to pass, that the Judges did expound the matter unto the people, and did cry out against Nephi, saying, Behold we know that this Nephi must have agreed with some one to slay the Judge, and then he might declare it unto us, that he might convert us unto his faith, that he might raise himself to be a great man, chosen of God, and a prophet;

links.text: But there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one:

provenance.other: “some great one” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the great power of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:9 and 8:10. The Book of Mormon reproduces neither string; it has 'raise himself to be a great man, chosen of God, and a prophet' and, at 9:41, 'he is a god'.
provenance.significance: Acts 8:9-11 is the KJV's one full account of the charge the judges lay here: a man who arranges a marvel so that a city will conclude he is great and divinely empowered, and whom the people accordingly call the great power of God, from the least to the greatest. Helaman 9 supplies both halves — the accusation at 9:16 and the popular verdict at 9:41, 'he is a god, for except he was a god, he could not know of all things' — and puts them on opposite sides of a demonstration that the marvel was genuine. The chapter is therefore constructed as an answer to Acts 8: the same evidence that made Simon a sorcerer makes Nephi a prophet, and the difference the text offers is that Nephi refuses the credit at 9:36, 'save it were given unto me by the power of God', which is Acts 8:10's phrase given back to God.

links.note: 'This Nephi must have agreed with some one to slay the Judge, and then he might declare it unto us … that he might raise himself to be a great man, chosen of God, and a prophet.' Proposed on the shape of the accusation rather than on its words. What the judges describe is Simon Magus's career as Acts 8 describes it, down to the two elements Luke's singletons name — self-promotion to greatness and a crowd's conclusion that the man is divine power — and Helaman supplies the second at 9:41. Offered under CONVENTIONS §0a as an interesting and defensible reading.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is a single common adjective. Accusing a wonder-worker of fraud is a stock scene and the Book of Mormon has its own vocabulary for it; a reader who requires shared wording should decline this row and read 9:16 as the narrator's own invention.

pericopes.text: and now behold we will detect this man, and he shall confess his fault and make known unto us the true murderer of this Judge.

And it came to pass that the five were liberated on the day of the burial. Nevertheless, they did rebuke the Judges in the words which they had spoken against Nephi, and did contend with them one by one, insomuch that they did confound them.

Nevertheless, they caused that Nephi should be taken and bound and brought before the multitude, and they began to question him in divers ways, that they might cross him, that they might accuse him to death;

links.text: Laying wait for him, and seeking to catch something out of his mouth, that they might accuse him.

provenance.other: “that they might accuse him” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 12:10, Mark 3:2 and Luke 11:54. The first two are sabbath-healing traps; only Luke 11:54 is an interrogation, and only Luke 11:53 supplies the method — 'began to urge him vehemently, and to provoke him to speak of many things'.
provenance.significance: Luke 11:53-54 follows immediately on the woes against the lawyers, and it is the lawyers who lay the trap; Helaman 9:19 is a bench of judges doing the same thing to a man who has just pronounced woes on them. Chapter 7:4 borrowed 'the power and authority' from Luke 20:20, which is the same manoeuvre in the same Gospel — spies feigning themselves just men to take hold of his words. So the catalogue's two entrapment links in Helaman both come from Luke, and Luke is the evangelist who twice makes questioning a preacher into a legal procedure.
