What Helaman adds is the object: not delivery to a governor but accusation 'to death', which is where Luke's sequence ends anyway.

links.note: 'They began to question him in divers ways, that they might cross him, that they might accuse him to death.' Four words shared with three KJV verses, and the case for Luke 11:54 rests on which of the three it is: the Book of Mormon's judges question and cross-examine, which is Luke's scene and not Matthew 12's or Mark 3's, where the trap is a healing and not a word. 'Cross him' is not KJV vocabulary and is one of the chapter's several courtroom terms with no biblical parent — 'detect this man' at 9:17 is another. The borrowed clause sits inside a paragraph whose other elements, binding the prisoner and bringing him before the multitude, are the Gospel arrest formula generally rather than any one verse.

pericopes.text: saying unto him, Thou art confederate; who is this man that hath done this murder? Now tell us, and acknowledge thy fault, saying, Behold here is money; and also we will grant unto thee thy life if thou wilt tell us and acknowledge the agreement which thou hast made with him.

But Nephi saith unto them, O ye fools, ye uncircumsised of heart, ye blind, and ye stiff-necked people, do ye know how long the Lord your God will suffer you that ye shall go on in this your ways of sin?

links.text: Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.

provenance.route: Leviticus 26:41 / Deuteronomy 10:16 → Acts 7:51 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “stiffnecked and uncircumcised” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The pairing exists nowhere else: 'uncircumcised in heart' is in three verses, Acts 7:51 and Ezekiel 44:7 and 44:9, and the Old Testament's only text that puts the two ideas together is Deuteronomy 10:16, which does it as an imperative — 'circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked'. “Ye fools and blind” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:17 and 23:19.
provenance.significance: Stephen's is the KJV's one speech in which a man on trial before a council turns and abuses his judges, and it is the speech that gets him killed. Helaman 9:19-21 has put Nephi in exactly that position — taken, bound, brought before the multitude, questioned so that they might accuse him to death — and the words he answers with are Stephen's. Recover Acts 7 and the borrowing carries a prediction with it: Stephen's next sentence asks which of the prophets their fathers did not persecute, and the chapter ends in a stoning. Helaman's ends the other way, with the prophet released and the judges confounded, which is the Book of Mormon's answer to the scene rather than its repetition of it. The Matthew 23 clause is the same manoeuvre in the same key: 'ye fools and blind' is Jesus abusing the men who will condemn him.

links.note: 'O ye fools, ye uncircumsised of heart, ye blind, and ye stiff-necked people.' A four-term insult assembled from the KJV's two great denunciations of a religious court. Acts 7:51 is the only verse that joins stiffneckedness to uncircumcision of heart, and Matthew 23:17 the only formula 'ye fools and blind'; Helaman interleaves them — fools, uncircumcised, blind, stiffnecked — so that each source's pair is split by the other's. mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between Deuteronomy 10:16 and Acts 7:51, because the Book of Mormon reproduces no clause the two share; the mediation is argued instead from the collocation, which is Acts's alone, and from the adjectival grammar, which is Acts's and not Deuteronomy's imperative. The 1830's 'uncircumsised' is a compositor's spelling.

links.text: Then Jesus answered and said, O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? how long shall I suffer you? bring him hither to me.

provenance.other: “how long shall I suffer you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 17:17 and Mark 9:19, which are the same saying. Luke 9:41 has it too in substance but reads 'how long shall I be with you, and suffer you'.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one exasperated 'how long shall I suffer you' is spoken over a failure of faith — the disciples could not cast out the spirit — and it opens with 'O faithless and perverse generation'. Helaman transfers the question from Christ to God and from faithlessness to sin: 'do ye know how long the Lord your God will suffer you that ye shall go on in this your ways of sin?' The change of speaker is the interesting part. In the Gospels the one who has to put up with the generation is the one standing in front of it; here the prophet asks the question on God's behalf, which is what a man who has just been called a pretended prophet (9:27) needs the sentence to do.
provenance.alternative: Mark 9:19 is verbally identical at the borrowed clause and cannot be excluded; Matthew is named because Matthew 23:17 is already in the same Book of Mormon sentence.

links.note: 'Do ye know how long the Lord your God will suffer you that ye shall go on in this your ways of sin?' Six words shared with a Synoptic doublet, restated as an indirect question. Moderate: the clause is short, the two candidate verses cannot be told apart, and 'suffer' in the sense of tolerate is common KJV usage. It is kept because it stands in the same sentence as two other denunciation formulas and because the verse is otherwise a pure catena of borrowed abuse.

pericopes.text: O ye had ought to begin to howl and mourn, because of the great destruction at this time which doth await you, except ye shall repent.

links.text: Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you.

provenance.other: “weep and howl” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Joel 1:5 and James 5:1, and Joel's is imperative to drunkards about wine. James 5:1 is the New Testament's only 'howl', and the only KJV verse that pairs the howling with a coming calamity addressed to the rich.
provenance.significance: James 5:1-9 is a single paragraph, and Helaman has now borrowed from both ends of it: 5:9's judge standing before the door at 8:27, and 5:1's weeping and howling here, fourteen verses of Book of Mormon later and in the same confrontation. Between them James says the rich have heaped treasure together for the last days, which is 8:25's heaping up of wrath. What the recovered context supplies is the addressee. James is denouncing rich men who have kept back the labourers' hire; Helaman's audience is a bench of judges who let the guilty go for money (7:5). The catalogue's Helaman 7-9 links keep landing on the KJV's passages about venal wealth, and James 5 is the largest of them.

links.note: 'O ye had ought to begin to howl and mourn, because of the great destruction at this time which doth await you, except ye shall repent.' James 5:1's structure entire: the imperative pair, the causal 'for/because', and the calamity that is coming upon you. 'Mourn' stands where James has 'weep', which is the one substitution, and it is the word Helaman has been using since 7:11. The strength of the row is that this is the third borrowing from James 5 in two chapters — 8:25, 8:27 and here — which is the recurrence criterion doing real work rather than decorating a single match.

pericopes.text: Behold, ye say that I have agreed with a man, that he should murder Seezoram, our Chief Judge. But behold, I say unto you, that this is because I have testified unto you, that ye might know concerning this thing; yea, even for a witness unto you, that I did know of the wickedness and abominations which is among you.
And because I have done this, ye say that I have agreed with a man that he should do this thing; yea, because I shewed unto you this sign, ye are angry with me, and seek to destroy my life.
And now behold, I will shew unto you another sign, and see if ye will in this thing seek to destroy me.
Behold I say unto you, Go to the house of Seantum, which is the brother of Seezoram, and say unto him,
Hath Nephi, the pretended prophet, which doth prophesy so much evil concerning this people, agreed with thee, in the which ye have murdered Seezoram, which is your brother?
And behold, he shall say unto you, Nay.
And ye shall say unto him, Have ye murdered your brother?
And he shall stand with fear, and wist not what to say. And behold, he shall deny unto you; and he shall make as if he were astonished; nevertheless, he shall declare unto you that he is innocent.

links.text: For he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid.

provenance.other: “wist not what to say” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Mark 14:40 has the nearest variant, 'neither wist they what to answer him', and the Book of Mormon has Mark 9:6's form.
provenance.significance: Mark 9:6 explains Peter's blurting at the Transfiguration: he did not know what to say, because they were sore afraid. Helaman 9:30 borrows the clause for a murderer's moment of exposure, and keeps the causal companion — 'he shall stand with fear, and wist not what to say' — so the fear-then-speechlessness order survives the transfer intact. The metalepsis is unflattering to no one and quietly good: the KJV's one sentence about a man with nothing to say is about a disciple in the presence of glory, and it is spent here on a fratricide in the presence of a prophet who already knows.
provenance.alternative: An archaic KJV verb of this kind is also the sort of thing a nineteenth-century writer imitating scripture would reach for without a particular verse in mind; the reason for naming Mark 9:6 is that the four-word string is unique to it and the accompanying fear clause is unique to it too.

links.note: 'And he shall stand with fear, and wist not what to say.' A five-word run on a KJV singleton, inside a prophecy given in advance and fulfilled at 9:37. 'Wist' occurs nowhere in Helaman except here, which is worth noting: the writer has reached for a verb he does not otherwise use, at the exact point where the KJV has one sentence containing it. The n-gram stream ranked it first in the verse and this time the ranking is right.

pericopes.text: But behold, ye shall examine him, and ye shall find blood upon the skirts of his cloak.

links.text: Also in thy skirts is found the blood of the souls of the poor innocents: I have not found it by secret search, but upon all these.

provenance.other: “in thy skirts” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 2:34 and Ezekiel 5:3, and only Jeremiah's has blood in them. It is the Bible's one instance of blood found on a garment's skirt as evidence of a murder.
provenance.significance: This is the batch's best metalepsis after 8:27. Jeremiah 2:34 is not merely the one verse where blood is found in the skirts; its second clause is 'I have not found it by secret search, but upon all these' — that is, the evidence did not have to be hunted for, it was in plain view. Helaman 9:31 sends the judges to find exactly that, on the strength of a prophet's word and without a search, and the whole chapter is an argument about how Nephi could have known without being complicit. Jeremiah's clause answers the question the judges are asking at 9:16-17 and answers it in God's voice: the blood is not found by secret search. Neither text says this. The pair does.

links.note: 'Ye shall examine him, and ye shall find blood upon the skirts of his cloak.' The KJV has one verse in which incriminating blood is found in a man's skirts, and the Book of Mormon reproduces its noun, its preposition and its verb, changing the possessive garment to a cloak. What makes the row strong is not the three words but the second half of Jeremiah's verse, which speaks directly to the chapter's forensic problem. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And when ye have seen this, ye shall say, From whence cometh this blood? Do we not know that it is the blood of your brother?

links.text: And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother’s keeper?

provenance.other: “Where is Abel thy brother” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “thy brother's blood” occurs in exactly two, Genesis 4:10 and 4:11, both of the same interrogation.
provenance.significance: Genesis 4:9-10 is the Bible's first murder inquiry and its shape is the shape of Helaman 9:29-35: the question that already knows the answer ('Have ye murdered your brother?'), the denial ('he shall deny unto you'), and then the blood itself as the witness that overrides the denial ('Do we not know that it is the blood of your brother?'). Cain's blood cries from the ground and Seantum's is on his cloak, but both are evidence God has and the interrogator has not obtained. The metalepsis reaches further than the wording: Genesis 4:10's next verse curses Cain to be a fugitive, and Helaman 9:8 has already had the crowd conclude that God smote the five 'that they could not flee from us'. The chapter's whole apparatus of fratricide, denial and blood-that-speaks is Genesis 4 run as a procedure.

links.note: 'From whence cometh this blood? Do we not know that it is the blood of your brother?' The chapter asks Genesis 4:9's question at 9:29 — 'Have ye murdered your brother?' — receives Cain's answer at 9:28 and 9:30, and then produces Genesis 4:10's evidence here. The link is filed at 9:32 because that is where the two Genesis verses meet in one sentence, with 9:29 and 9:35 recorded as recurrences. The verbal contact is 'thy brother's blood' rewritten as 'the blood of your brother'; the argument is the sequence, which no other KJV passage supplies.

pericopes.text: And then shall he tremble, and shall look pale, even as if death had come upon him.
And then shall ye say, Because of this fear and this paleness which hath come upon your face, behold, we know that thou art guilty.

links.text: Ask ye now, and see whether a man doth travail with child? wherefore do I see every man with his hands on his loins, as a woman in travail, and all faces are turned into paleness?

provenance.other: “paleness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The word is not otherwise in the Authorized Version at all, in any inflection.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 30:6-7 is the day of Jacob's trouble, and the paleness in it is terror at a coming judgment, seen on every face at once. Helaman narrows it to one face and makes it forensic: the paleness is not a response to a prophecy but the evidence that convicts a murderer, and the judges are told in advance to read it as such. A word the KJV uses once, for a nation, is spent here on a single man's guilt.

links.note: 'Because of this fear and this paleness which hath come upon your face, behold, we know that thou art guilty.' A one-word borrowing, and the word occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Filed as an echo at moderate: a single noun, however rare, cannot demonstrate dependence, and 'look pale' at 9:33 is not KJV wording at all. It is worth a row because the writer needed a noun for the thing and the English Bible offered him precisely one.

pericopes.text: And then shall greater fear come upon him; and then shall he confess unto you, and deny no more that he hath done this murder.

And then shall he say unto you, That I, Nephi, know nothing concerning the matter, save it were given unto me by the power of God. And then shall ye know that I am an honest man, and that I am sent unto you from God.

And it came to pass that they went and did, even according as Nephi had said unto them. And behold, the words which he had said, were true: for according to the words, he did deny; and also according to the words, he did confess.
And he was brought to prove that he himself was the very murderer, insomuch that the five were set at liberty; and also was Nephi.

And there were some of the Nephites which believed on the words of Nephi; and there were some also, which believed, because of the testimony of the five, for they had been converted while they were in prison.
And now there were some among the people, which said that Nephi was a prophet;

and there were others which said, Behold, he is a god, for except he was a god, he could not know of all things. For behold, he hath told us the thoughts of our hearts, and also hath told us things; and even he hath brought unto our knowledge the true murderer of our Chief Judge.

links.text: Howbeit they looked when he should have swollen, or fallen down dead suddenly: but after they had looked a great while, and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.

provenance.other: “said that he was a god” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Acts 14:11's Lystra crowd say 'the gods are come down to us in the likeness of men', and Acts 12:22's say 'It is the voice of a god, and not of a man'; only Acts 28:6 has the bare predication.
provenance.significance: All three of Luke's crowd-deification scenes are corrections, and Acts 28:6 is the mildest: Paul does not rebuke Malta as he rebukes Lystra, and Luke leaves the verdict standing without comment. Helaman 9:40-41 does the same — the narrator reports the two opinions, prophet and god, and moves on to chapter 10 without adjudicating, where the voice that comes to Nephi settles it by calling him blessed rather than divine. The borrowing brings with it the reason a crowd reaches the wrong conclusion in Acts: they inferred divinity from an escape they could not explain, which is exactly the inference at 9:41, 'except he was a god, he could not know of all things'.

links.note: 'Behold, he is a god, for except he was a god, he could not know of all things.' Five words on a KJV singleton, with the tense shifted from the narrator's report to the crowd's own speech. Moderate rather than high because the words are common and a crowd calling a wonder-worker a god needs no source; what argues for Acts 28:6 is that the KJV says it in one place, that Helaman uses the same predication twice in one sentence, and that the chapter has already borrowed the accusation of self-deification from Acts 8:9 at 9:16.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there arose a division among the people, insomuch that they divided hither and thither, and went their ways, leaving Nephi alone, as he was standing in the midst of them.

links.text: So there was a division among the people because of him.

provenance.other: “a division among the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 7:43. John uses the noun of the crowd twice more (9:16, 10:19) but never in this phrase; elsewhere the KJV's word for a split people is 'divided' or 'strife'.
provenance.significance: Recover John 7 and the parallel is not merely verbal. The division there is over whether a man teaching in the temple is the Christ; it happens while the officers sent to arrest him fail to take him (7:44-46), and the chapter ends 'every man went unto his own house' (7:53) before Jesus goes to the mount of Olives. Helaman 10 runs the same sequence in the same order: a division among the people (10:1), the prophet left alone and going toward his own house (10:2), and at 10:15-16 officers who 'could not take him'. The borrowed clause is the head of a borrowed scene.

links.note: 'There arose a division among the people, insomuch that they divided hither and thither, and went their ways, leaving Nephi alone.' The one KJV verse with this phrase is the crowd's split over Jesus in the temple, and what follows in Helaman 10 follows what follows in John 7 — the failed arrest at 10:15-16 in particular. The n-gram stream ranked it; the sequence is what makes it a link rather than a coincidence.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Nephi went his way towards his own house, pondering upon the things which the Lord had shewn unto him.

And it came to pass as he was thus pondering,—being much cast down because of the wickedness of the people of the Nephites, their secret works of darkness, and their murderings, and their plunderings, and all manner of iniquities—and it came to pass as he was thus pondering in his heart, behold, a voice came unto him, saying:

links.text: But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.

provenance.other: The verb is nearly absent from the KJV. “pondered” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 2:19; the imperative 'ponder' occurs in two, Proverbs 4:26 and 5:6, both of paths rather than of sayings. There is no KJV 'pondering'. So the KJV's single instance of pondering something one has been told is Mary's.
provenance.significance: Nephi walks home 'pondering upon the things which the Lord had shewn unto him', then 'as he was thus pondering in his heart' a voice from heaven addresses him by name and calls him blessed. That is the shape of Luke 1-2 and not of any Old Testament call: Mary keeps the things she has been told and ponders them in her heart, and the words spoken over her are 'Blessed art thou among women'. The blessing formula arrives one verse later at 10:4, which is where the borrowing becomes hard to write off.

links.note: Two contacts, neither decisive alone: the rare verb, and the phrase 'in his heart' governing it. What raises it above coincidence is what stands next to it — the voice of 10:4 opens 'Blessed art thou, Nephi', and the KJV pairs pondering-in-the-heart with a 'Blessed art thou' address exactly once, in Luke's infancy narrative. 1830 reads 'shewn' at 10:2 where 1920 reads 'shown', keeping the KJV's orthography (CONVENTIONS §8).
links.whyNot: 'Ponder' is ordinary nineteenth-century English and needs no KJV source at all; the Book of Mormon uses it freely elsewhere. If the word came in from the language rather than the book, the Luke contact evaporates and only 'in his heart' is left, which is nothing.

pericopes.text: Blessed art thou, Nephi, for those things which thou hast done: for I have beheld how thou hast with unwearyingness declared the word which I have given unto thee, unto this people. And thou hast not feared them, and hast not sought thine own life, but hath sought my will, and to keep my commandments.

links.text: And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.

provenance.other: “Blessed art thou” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Psalm 119:12 (O LORD), Ecclesiastes 10:17 (O land), Luke 1:28 and 1:42 (among women), and Matthew 16:17. Matthew 16:17 is the only one of the five in which the formula is followed by a person's name.
provenance.significance: This is the first term of a three-verse sequence, and the sequence is the argument. Matthew 16 runs: 'Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona' (17) → 'thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church' (18) → 'I will give unto thee the keys … whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven' (19). Helaman 10 runs: 'Blessed art thou, Nephi' (4) → 'Behold, thou art Nephi, and I am God' (6) → 'whatsoever ye shall seal on earth, shall be sealed in heaven' (7). Three elements, same order, no other KJV passage containing any two of them. What the transfer does is worth saying: the naming clause is rewritten so that the answering half is not a new name for the man but the identity of the speaker — 'thou art Nephi, and I am God' — which removes the rock and the church and leaves the commission standing on the asymmetry between the two.

links.note: 'Blessed art thou, Nephi, for those things which thou hast done.' Taken alone this is a five-verse formula and would not be a link. It is a link because of what comes with it: the only KJV verse that addresses a named man as 'Blessed art thou' is the one that continues 'thou art Peter' and 'whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth', and Helaman 10:6 and 10:7 supply both continuations in Matthew's order. Adjudicated here as the head of the sequence; 10:7 carries the verbal case.

links.text: I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.

provenance.other: “mine own will” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 5:30 and John 6:38, and in both the clause is the same antithesis: not my own will, but the will of him that sent me. The Book of Mormon inverts the persons — the messenger is praised in the second person for not having sought his own — and substitutes 'life' for 'will' in the first limb while keeping 'will' in the second.
provenance.significance: The antithesis is the Johannine Son's self-description, and the voice that speaks it here speaks it about Nephi. Note also that the substitution is not idle: 'hast not sought thine own life' is what makes the formula fit a prophet standing in front of a crowd that will shortly try to imprison him (10:15), where 'own will' would not.

links.note: 'Thou hast not feared them, and hast not sought thine own life, but hath sought my will, and to keep my commandments.' The not-X-but-my-will construction is the Fourth Gospel's, twice, and nowhere else in the KJV. 1830's 'hath sought' — a plain grammatical slip that 1920 corrected to 'hast' — is worth recording here because it shows the clause being assembled rather than copied (CONVENTIONS §8).
links.whyNot: No phrase is reproduced. The shared material is a rhetorical shape plus the two words 'my will', and self-denial before God is common enough in scripture that a writer could reach this sentence without John.

pericopes.text: And now because thou hast done this with such unwearyingness, behold, I will bless thee forever; and I will make thee mighty in word and in deed, in faith and in works; yea, even that all things shall be done unto thee according to thy word, for thou shalt not ask that which is contrary to my will.

links.text: And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds.

provenance.other: The KJV has the collocation twice and in two orders. “mighty in words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:22, of Moses — 'mighty in words and in deeds'. “mighty in deed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:19, of Jesus — 'a prophet mighty in deed and word before God'. Helaman 10:5 reads 'mighty in word and in deed', which is Acts 7:22's order with Luke 24:19's singular nouns.
provenance.alternative: Luke 24:19, if the singulars are thought to weigh more than the order. The two verses are by the same author and the phrase is idiomatic to him; a case can be made either way, which is why the row records both.
provenance.significance: Word before deed is Moses's order, and Moses is who this promise is making Nephi into: the next verse gives him power to 'smite the earth with famine, and with pestilence', which is the Egyptian plague repertoire, and chapter 11 will have him shut the heavens. Stephen's speech is also the passage this catalogue keeps finding behind Nephite call narratives (see 1 Nephi 17:8's 'which I shall shew thee', Acts 7:3). The alternative order would make him a prophet like Jesus instead; the text as it stands chose Moses.

links.note: 'I will make thee mighty in word and in deed, in faith and in works.' The KJV supplies this collocation exactly twice, once of Moses and once of Jesus, and the two differ in the order of the nouns. The Book of Mormon has Moses's order. That is a small datum and it points the same way the rest of the chapter does.

links.text: If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you.

provenance.route: John 15:7 (+ 1 John 5:14 for the proviso) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “it shall be done unto” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Obadiah 1:15 (retribution, 'as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee') and John 15:7. Only John's is a promise about asking. The proviso attached to it in Helaman — that he will not ask contrary to God's will — is the qualification 1 John 5:14 puts on the same promise: 'if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us'.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's move is to make the Johannine safeguard structural rather than conditional. In 1 John the answer depends on whether the asking happens to accord with God's will; here God guarantees in advance that it will — 'for thou shalt not ask that which is contrary to my will' — which converts a condition on prayer into a description of a man. That is the theological content of the whole promise, and the two New Testament verses are what it is built out of.

links.note: 'All things shall be done unto thee according to thy word, for thou shalt not ask that which is contrary to my will.' The unlimited-asking promise and its will-of-God proviso are a recognizable Johannine pair (John 15:7, 15:16; 1 John 5:14), and the sentence has both halves in order. The verbal contact is short and the argument rests on the pairing rather than on any one phrase.

pericopes.text: Behold, thou art Nephi, and I am God. Behold, I declare it unto thee in the presence of mine angles, that ye shall have power over this people, and shall smite the earth with famine, and with pestilence, and destruction, according to the wickedness of this people.

links.text: These have power to shut heaven, that it rain not in the days of their prophecy: and have power over waters to turn them to blood, and to smite the earth with all plagues, as often as they will.

provenance.other: “smite the earth” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Isaiah 11:4 (with the rod of his mouth), Malachi 4:6 (with a curse), and Revelation 11:6. “have power over” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Esther 9:1, Daniel 11:43, and Revelation 11:6. Revelation 11:6 is the only KJV verse that has both, and it has them in Helaman 10:6's order — power over, then smite the earth with.
provenance.significance: Revelation 11:6 describes the two witnesses: 'These have power to shut heaven, that it rain not in the days of their prophecy: and have power over waters to turn them to blood, and to smite the earth with all plagues, as often as they will.' Helaman 10:6-7 gives Nephi that grant, and Helaman 11 spends it exactly as the verse specifies — at 11:4 he asks that the rain be withheld, at 11:5 a famine follows, at 11:17 he asks for the rain back. So the prophet who is being made into Moses in 10:5 is being equipped out of the Apocalypse, and the passage the equipment comes from is about two prophets whose city kills them and whose corpses lie in the street. That is a reading of Helaman 10:15-16, where the crowd tries to seize him and cannot.

links.note: 'Ye shall have power over this people, and shall smite the earth with famine, and with pestilence, and destruction.' Two three-verse KJV phrases meet in one verse of the KJV and in one verse of the Book of Mormon, in the same order. The confirmation is at one remove: the powers named in Revelation 11:6 that Helaman 10:6 does not list are the ones Nephi goes on to exercise in chapter 11.

links.text: Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth.

provenance.other: “presence of the angels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 15:10. The nearest competitor is Luke 12:8-9's 'before the angels of God'. The genitive that Helaman 10:6 actually has — 'in the presence of mine angels', with the first-person possessive — has no KJV parallel at all; the KJV's one 'in the presence of mine' is Psalm 23:5's 'mine enemies'.
provenance.significance: If the phrase is Luke's, the declaration is being made in the setting Luke reserves for joy over one sinner who repents — which is the errand Nephi is being sent on two verses later ('Except ye repent, ye shall be smitten'). The 1830 prints 'angles', a compositor's transposition corrected in 1920; it is worth noting because it shows the word was set from dictation or from a hand, not copied from a Bible page.

links.note: 'I declare it unto thee in the presence of mine angles.' Recorded rather than argued. The prepositional phrase is Lukan in the KJV and nowhere else, but the possessive that makes Helaman's version distinctive is not in the KJV at all, so the borrowing, if there is one, has been reworked past the point where it can be demonstrated.
links.whyNot: 'In the presence of' is among the commonest prepositional phrases in the KJV (Genesis 23:11, Psalm 23:5 and dozens more), and angels attending a divine declaration is a scriptural commonplace requiring no particular source. The only distinctive element — 'mine angels' — is precisely the element the KJV does not have.

pericopes.text: Behold, I give unto you power, that whatsoever ye shall seal on earth, shall be sealed in heaven; and whatsoever ye shall loose on earth, shall be loosed in heaven; and thus shall ye have power among this people.

links.text: Verily I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever ye shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.

provenance.route: Matthew 18:18 (wording and number) + Matthew 16:19 (setting) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “loosed in heaven” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 16:19 and Matthew 18:18, and they differ in exactly one respect that matters here: 16:19 is singular throughout ('whatsoever THOU shalt bind … THOU shalt loose'), 18:18 plural ('whatsoever YE shall bind … YE shall loose'). Helaman 10:7 is plural — 'whatsoever ye shall seal … whatsoever ye shall loose' — and so reproduces Matthew 18:18's pronoun, not Matthew 16:19's, in a speech addressed to one man. The opening clause is a third verse again: “Behold, I give unto you power” is Luke 10:19's, the commission of the seventy.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 16:19 alone, which is the passage the surrounding verses are following (see 10:4). The pronoun rules it out as the source of this verse's wording while leaving it as the source of its setting.
provenance.significance: The one word that is not the KJV's is the one the passage exists to change: 'bind' becomes 'seal', in both verbs' first limb, while 'loose' is kept. Bind/loose is a matched pair of rabbinic legal verbs; seal/loose is not a pair at all, and the substitution pulls the grant out of the courtroom and into the language of documents and covenants. Recover Matthew 18 and the context sharpens it further — 18:18's promise is given to a congregation that has just been told how to expel an unrepentant member (18:15-17), which is the situation Nephi is in from 10:11 onward. The reader who follows the echo home finds a text about a community's power over its own impenitent.

links.note: Fourteen consecutive words of Matthew 18:18 with one substitution ('seal' for 'bind') and one omission. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for his KJV-quotation list, so this is not one of his 36; it is catalogued as a quotation on CONVENTIONS §2's grounds, since a clause is reproduced from an identifiable verse. The mediation datum is the pronoun: the frame around this verse is Matthew 16's singular address to a named man (10:4, 10:6), but the clause itself is Matthew 18's plural, and the Book of Mormon keeps the plural even though its speaker is addressing one person.

pericopes.text: And thus, if ye shall say unto this temple, It shall be rent in twain, and it shall be done.

links.text: And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;

provenance.route: Matthew 27:51 / Mark 15:38 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “rent in twain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 27:51 and Mark 15:38, and both are the same event: the veil of the temple at the moment of the crucifixion. Luke's parallel at 23:45 avoids the phrase ('rent in the midst'). There is no KJV instance of the phrase applied to anything but that veil.
provenance.significance: Nephi is given power to say to a temple the two words the King James Bible says about a temple exactly once, and the once is Golgotha. The metalepsis is unusually clean because the borrowing is anticipatory in the text's own chronology: what Nephi could do by a word, God will do at the death of Christ, and 3 Nephi 8 will report the fulfilment. The sentence is also the first of the three impossibilities of 10:8-10, and it is the only one not drawn from the Gospel faith-sayings — the mountain and the smiting come from Matthew 21:21 (see 10:9). This one comes from the passion narrative, which is a different kind of borrowing lodged inside a series of the other kind.

links.note: 'If ye shall say unto this temple, It shall be rent in twain, and it shall be done.' The frame is Matthew 21:21's (see the following verse); the content of the impossibility is not. 'Rent in twain' belongs to one event in the KJV, and the object it belongs to is a temple, which is the object here. The 1830 keeps a conjunction ('and it shall be done') that 1920 deletes in both 10:8 and 10:9, restoring Matthew 21:21's asyndeton — a change away from the running text and toward the source.

pericopes.text: And if ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou cast down and become smooth, and it shall be done.

links.text: Jesus answered and said unto them, Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith, and doubt not, ye shall not only do this which is done to the fig tree, but also if ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; it shall be done.

provenance.route: Matthew 21:21 (frame) + Luke 3:5 (the levelling word) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “if ye shall say unto this mountain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 21:21. The saying exists in three KJV forms and the pronouns separate them: Matthew 17:20 'ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence'; Mark 11:23 'whosoever shall say unto this mountain'; Matthew 21:21 'if ye shall say unto this mountain'. The Book of Mormon has Matthew 21:21's conditional-plural, and closes with that verse's 'it shall be done' rather than Mark's 'he shall have whatsoever he saith'.
provenance.alternative: Mark 11:23, which the n-gram stream ranked second here. It shares 'say unto this mountain, Be thou' but not the conditional, and its apodosis is different.
provenance.significance: Where Matthew's mountain is 'removed' and 'cast into the sea', Helaman's is 'cast down and become smooth' — and that second verb is the one place the sentence leaves Matthew. mediation-check.py returns a decisive result for Luke 3:5 over Isaiah 40:4 on it: Isaiah 40:4 levels the ground into 'plain', Luke 3:5 renders the same prophecy 'the rough ways shall be made smooth', and “made smooth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 3:5. The backbone under that verdict is thin — Helaman shares only 'mountain' and 'smooth' with either verse, and the seven words the tool counts are shared between Isaiah and Luke rather than with the Book of Mormon — so it is offered as a secondary contact, not as the verse's source. What it suggests is that the faith-saying has been finished with the Baptist's levelling prophecy in its Lukan form. The catalogue adjudicated that same Isaiah-via-Luke 'smooth' at 1 Nephi 17:46.
provenance.mt: Isaiah 40:4 — 'and the rough places plain', against Luke 3:5's 'the rough ways shall be made smooth'.

links.note: Six consecutive words of Matthew 21:21, from the only KJV verse that has them, closing with that verse's apodosis. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and so not one of his 36. The interest is in the one clause that is not Matthew's: 'become smooth', where the levelling vocabulary is Luke 3:5's rendering of Isaiah 40:4 rather than Isaiah's own.

pericopes.text: And behold, if ye shall say, That God shall smite this people, it shall come to pass.—
And now behold, I command you that ye shall go and declare unto this people, that thus saith the Lord God, who is the Almighty: Except ye repent, ye shall be smitten, even unto destruction.

And behold, now it came to pass that when the Lord had spoken these words unto Nephi, he did stop, and did not go unto his own house, but did return unto the multitudes which were scattered about upon the face of the land, and began to declare unto them the word of the Lord, which had been spoken unto him concerning their destruction, if they did not repent.

Now behold, notwithstanding that great miracle which Nephi had done in telling them concerning the death of the Chief Judge, they did harden their hearts, and did not hearken unto the words of the Lord;
therefore Nephi did declare unto them the word of the Lord, saying: Except ye repent, thus saith the Lord: Ye shall be smitten even unto destruction.—

And it came to pass that when Nephi had declared unto them the word, behold, they did still harden their hearts, and would not hearken unto his words; therefore they did revile against him, and did seek to lay their hands upon him, that they might cast him into prison.
But behold, the power of God was with him, and they could not take him to cast him into prison: for he was taken by the spirit, and conveyed away out of the midst of them.

links.text: And he that was healed wist not who it was: for Jesus had conveyed himself away, a multitude being in that place.

provenance.route: John 5:13 (the verb) + Acts 8:39-40 (the mode and its sequel) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “conveyed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 5:13 — 'for Jesus had conveyed himself away, a multitude being in that place'. The Book of Mormon's 'conveyed away out of the midst of them' has the KJV's single instance of the verb in the KJV's own sense, escape from a crowd, and adds the adverb the KJV attaches to it. Separately, “caught away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:39, where the Spirit of the Lord removes Philip from the road.
provenance.significance: Two rare KJV escapes are being used at once and they do different work. John 5:13 supplies the word and the situation — a multitude, and a man who is simply not there any more. Acts 8:39-40 supplies the mechanism and the consequence: Philip is carried off by the Spirit and is next found 'preaching in all the cities'. Helaman 10:17 is that sequel verbatim in substance — 'he did go forth in the spirit, from multitude to multitude, declaring the word of God'. So the verse is a Johannine disappearance completed by a Lukan itinerary, and the crowd that could not take him is left, as in John 7:44-46, holding nothing.

links.note: 'They could not take him to cast him into prison: for he was taken by the spirit, and conveyed away out of the midst of them.' The KJV uses 'convey' once in all sixty-six books, of Jesus slipping away from a crowd; the Book of Mormon uses it here, of a prophet slipping away from a crowd. The next verse then supplies Philip's sequel. Note that the failed arrest ('they could not take him') closes the John 7 frame opened at 10:1.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that thus he did go forth in the spirit, from multitude to multitude, declaring the word of God, even until he had declared it unto them all, or sent it forth among all the people.
And it came to pass that they would not hearken unto his words; and there began to be contentions, insomuch that they were divided against themselves, and began to slay one another with the sword.

links.text: And if a kingdom be divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.

provenance.route: Mark 3:24-25 / Matthew 12:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “divided against” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses. Six of the seven are the Beelzebub saying in its three Synoptic forms (Matthew 12:25, 12:26; Mark 3:24, 3:25; Luke 11:17, 11:18); the seventh is Luke 12:53, the household divided by the gospel. The reflexive plural Helaman has, 'divided against themselves', is in none of them — the KJV's forms are 'against itself' and 'against himself'.
provenance.significance: The Beelzebub saying's point is that a kingdom so divided 'cannot stand', and the Book of Mormon supplies the consequence the saying withholds: they 'began to slay one another with the sword'. Read with 10:1, the chapter is framed by two divisions — John 7:43's division over a prophet's words at the beginning, and the Synoptic kingdom-divided at the end — and the second is what the first becomes when the words are refused.

links.note: 'They were divided against themselves, and began to slay one another with the sword.' The idiom is the Gospels' and effectively only the Gospels', though the Book of Mormon's reflexive plural matches no single verse. Recorded because the chapter's closing sentence is doing with the phrase what the Synoptic saying says it does — a divided house falls.
links.whyNot: 'Divided against' is available as plain English and the exact form here is in no KJV verse, so the link rests on a distribution rather than on a string. A reader could reasonably say the Book of Mormon simply describes a civil war.

pericopes.text: And thus ended the seventy and first year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.

And now it came to pass in the seventy and second year of the reign of the Judges, that the contentions did increase, insomuch that there were wars throughout all the land, among all the people of Nephi.
And it was this secret band of robbers which did carry on this work of destruction and wickedness. And this war did last all that year. And in the seventy and third year it did also last.
And it came to pass that in this year, Nephi did cry unto the Lord, saying:

O Lord, do not suffer that this people shall be destroyed by the sword; but O Lord, rather let there be a famine in the land, to stir them up in remembrance of the Lord their God, and perhaps they will repent and turn unto thee;

links.text: So Gad came to David, and told him, and said unto him, Shall seven years of famine come unto thee in thy land? or wilt thou flee three months before thine enemies, while they pursue thee? or that there be three days’ pestilence in thy land? now advise, and see what answer I shall return to him that sent me.

provenance.route: 2 Samuel 24:13-14 → Book of Mormon (form, not wording)
provenance.other: No clause is shared. The three scourges named — famine, the sword or enemies, and pestilence — are the Jeremian triad, and “the famine and the pestilence” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 24:10 and 29:17, both of which read 'the sword, the famine, and the pestilence'.
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly one scene in which a man is put to choosing among the three scourges: Gad offers David famine, flight before enemies, or pestilence, and David answers 'let us fall now into the hand of the LORD; for his mercies are great: and let me not fall into the hand of man.' Helaman 11:4 makes the same election and gives the same reason in different words — not the sword (which is the hand of man, wielded here by the Gadianton band) but famine, because famine will 'stir them up in remembrance of the Lord their God'. The transposition is that David chooses a punishment for a sin he has committed, while Nephi chooses one for a people who have not yet repented; the mercy David trusts is the mercy Nephi is counting on to work backwards, as a means of repentance rather than a mitigation of sentence.

links.note: 'Do not suffer that this people shall be destroyed by the sword; but O Lord, rather let there be a famine in the land.' No wording is borrowed and the link is offered on form alone: the sword-or-famine election belongs to one biblical episode, and the reason given for the choice is David's reason. Filed as figural for that reason, at moderate rather than higher, since the triad of scourges was available to any reader of Jeremiah without David's scene attached to it.

pericopes.text: and so it was done, according to the words of Nephi.— And there was a great famine upon the land, among all the people of Nephi. And thus, in the seventy and fourth year, the famine did continue, and the work of destruction did cease by the sword, but became sore by famine.

links.text: And Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead, said unto Ahab, As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.

provenance.other: “according to my word” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 17:1, where it is Elijah's claim that the drought he has just announced will end only at his say-so. Helaman 11:5 has 'according to the words of Nephi' and Helaman 11:13 has 'according to my words'; the singular-to-plural shift is the only change. The KJV has no other instance of a drought or famine made contingent on a named man's word.
provenance.significance: This is the head of the chapter's controlling borrowing, and it should be read against Helaman 10:6. There the grant came out of Revelation 11:6, where the two witnesses 'have power to shut heaven, that it rain not in the days of their prophecy' — a verse that is itself the Apocalypse's compression of Elijah. Helaman 11 then spends the grant in Elijah's own terms: withheld rain at the prophet's word (11:5, from 1 Kings 17:1), the widow's confession that he is a man of God (11:8, from 1 Kings 17:24), the promise to send rain upon the earth (11:13, from 1 Kings 18:1), and the fulfilment (11:17). So chapter 10 licenses the prophet from Revelation and chapter 11 performs him from Kings, which is a two-stage borrowing the reader can only see by reading both chapters.

links.note: 'And so it was done, according to the words of Nephi. And there was a great famine upon the land.' The one KJV verse in which weather is made contingent on a prophet's word is Elijah's oath before Ahab, and the Book of Mormon reproduces the operative phrase. Everything else in the chapter's drought sequence comes from the same two chapters of Kings.

pericopes.text: And this work of destruction did also continue in the seventy and fifth year. For the earth was smitten, that it was dry, and did not yield forth grain in the season of grain; and the whole earth was smitten, even among the Lamanites as well as among the Nephites, so that they were smitten that they did perish by thousands, in the more wicked parts of the land.
And it came to pass that the people saw that they were about to perish by famine, and they began to remember the Lord their God; and they began to remember the words of Nephi.

And the people began to plead with their Chief Judges and their leaders, that they would say unto Nephi, Behold, we know that thou art a man of God, and therefore cry unto the Lord our God, that he turn away from us this famine, lest all the words which thou hast spoken concerning our destruction, be fulfilled.

links.text: And the woman said to Elijah, Now by this I know that thou art a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in thy mouth is truth.

provenance.other: “thou art a man of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 17:24. 'A man of God' by itself occurs in ten, but only here is it a second-person confession, and only here does the confession carry the clause the Book of Mormon also has — 'Now by this I know that thou art a man of God' against 'Behold, we know that thou art a man of God'.
provenance.significance: The speaker in 1 Kings is the widow of Zarephath, and what she is confessing is that a prophet who brought a famine can be trusted about life — she says it over her son restored. Helaman 11:8 puts the same nine words in the mouth of a starving nation asking that prophet to lift the famine he called down. The metalepsis is that the widow's clause continues 'and that the word of the LORD in thy mouth is truth', which is exactly what the Nephites go on to say in their own idiom: 'lest all the words which thou hast spoken concerning our destruction, be fulfilled.' They concede the truth of the word in order to ask that it not be kept.

links.note: Nine consecutive words, from the only KJV verse that has them, spoken in the same situation — a famine called down by a prophet, and a confession made to him about it. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and so not among his 36; a quotation on CONVENTIONS §2's grounds, since a whole clause is reproduced from an identifiable verse. The machine ranked it, at a nine-word longest run, and it is the highest-value candidate in the dossier for this chapter.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Judges did say unto Nephi, according to the words which had been desired.— And it came to pass that when Nephi saw that the people had repented, and did humble themselves in sackcloth, he cried again unto the Lord, saying:

O Lord, behold this people repenteth; and they have swept away the band of Gadianton from amongst them, insomuch that they have become extinct, and they have concealed their secret plans in the earth.
Now, O Lord, because of this their humility, wilt thou turn away thine anger, and let thine anger be appeased in the destruction of those wicked men whom thou hast already destroyed?
O Lord, wilt thou turn away thine anger, yea, thy fierce anger, and cause that this famine may cease in this land?

links.text: Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?

provenance.other: “turn away from his fierce anger” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:9. 'Fierce anger' alone occurs in twenty, mostly Jeremiah, but nowhere else in the KJV is it the object of 'turn away' in a plea that the threatened destruction be withdrawn. The Book of Mormon asks it three times — 11:11, 11:12 and 11:16 — with 'thy fierce anger' at 11:12.
provenance.significance: The whole episode is Jonah 3 with the prophet's temper reversed. Nineveh's king proclaims a fast and sackcloth; Helaman 11:9 has the people 'humble themselves in sackcloth'. Nineveh asks 'who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?'; Nephi asks 'wilt thou turn away thine anger, yea, thy fierce anger?'. Jonah 3:10 grants it, and Helaman 11:17 grants it. What the borrowing changes is the intercessor: in Jonah the prophet is angry that the city is spared, and here the prophet is the one asking, having called the calamity down himself in order to produce exactly this repentance. Helaman 11:16 — 'try again if they will serve thee' — is the sentence Jonah could not say.

links.note: 'Wilt thou turn away thine anger, yea, thy fierce anger, and cause that this famine may cease in this land?' The clause is Nineveh's from the one KJV verse that has it, and the sackcloth three verses earlier is Nineveh's too. Adjudicated here rather than at 11:11 because 11:12 is where 'fierce' appears; 11:11 and 11:16 are the same prayer repeated and are recorded as recurrences.

pericopes.text: O Lord, wilt thou hearken unto me, and cause that it may be done according to my words, and send forth rain upon the face of the earth, that she may bring forth her fruit and her grain, in the season of grain?

links.text: And it came to pass after many days, that the word of the LORD came to Elijah in the third year, saying, Go, shew thyself unto Ahab; and I will send rain upon the earth.

provenance.route: 1 Kings 18:1 (the rain) + 1 Kings 17:1 (the word) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “send rain upon the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 18:1 — the word of the LORD to Elijah in the third year of the drought, 'Go, shew thyself unto Ahab; and I will send rain upon the earth'. The looser 'rain upon the earth' occurs in five (Genesis 2:5, 7:4, 1 Kings 17:14, 18:1, Job 5:10), and only 1 Kings 18:1 has the verb. Helaman 11:13 reads 'send forth rain upon the face of the earth'.
provenance.alternative: James 5:17, the New Testament's summary of the same drought. mediation-check.py returns 1 decisive point for 1 Kings 17:1 over James 5:17 on this verse — the Book of Mormon has 'according to my word(s)', which is Kings's phrase and has no counterpart in James. The backbone under that verdict is one word ('years'), so it is thin; but the phrase it turns on is a KJV singleton, which is the kind of evidence a thin backbone does not weaken.
provenance.significance: The direction of the borrowing is worth naming. In 1 Kings 18:1 God tells Elijah he will send rain; here Nephi asks God to send it. The Book of Mormon has consistently moved the initiative to the prophet across this chapter — Elijah announces a drought God has decided on, Nephi requests one (11:4) — and this verse completes the pattern by turning God's promise into the prophet's petition. The petition is then granted at 11:17 in the New Testament's words rather than in Kings's, which is the finding recorded there.

links.note: Two Elijah phrases in one sentence, both from the drought cycle: the rain of 1 Kings 18:1 and the 'according to my word' of 1 Kings 17:1, which Helaman pluralizes. The mediation test against James 5:17 comes out for Kings here, and comes out for James four verses later — see 11:17.

pericopes.text: O Lord, thou didst hearken unto my words when I said, Let there be a famine, that the pestilence of the sword might cease; and I know that thou wilt, even at this time, hearken unto my words: for thou saidst, That if this people repent, I will spare them;
yea, O Lord, and thou seest that they have repented, because of the famine, and the pestilence and destruction which has come unto them.

links.text: Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Behold, I will send upon them the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, and will make them like vile figs, that cannot be eaten, they are so evil.

provenance.other: “the famine and the pestilence” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 24:10 and 29:17, and in both it is the tail of the fixed triad 'the sword, the famine, and the pestilence'. Helaman 11:15 has 'the famine, and the pestilence and destruction', substituting the Book of Mormon's own third term for the KJV's first.
provenance.significance: The chapter takes the Jeremian triad apart and reassembles it, and the seam shows at 11:14, where Nephi says he asked for a famine 'that the pestilence of the sword might cease'. 'Pestilence of the sword' is not a KJV phrase and not an English one: it is two members of the triad fused, the sword having been renamed with the noun that stood beside it. Read alongside 11:4, where the sword is traded for the famine, the chapter's argument is that the three scourges are interchangeable currency, which is precisely what Jeremiah's fixed formula assumes and never says.

links.note: The triad is formulaic in Jeremiah and would not on its own be a link. What makes it worth a row is 11:14's 'the pestilence of the sword', a fusion that only makes sense if the three terms were present together as a set, and the substitution here of 'destruction' for 'the sword' in the same set.
links.whyNot: Sword, famine and pestilence appear together some twenty times in Jeremiah and Ezekiel; no particular verse can be identified, and the Book of Mormon may simply have absorbed the formula rather than any occurrence of it.

pericopes.text: And now, O Lord, wilt thou turn away thine anger, and try again if they will serve thee? And if so, O Lord, thou canst bless them according to thy words which thou hast said.

And it came to pass that in the seventy and sixth year, the Lord did turn away his anger from the people, and caused that rain should fall upon the earth, insomuch that it did bring forth her fruit in the season of her fruit. And it came to pass that it did bring forth her grain, in the season of her grain.

links.text: And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth brought forth her fruit.

provenance.route: 1 Kings 17-18 via James 5:17-18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Both halves of James 5:18 are KJV singletons: “the heaven gave rain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “brought forth her fruit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both James 5:18. Helaman 11:13 asks that the earth 'may bring forth her fruit', and 11:17 reports that 'it did bring forth her fruit in the season of her fruit' — the feminine possessive included, which is what makes the contact specific rather than generic. 1 Kings 18:45, the narrative fulfilment in Kings, has no fruit and no earth: 'the heaven was black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain'.
provenance.alternative: 1 Kings 18:45. mediation-check.py returns divergences pointing both ways here, and the split is instructive rather than genuinely balanced. The one decisive point it scores for Kings is 'it came to pass in the mean while that' against James's 'he prayed again and' — but 'and it came to pass' is the Book of Mormon's own universal connective, present in something like a third of its verses, so the tool is matching Nephite boilerplate rather than Elijah. The point scored for James rests on a KJV singleton. Weighed rather than counted, this verse is James's.
provenance.significance: Chapter 11 is structurally James 5:17-18 and not 1 Kings: prophet prays that it not rain (11:4), it does not rain, 'he cried AGAIN unto the Lord' (11:9, against James's 'he prayed again'), and the earth brings forth her fruit (11:17). James is the only place in the Bible where the Elijah drought is told as a two-prayer sequence, because James is telling it to make a point about the prayer of a righteous man availing much (5:16) — which is the point of Helaman 11 and is not the point of 1 Kings 17-18, where Elijah's second prayer is a posture on Carmel and the narrative interest is the contest with Baal. So the chapter's frame is the epistle's compression, filled in with wording from Kings at 11:5, 11:8 and 11:13. Note also what James supplies that Kings does not: the phrase 'the earth brought forth her fruit', which is why Helaman's earth is a 'she'.

links.note: 'The Lord did turn away his anger from the people, and caused that rain should fall upon the earth, insomuch that it did bring forth her fruit in the season of her fruit.' The fulfilment is told in James's words, not Kings's — Kings's rain scene has clouds, wind and Ahab riding to Jezreel, and no fruit at all. The mediation test splits, and the note above says why the split resolves for James: the tool's vote for Kings is a match on 'it came to pass', which is Mormon's connective and not a borrowing from anywhere.

pericopes.text: And behold, the people did rejoice, and glorify God; and the whole face of the land was filled with rejoicing; and they did no more seek to destroy Nephi, but they did esteem him as a great prophet, and a man of God, having great power and authority given unto him from God.

links.text: And there came a fear on all: and they glorified God, saying, That a great prophet is risen up among us; and, That God hath visited his people.

provenance.other: “a great prophet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 7:16, and that same verse also supplies the crowd's reaction the Book of Mormon puts beside it: 'they glorified God, saying, That a great prophet is risen up among us'. Helaman 11:18 has 'the people did rejoice, and glorify God … and they did esteem him as a great prophet'. Two elements, one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Luke 7:16 is the crowd at Nain, after Jesus raises the widow's son. That is the same episode 1 Kings 17:24 belongs to at the other end of the borrowing — the widow's son restored, and the woman's confession 'thou art a man of God' — and Luke has deliberately written Nain as an Elijah scene. Helaman 11 takes the widow's confession at 11:8 and the crowd's acclamation at 11:18 and puts them ten verses apart around the same prophet, which is what Luke does with them across a single pericope. The Book of Mormon's addition, 'and a man of God', joins the two verses explicitly.

links.note: 'The people did rejoice, and glorify God … they did esteem him as a great prophet, and a man of God.' The KJV's one 'great prophet' is Luke 7:16, and it comes with the glorifying already attached; the trailing 'man of God' returns to 1 Kings 17:24, quoted at 11:8. Whether or not the writer knew that Luke 7 is itself modelled on 1 Kings 17, the two verses have arrived here together.

pericopes.text: And behold, Lehi, his brother, was not a whit behind him as to things pertaining to righteousness.

links.text: For I suppose I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles.

provenance.other: “not a whit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 11:5 — 'For I suppose I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles'. The idiom appears nowhere else in the King James Bible in any form, and Paul's own restatement at 12:11 drops it ('in nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles'). Helaman 11:19 reads 'was not a whit behind him', reproducing the whole idiom including the preposition. The 1830 and 1920 texts are identical here.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a defence of his own standing against apostles he will not name; the Book of Mormon makes it a narrator's compliment paid by one brother to another, and in doing so removes the sting the phrase carries in Paul, where 'I suppose' is doing heavy ironic work. It is also worth noting what the borrowing measures: Paul's comparison is with 'the very chiefest apostles', and Lehi's is with Nephi, which quietly puts Nephi in that class. The catalogue would not press the point except that Helaman 10:7 has already given Nephi the sealing keys of Matthew 16:19.
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 12:11, if the sense rather than the idiom is thought decisive; but the idiom is what Helaman 11:19 actually has.

links.note: A four-word English idiom that occurs once in the KJV, reproduced whole with its preposition. This is as clean a borrowing as the chapter contains and it is doing no thematic work at all — which is itself the finding, since a phrase used simply because it was available says something about how the text's English was assembled.

pericopes.text: And thus it did come to pass that the people of Nephi began to prosper again in the land, and began to build up their waste places, and began to multiply and spread, even until they did cover the whole face of the land, both on the northward and on the southward, from the sea west, to the sea east.

links.text: And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.

provenance.other: “waste places” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all in Isaiah (5:17, 51:3, 52:9, 58:12), and “build the old waste places” occurs in exactly one, Isaiah 58:12. Helaman 11:20 reads 'began to build up their waste places'. Isaiah 61:4 has the same promise with different nouns ('they shall build the old wastes').
provenance.significance: Isaiah 58 is the fast chapter — the fast God chooses is to loose the bands of wickedness and deal bread to the hungry — and its promise of rebuilt waste places is the reward for that fast. Helaman 11 has just come through a famine ended by a people who 'humble themselves in sackcloth' (11:9), which is the fast Isaiah 58:5 dismisses as insufficient. The Book of Mormon gives them Isaiah 58:12's reward anyway, which is either a reading of the chapter or an unwitting collision with it; the note declines to decide.

links.note: 'They began to build up their waste places, and began to multiply and spread.' The phrase is Isaiah's exclusively, and Isaiah 58:12 is the only verse in which it is the object of 'build'. Moderate rather than high because 'waste places' is a natural English phrase for ruined country and the Book of Mormon adds 'up' and drops 'old'.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the seventy and sixth year did end in peace. And the seventy and seventh year began in peace; and the church did spread throughout the face of all the land; and the more part of the people, both the Nephites and the Lamanites, did belong to the church; and they did have exceeding great peace in the land. And thus ended the seventy and seventh year.
And also they had peace in the seventy and eighth year, save it were a few contentions concerning the points of doctrine which had been laid down by the prophets.

And in the seventy and ninth year, there began to be much strife. But it came to pass that Nephi and Lehi, and many of their brethren, which knew concerning the true points of doctrine, having many revelations daily, therefore they did preach unto the people, insomuch that they did put an end to their strife in that same year.

And it came to pass that in the eightieth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi, there were a certain number of the dissenters from the people of Nephi, which had some years before gone over unto the Lamanites, and took upon themselves the name of Lamanites; and also, a certain number which were real descendants of the Lamanites, being stirred up to anger by them, or by those dissenters, therefore they commenced a war with their brethren.

And they did commit murder and plunder; and then they would retreat back into the mountains, and into the wilderness and secret places, hiding themselves that they could not be discovered, receiving daily an addition to their numbers, inasmuch as there were dissenters that went forth unto them;

and thus in time, yea, even in the space of not many years, they became an exceeding great band of robbers; and they did search out all the secret plans of Gadianton; and thus they became robbers of Gadianton.
Now behold, these robbers did make great havoc, yea, even great destruction among the people of Nephi, and also among the people of the Lamanites.

links.text: As for Saul, he made havock of the church, entering into every house, and haling men and women committed them to prison.

provenance.other: “havock” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:3, of Saul persecuting the church; the word occurs nowhere else in the King James Bible in any spelling. The Book of Mormon has 'did make great havoc', modernizing the -ck. Both 1830 and 1920 print 'havoc'.
provenance.significance: Acts 8 is the chapter these two Helaman chapters keep returning to. Helaman 10:16-17 has Nephi taken by the Spirit and set down preaching from multitude to multitude, which is Philip at Acts 8:39-40; Helaman 10:15 has a crowd trying to put him in prison, which is what Acts 8:3 says Saul did with men and women; and now the robbers 'make great havoc' in Saul's word. Whether or not any one of these is deliberate, one short chapter of Acts is supplying vocabulary at three points in a row.

links.note: A KJV hapax reused. On its own this would be a weak row — 'havoc' is ordinary English and the Book of Mormon has dropped the King James spelling, which is the usual sign that a word came in from the language rather than from the page. It is recorded because of company: Acts 8 has already furnished Helaman 10:16-17 with Philip's translation by the Spirit and his subsequent circuit of preaching.
links.whyNot: 'Make havoc' was current English in 1829 and needed no biblical source; the modernized spelling weakens rather than supports a KJV route; and the sense is opposite in agent — Saul persecutes the church, the Gadianton robbers plunder a nation.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that it was expedient that there should be a stop put to this work of destruction; therefore they sent an army of strong men into the wilderness, and upon the mountains, to search out this band of robbers, and to destroy them.
But behold, it came to pass that in that same year, they were driven back even into their own lands. And thus ended the eightieth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.
And it came to pass in the commencement of the eighty and first year, they did go forth again against this band of robbers, and did destroy many; and they were also visited with much destruction;

and they were again obliged to return out of the wilderness, and out of the mountains, unto their own lands, because of the exceeding greatness of the numbers of those robbers which infested the mountains and the wilderness.—

And it came to pass that thus ended this year. And the robbers did still increase and wax strong, insomuch that they did defy the whole armies of the Nephites, and also of the Lamanites; and they did cause great fear to come unto the people, upon all the face of the land;

yea, for they did visit many parts of the land, and did do great destruction unto them; yea, did kill many, and did carry away others captive into the wilderness; yea, and more especially their women and their children.
Now this great evil, which came unto the people because of their iniquity, did stir them up again in remembrance of the Lord their God.
And thus ended the eighty and first year of the reign of the Judges.

And in the eighty and second year, they began again to forget the Lord their God. And in the eighty and third year, they began to wax strong in iniquity.— And in the eighty and fourth year, they did not mend their ways.
And it came to pass in the eighty and fifth year, they did wax stronger and stronger in their pride, and in their wickedness; and thus they were ripening again for destruction.
And thus ended the eighty and fifth year.

And thus we can behold how false, and also the unsteadiness of the hearts of the children of men; yea, we can see that the Lord in his great infinite goodness, doth bless and prosper those who put their trust in him;

yea, and we may see at the very time when he doth prosper his people; yea, in the increase of their fields, their flocks, and their herds, and in gold, and in silver, and in all manner of precious things of every kind and art; sparing their lives, and delivering them out of the hands of their enemies; softening the hearts of their enemies, that they should not declare wars against them; yea, and in fine, doing all things for the welfare and happiness of his people; yea, then is the time that they do harden their hearts, and do forget the Lord their God, and do trample under their feet the Holy One; yea, and this because of their ease, and their exceeding great prosperity.

links.text: And when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, and thy silver and thy gold is multiplied, and all that thou hast is multiplied;

provenance.other: Three separate counts converge on one paragraph of Deuteronomy. “thy flocks multiply” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 8:13, which is also the KJV's inventory of prosperity — herds, flocks, silver, gold — and Helaman 12:2 has the same four in the same pairs ('their flocks, and their herds, and in gold, and in silver'). “thine heart be lifted up” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 8:14, and Helaman 12:5 has 'how quick to be lifted up in pride'. “forget the Lord thy God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 8:14 and 8:19, and Helaman 12:2 has 'do forget the Lord their God'.
provenance.significance: This is the passage the Book of Mormon's whole cyclical philosophy of history is built out of, and it is worth saying that it is one paragraph rather than a general biblical atmosphere. Deuteronomy 8:11-17 gives the sequence exactly as Helaman 12:2 gives it: eat and be full, build houses, multiply herds and flocks and silver and gold, and then — 'then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God'. Mormon's contribution is the word 'then' made explicit and temporal: 'yea, then is the time that they do harden their hearts'. Where Moses warns a people about a danger, Mormon reports it as a law that has already operated, which is what turns a paranesis into a theory of history. Deuteronomy 8:17's 'My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth' is the sentence Helaman 12:2 replaces with 'their ease, and their exceeding great prosperity'.

links.note: 'In the increase of their fields, their flocks, and their herds, and in gold, and in silver … yea, then is the time that they do harden their hearts, and do forget the Lord their God.' Deuteronomy 8:13-14 in order, with two KJV singletons inside it and the third element ('lifted up') three verses later at 12:5. Nothing else in the KJV runs prosperity → forgetting in this vocabulary.

links.text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.

provenance.other: “trample them under their feet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:6, and so does the shorter “under their feet”; the KJV's other three uses of 'trample' are 'under feet' (Psalm 91:13) and 'in my fury' (Isaiah 63:3). Helaman 12:2 reads 'trample under their feet the Holy One'. The object matters as much as the verb: the thing trampled in Matthew 7:6 is 'that which is holy', a phrase occurring in exactly two KJV verses.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:6 is about giving holy things to those who will not know what they are: pearls before swine, and holy things to dogs, who trample them and turn and rend the giver. Helaman 12:2 puts the Holy One himself in the place of the trampled holy thing, so that the people who have been given prosperity are the dogs of the saying. That reading is available only by recovering the source — nothing in Helaman 12 mentions dogs or swine — and it sharpens the preceding clause, since the list of gifts in 12:2 is precisely a list of holy things given to people who will not know what they are.

links.note: 'They do trample under their feet the Holy One.' Five words from the KJV's only instance of the phrase, with the source verse's object ('that which is holy') converted into a person. The Book of Mormon uses 'trample under their feet' elsewhere; this is the Helaman occurrence and the argument is made here.

pericopes.text: And thus we see, that except the Lord doth chasten his people with many afflictions, yea, except he doth visit them with death, and with terror, and with famine, and with all manner of pestilences, they will not remember him.

links.text: And when the LORD raised them up judges, then the LORD was with the judge, and delivered them out of the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge: for it repented the LORD because of their groanings by reason of them that oppressed them and vexed them.

provenance.route: Judges 2:14-19 → Book of Mormon (structure, with one phrase)
provenance.other: “hands of their enemies” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 2:14; the singular “out of the hand of their enemies” occurs in exactly two, Judges 2:18 and Nehemiah 9:27, both of them statements of the deliverance cycle. Helaman 12:2 has 'delivering them out of the hands of their enemies', which is Judges 2:18's clause with Judges 2:14's plural noun.
provenance.significance: Judges 2:14-19 is the Old Testament's one explicit statement that the cycle repeats: God sells them into the hands of their enemies, raises a judge, delivers them out of the hand of their enemies, and 'when the judge was dead … they returned, and corrupted themselves more than their fathers'. Helaman 12:1-3 states the same law in the same order and adds the theological conclusion Judges leaves implicit — that the affliction is not merely punitive but is the only instrument that works: 'except the Lord doth chasten his people with many afflictions … they will not remember him.' Note the setting: Helaman's own chapters are dated by the reign of the judges, and the chapter that states the Judges cycle is the summary of a book of Nephite judges. Whether that is design or coincidence, it is the right frame in which to read the borrowing.

links.note: Filed as figural because the argument is the shape rather than the wording — one clause of Judges 2:18 appears at 12:2 and nothing else is reproduced.
