What is being borrowed is the deliverance-and-relapse cycle as an explicit doctrine, which the KJV states outright in exactly one passage, and which Helaman 12 states as its thesis.
links.whyNot: The prosperity-and-forgetting law is already fully supplied by Deuteronomy 8:11-17, catalogued at 12:2 on much stronger verbal grounds, and a reader could reasonably hold that Judges 2 adds nothing the Deuteronomy passage has not already given.

pericopes.text: O how foolish, and how vain, and how evil, and devilish, and how quick to do iniquity, and how slow to do good, are the children of men; yea, how quick to hearken unto the words of the evil one, and to set their hearts upon the vain things of the world;

yea, how quick to be lifted up in pride; yea, how quick to boast, and do all manner of that which is iniquity; and how slow are they to remember the Lord their God, and to give ear unto his counsels; yea, how slow to walk in wisdom’s paths!

Behold, they do not desire that the Lord their God, who hath created them, should rule and reign over them, notwithstanding his great goodness and his mercy towards them; they do set at nought his counsels, and they will not that he should be their guide.

links.text: But ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof:

provenance.other: “set at nought” occurs in exactly five KJV verses (Proverbs 1:25; Mark 9:12; Acts 4:11, 19:27; Romans 14:10), and Proverbs 1:25 is the only one of the five whose object is counsel — 'ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof'. Helaman 12:6 reads 'they do set at nought his counsels'. Proverbs 1:30 restates it: 'They would none of my counsel: they despised all my reproof.'
provenance.significance: Read with the verse before it, the borrowing is larger than the phrase. Helaman 12:5 ends 'how slow to walk in wisdom's paths', and Proverbs 1-4 is the KJV's one sustained personification of Wisdom as a speaker with paths ('her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace', 3:17). Helaman 12:5-6 therefore has Wisdom's paths and Wisdom's complaint in consecutive verses, and turns her first-person rebuke into a third-person description of the same refusal. The Book of Mormon's addition — 'they will not that he should be their guide' — is what Proverbs 1:33 promises to those who do listen.

links.note: 'They do set at nought his counsels, and they will not that he should be their guide.' The idiom is available from four New Testament verses as well, but only Proverbs 1:25 attaches it to counsel, and only Proverbs supplies the wisdom's-paths image standing in the previous verse. Moderate rather than high because 'set at nought' was ordinary English and the plural 'counsels' is the Book of Mormon's own.

pericopes.text: O how great is the nothingness of the children of men; yea, even they are less than the dust of the earth.
For behold, the dust of the earth moveth hither and thither, to the dividing asunder, at the command of our great and everlasting God;

links.text: For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

provenance.other: “dividing asunder” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 4:12. 'Asunder' by itself occurs in twenty-one, always with a different verb — break, cleave, part, cut, divide it asunder — and never in this nominal form. Helaman 12:8 reads 'the dust of the earth moveth hither and thither, to the dividing asunder, at the command of our great and everlasting God'.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one 'dividing asunder' is what the word of God does — 'For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit' — and Helaman 12:8 is the opening term of a passage about nothing but that: 'at his voice doth the hills and the mountains tremble' (12:9), 'by the power of his voice' three times over (12:10-12), 'if he saith unto the earth, Move, and it is moved' (12:13). So the borrowed phrase names the faculty the following ten verses illustrate, and it does so at the exact hinge where the sermon turns from human nothingness to divine speech. Hebrews 4:12's other half — 'a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart' — is the subject of everything Helaman 12 has said up to this point.

links.note: Two words, but they are the KJV's only instance of them, and they sit at the head of a fourteen-verse meditation on the power of God's voice — which is what Hebrews 4:12 attributes them to. Filed as echo because no clause is reproduced and the syntax has been changed past recovery: Hebrews's phrase is a genitive of what the word divides, Helaman's is an adverbial of result.
links.whyNot: 'Divide asunder' is common enough English that the participle could be independent, and Helaman's phrase is doing a different grammatical job. If the contact is accidental the verse loses nothing, since its argument stands on its own.

pericopes.text: yea, behold, at his voice doth the hills and the mountains tremble and quake;

links.text: The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is burned at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein.

provenance.other: “the mountains quake” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the hills melt” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse, Nahum 1:5 — the KJV's only line pairing quaking mountains with hills. Helaman 12:9 reads 'at his voice doth the hills and the mountains tremble and quake'. Nahum 1:5 continues 'and the earth is burned at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein', against Helaman 12:11's 'by the power of his voice, doth the whole earth shake'.
provenance.significance: Nahum 1:2-6 is the KJV's most compressed theophany, and its rhetorical question is 'Who can stand before his indignation?' — which is the question Helaman 12:7-8 has just answered from the other end, with man 'less than the dust of the earth'. What Helaman adds is the mechanism: Nahum's mountains quake 'at him', Helaman's quake 'at his voice', and the next three verses insist on it — 'by the power of his voice' — so that a theophany of presence has been rewritten as a theophany of speech. That is the same move the Hebrews 4:12 echo makes one verse earlier and the same one Matthew 21:21 supplies at 12:17.

links.note: 'At his voice doth the hills and the mountains tremble and quake.' Both of the KJV's relevant singletons are in Nahum 1:5, and the Book of Mormon has both nouns and the verb. The substitution of 'tremble' for 'melt' is what lets the sentence keep both mountains and hills in one predicate where Nahum splits them.

pericopes.text: and by the power of his voice, they are broken up and become smooth, yea, even like unto a valley;

links.text: Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth;

provenance.route: Isaiah 40:4 via Luke 3:5 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “made smooth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 3:5, which is Luke's rendering of Isaiah 40:4; Isaiah's own KJV wording is 'the rough places plain', and 'smooth' is nowhere in Isaiah 40. Helaman 12:10 reads 'they are broken up and become smooth, yea, even like unto a valley', and Luke 3:5 is also the verse that supplies the valley: 'Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low'.
provenance.significance: This is the third appearance of the Lukan 'smooth' in the catalogue and the pattern is now visible. 1 Nephi 17:46 has 'rough places be made smooth, and smooth places shall be broken up'; Helaman 10:9 has a mountain told to 'be thou cast down and become smooth'; Helaman 12:10 has both of 1 Nephi 17:46's verbs together — 'broken up and become smooth'. Each time the levelling is an assertion of divine power over terrain rather than a prophecy of a road for the Lord, which is what it is in Isaiah and in Luke. The Book of Mormon has taken the Baptist's prophecy and used it as evidence in a natural-theology argument, and it has taken it in the New Testament's word and not the Old Testament's.
provenance.mt: Isaiah 40:4 — 'and the rough places plain', against Luke 3:5's 'the rough ways shall be made smooth'.

links.note: 'By the power of his voice, they are broken up and become smooth, yea, even like unto a valley.' The mediation datum is one word and it is decisive on rarity: the KJV's only 'made smooth' is Luke's, not Isaiah's. Written as a fresh row rather than a bare recurrence because the pairing with 'broken up' is new here and reproduces 1 Nephi 17:46's pair exactly, across a book boundary (ADJUDICATING §4).

pericopes.text: yea, by the power of his voice, doth the whole earth shake;
yea, by the power of his voice, doth the foundations rock, even to the very centre;
yea, and if he saith unto the earth, Move, and it is moved;
yea, if he saith unto the earth, Thou shalt go back, that it lengthen out the day for many hours, and it is done;
and thus according to his word, the earth goeth back, and it appeareth unto man that the sun standeth still; yea, and behold, this is so: for sure it is the earth that moveth, and not the sun.

links.text: And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day.

provenance.route: Joshua 10:12-14 (the standing still) + 2 Kings 20:11 / Isaiah 38:8 (the going back) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the sun stood still” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 10:13, where it occurs twice. Joshua 10:13 also has 'hasted not to go down about a whole day', against Helaman 12:14's 'that it lengthen out the day for many hours'. The other element is not Joshua's: the sun or its shadow going BACK is the sign given to Hezekiah, where the LORD 'brought the shadow ten degrees backward' (2 Kings 20:11) and 'the sun returned ten degrees' (Isaiah 38:8). Helaman 12:14-15 has both — 'Thou shalt go back' from Hezekiah's sign, 'the sun standeth still' from Joshua's.
provenance.significance: The two miracles are welded together and then explained, which is the striking thing here. Helaman 12:15 does not merely report the sign; it offers a cosmology to account for it — 'it appeareth unto man that the sun standeth still; yea, and behold, this is so: for sure it is the earth that moveth, and not the sun.' The verse takes the KJV's two solar miracles, keeps their words, and reassigns their mechanism from the sun to the earth, so that Joshua's language is preserved as a report of appearances while the physics behind it is corrected. That is a use of scripture the catalogue has not met before: the borrowing is quoted in order to be glossed as phenomenological. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Joshua 10:12-14 at this verse.
provenance.alternative: 2 Kings 20:11 / Isaiah 38:8 alone, if the 'go back' of 12:14 is weighted above the 'standeth still' of 12:15. Both are present and the row treats them as a composite.

links.note: 'And thus according to his word, the earth goeth back, and it appeareth unto man that the sun standeth still.' The KJV's one 'the sun stood still' is Joshua 10:13, and the lengthened day comes with it; the going back is Hezekiah's sign from a different book. Hardy's cross-reference at this verse points to Joshua 10:12-14 and is the reason this row is not `citationsPending`.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Hel 12.15 (cross-reference to Joshua 10:12-14)

pericopes.text: And behold, also, if he saith unto the waters of the great deep, Be thou dried up, and it is done.

links.text: Art thou not it which hath dried the sea, the waters of the great deep; that hath made the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed to pass over?

provenance.other: “waters of the great deep” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 51:10 — 'Art thou not it which hath dried the sea, the waters of the great deep' — and that verse also supplies the Book of Mormon's verb. 'The great deep' without 'waters' occurs in exactly three (Genesis 7:11, Isaiah 51:10, Amos 7:4), and only Isaiah's is dried up. Helaman 12:16 reads 'if he saith unto the waters of the great deep, Be thou dried up, and it is done'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 51:9-10 addresses the arm of the LORD and asks it to wake as in the days of Rahab and the dragon, and the drying of the sea it names is the Red Sea — 'that hath made the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed to pass over'. Helaman 12:16 keeps the phrase and drops the deliverance: the drying is offered as a specimen of power, with no Israel walking through it. Every one of the marvels in 12:13-17 has been stripped this way — Joshua's long day with no battle, Hezekiah's sign with no illness, the Exodus sea with no crossing — because the argument of the sermon is about the nothingness of man and not about salvation history. That systematic stripping is the finding, and it is only visible once the sources are identified.

links.note: Five words from the KJV's only instance of the phrase, with that verse's own verb ('dried') attached. The machine ranked Isaiah 51:10 first here, which it earned.

pericopes.text: Behold, if he saith unto this mountain, Be thou raised up, and come over and fall upon that city, that it be buried up, and behold it is done.

links.text: Jesus answered and said unto them, Verily I say unto you, If ye have faith, and doubt not, ye shall not only do this which is done to the fig tree, but also if ye shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; it shall be done.

provenance.route: Matthew 21:21 (frame, via Helaman 10:9) + Hosea 10:8 / Luke 23:30 (the falling) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The frame 'if he saith unto this mountain, Be thou … and behold it is done' is Helaman 10:9's, which is Matthew 21:21's; “if ye shall say unto this mountain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. What is new here is the mountain's errand. Matthew's mountain is 'removed' and 'cast into the sea'; Helaman's is 'raised up, and come over and fall upon that city, that it be buried up'. Mountains falling on people is a separate biblical topos — Hosea 10:8's 'they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us', quoted by Jesus at Luke 23:30 and by the kings of the earth at Revelation 6:16.
provenance.significance: The two sources are made to change places, and that is the point of the row. In Hosea, Luke and Revelation it is the guilty who beg the mountains to fall on them, as a mercy hiding them from the face of him that sitteth on the throne; here God commands the mountain to fall on the city as judgment. And the frame that carries it is the faith-saying, in which a mountain is moved by a believer's word. So a promise about faith and a plea for annihilation have been fused into a sentence about God burying a city — which 3 Nephi 8-9 will report happening.
provenance.alternative: A simple recurrence of the Helaman 10:9 formula, with no second source. The 'fall upon that city' clause is what argues against reading it that way.

links.note: Written as a link rather than left to `recurrenceRefs` because the second half of the sentence is not a repetition of anything in chapter 10. The mountain-formula returns, but its object has been changed from the sea to a city, and the changed object has its own biblical background. Moderate: no clause of Hosea, Luke or Revelation is reproduced, and the argument for their presence is the topos rather than the words.
links.whyNot: Helaman 10:9 has already established the mountain formula as this narrator's own, and ADJUDICATING §4's default is that a phrase re-used within a book is the writer using his formula. Only the falling-on-a-city clause resists that reading.

pericopes.text: And behold, if a man hideth up a treasure in the earth, and the Lord shall say, Let it be accursed, because of the iniquity of him that hath hid it up, behold, it shall be accursed;

links.text: When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight, then I coveted them, and took them; and, behold, they are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent, and the silver under it.

provenance.other: “hid in the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 7:21 — Achan's confession that the Babylonish garment, the silver and the wedge of gold 'are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent'. Helaman 12:18 reads 'if a man hideth up a treasure in the earth'. The other term of the sentence comes from the same episode: Joshua 6:18 warns 'keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest ye make yourselves accursed, when ye take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of Israel a curse', and Joshua 7:12-13 twice repeats that Israel cannot stand 'because ye were accursed'.
provenance.significance: Every element of Helaman 12:18-19 is in Joshua 7 and only there: valuables buried in the earth, a curse attaching to them because of the iniquity of the man who buried them, and the curse falling on the man rather than on the goods. What the Book of Mormon changes is the outcome. Achan's treasure is dug up, displayed before the LORD, and destroyed with him; Helaman 12:19 says the opposite — 'no man shall find thee from this time henceforth and forever, and behold, no man getteth it henceforth and forever'. The buried thing is not recovered, and the curse is a permanent concealment rather than an exposure. That inversion is what makes this passage the Book of Mormon's aetiology for the 'slippery treasures' of Mormon 1:18 and Helaman 13:31-36, and it is a reading of Achan's story turned inside out.

links.note: 'If a man hideth up a treasure in the earth, and the Lord shall say, Let it be accursed, because of the iniquity of him that hath hid it up, behold, it shall be accursed.' The KJV's one 'hid in the earth' is Achan's, and the accursed thing is Achan's chapter. The machine offered Ezekiel 9:9 and Luke 12:33 here; neither has a curse or buried spoil.

pericopes.text: and if the Lord shall say, Be thou accursed, that no man shall find thee from this time henceforth and forever, and behold, no man getteth it henceforth and forever.
And behold, if the Lord shall say unto a man, Because of thine iniquities thou shalt be accursed forever, and it shall be done.
And if the Lord shall say, Because of thine iniquities, thou shalt be cut off from my presence, and he will cause that it shall be so.—

links.text: Say unto them, Whosoever he be of all your seed among your generations, that goeth unto the holy things, which the children of Israel hallow unto the LORD, having his uncleanness upon him, that soul shall be cut off from my presence: I am the LORD.

provenance.other: “cut off from my presence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 22:3, where the priest who approaches the holy things in uncleanness is cut off. Within the Book of Mormon the phrase is Lehi's covenant formula, adjudicated at 2 Nephi 1:20 and 4:4, and it recurs in the third person ('cut off from the presence of the Lord') at 1 Nephi 2:21, 2 Nephi 5:20 and 9:6 and in Alma. Helaman 12:21 is its only occurrence in Helaman.
provenance.significance: The mediation call is the point of this row. Helaman 12:21 is not reaching past six hundred years of its own text to Leviticus; it is quoting the promise the Book of Mormon's own first prophet gave his sons — 'inasmuch as ye will not keep my commandments ye shall be cut off from my presence' — and applying it to any man whatever, at the close of a sermon on the human race. The clause's KJV origin is real and is recorded at 2 Nephi 1:20; what Helaman adds is the generalization, which is why the row is worth writing rather than leaving to a cross-reference. Note also what the generalization costs: in Leviticus and in 2 Nephi the cutting off is conditional on a covenant, and here it is stated of 'a man', with 'because of thine iniquities' as the whole of the condition.

links.note: 'If the Lord shall say, Because of thine iniquities, thou shalt be cut off from my presence.' The phrase is a KJV singleton but its proximate model is Lehi's, not Leviticus's, and the mediation field says so. Adjudicated as a link rather than as a bare recurrence because a reader of Helaman meets it here for the first time in this book (ADJUDICATING §4).

pericopes.text: And wo unto whom he shall say this, for it shall be unto him that will do iniquity, and he cannot be saved; therefore, for this cause, that men might be saved, hath repentance been declared.
Therefore, blessed are they who will repent, and hearken unto the voice of the Lord their God; for these are they that shall be saved.
And may God grant, in his great fulness, that men might be brought unto repentance and good works, that they might be restored unto grace, for grace according to their works.

links.text: And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.

provenance.other: Both distinctive phrases of Helaman 12:24 are KJV singletons and both are in one verse. “grace for grace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:16, and “his fulness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one: 'And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.' Helaman 12:24 reads 'may God grant, in his great fulness, that men might be brought unto repentance and good works, that they might be restored unto grace, for grace according to their works'.
provenance.alternative: None. Nothing else in the KJV supplies either phrase.
provenance.significance: The prepositions have been changed and they carry the argument. In John, 'of his fulness have all we received' — the fulness is the source out of which grace comes, and 'grace for grace' is grace succeeding grace, without measure or condition. Helaman 12:24 makes the fulness a manner ('in his great fulness') and attaches to the borrowed phrase a clause John does not have and would not accept: 'according to their works'. So the sentence takes the New Testament's least conditional statement about grace and conditions it, in a chapter whose closing quotation (12:26, from John 5:29) is likewise about what men have done. Whether that is a misreading of John or a deliberate correction of him is the question the row leaves open; what is not in doubt is that the two verses are the Fourth Gospel's.

links.note: Two KJV singletons from one verse, in the same order they occur in it. Frederick 2016 treats Helaman 12:24 in the same stretch of argument as John 1:1, 1:14, 1:16 and 1:17 (co-occurrence, per data/frederick-refs.json). That is a fact about where his discussion falls, not an attribution of this identification to him: his book is an argument about the presence of the Gospel of John in Latter-day Saint scripture and carries no list of proposed sources (CONVENTIONS §3a).
bibliography: Frederick 2016: Helaman 12:24 discussed in proximity to John 1:16

pericopes.text: And I would that all men might be saved. But we read that in that great and last day, there are some which shall be cast out; yea, which shall be cast off from the presence of the Lord;

yea, which shall be consigned to a state of endless misery, fulfilling the words which saith, They that have done good, shall have everlasting life; and they that have done evil, shall have everlasting damnation.— And thus it is. Amen.

links.text: And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.

provenance.route: John 5:29, with Daniel 12:2's adjective → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The frame is John's: 'they that have done good … and they that have done evil' is eleven consecutive words of John 5:29, and the Book of Mormon marks it as a quotation ('fulfilling the words which saith'). The predicate is not John's. John reads 'unto the resurrection of life' and 'unto the resurrection of damnation'; Helaman reads 'shall have everlasting life' and 'shall have everlasting damnation'. 'Everlasting life' is Daniel 12:2's phrase in the verse John 5:29 is built on — 'many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt' — and “everlasting damnation” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses. The Book of Mormon has coined it by putting Daniel's adjective on John's noun.
provenance.alternative: Daniel 12:2 alone. mediation-check.py returns divergences pointing both ways, which is correct and not a failure: the syntax is decisively John's and the adjective is decisively Daniel's, so the verse is a composite and the note says so rather than choosing.
provenance.significance: Mormon is quoting, and what he quotes does not exist. The formula 'fulfilling the words which saith' presents this as a citation of scripture, and the sentence cited is a conflation of a verse of John with a word from Daniel that produces a phrase — 'everlasting damnation' — the King James Bible never prints. Two things follow. First, this is a clean instance of the corpus's characteristic mode: not transcription but recomposition inside the KJV's own vocabulary. Second, the conflation is not arbitrary, since Daniel 12:2 is the passage John 5:28-29 is itself reworking; the Book of Mormon has, in effect, restored to John's sentence the adjective John's source used, which is either a very good ear or a very good accident. Hardy's apparatus cross-references John 5:29 here.
provenance.mt: Daniel 12:2 — 'some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.'

links.note: 'Fulfilling the words which saith, They that have done good, shall have everlasting life; and they that have done evil, shall have everlasting damnation.' Eleven words of John 5:29 under an explicit citation formula, with John's 'resurrection of' replaced twice by Daniel 12:2's 'everlasting'. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and so not among his 36. The closing 'cast off from the presence of the Lord' at 12:25 is the KJV's judgment idiom from 2 Thessalonians 1:9, where it stands beside 'everlasting destruction'.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Hel 12.26 (cross-reference to John 5:29)

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass in the eighty and sixth year, the Nephites did still remain in wickedness, yea, in great wickedness, while the Lamanites did observe strictly to keep the commandments of God, according to the law of Moses.

And it came to pass that in this year, there was one Samuel, a Lamanite, came into the land of Zarahemla, and began to preach unto the people. And it came to pass that he did preach many-day repentance unto the people, and they did cast him out, and he was about to return to his own land.
But behold, the voice of the Lord came unto him, that he should return again, and prophesy unto the people whatsoever things should come in his heart.

And it came to pass that they would not suffer that he should enter into the city; therefore he went and got upon the wall thereof, and stretched forth his hand and cried with a loud voice, and prophesied unto the people whatsoever things the Lord put into his heart;

and he said unto them, Behold, I, Samuel, a Lamanite, do speak the words of the Lord, which he doth put into my heart; and behold he hath put it into my heart to say unto this people, that the sword of justice hangeth over this people; and four hundred years passeth not away save the sword of justice falleth upon this people;

yea, heavy destruction awaiteth this people, and it surely cometh unto this people, and nothing can save this people, save it be repentance and faith on the Lord Jesus Christ, which surely shall come into the world, and shall suffer many things, and shall be slain for his people.

And behold, an angel of the Lord hath declared it unto me, and he did bring glad tidings to my soul. And behold, I was sent unto you to declare it unto you also, that ye might have glad tidings; but behold ye would not receive me,

links.text: And the angel answering said unto him, I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings.

provenance.other: “Glad tidings” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Luke 1:19, Luke 8:1, Acts 13:32, Romans 10:15), of which Luke 1:19 is the only one where an angel brings them and the only one that couples them with being sent.
provenance.significance: Samuel's credentials are Gabriel's. The angel of Luke 1 answers a doubting priest by naming himself, saying he was sent, and saying what he was sent with — glad tidings; Samuel, standing on a wall over a city that has already thrown him out, says the same three things in the same order. The suppressed correspondence is the reception: Gabriel strikes Zacharias dumb for not believing, and Samuel's hearers will spend chapter 16 shooting arrows at him. Compare Hays on metalepsis — the borrowed frame carries its own outcome with it.

links.note: 'An angel of the Lord hath declared it unto me, and he did bring glad tidings to my soul. And behold, I was sent unto you to declare it unto you also, that ye might have glad tidings.' Against Luke 1:19: 'I am Gabriel … and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings.' The three elements — angel, sent, glad tidings — are Luke's, and 'glad tidings' occurs in exactly four KJV verses of which this is the only angelic one. The Book of Mormon then does something Luke does not: it makes the prophet a relay, receiving the tidings and passing them on in the same words. Note that the immediately following verse borrows from two verses earlier in the same speech (13:8, Luke 1:17), which is the sequence argument for reading this as Luke 1 rather than the general KJV idiom.

pericopes.text: therefore thus saith the Lord, Because of the hardness of the hearts of the people of the Nephites, except they repent I will take away my word from them, and I will withdraw my spirit from them, and I will suffer them no longer, and I will turn the hearts of their brethren against them;

links.text: And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.

provenance.route: Malachi 4:6 → Luke 1:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Turn the hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:17. Malachi 4:6, which Luke is quoting, has the singular — 'turn the heart of the fathers to the children' — and so does 3 Nephi 25:6 when the Book of Mormon transcribes Malachi outright.
provenance.significance: The Elijah promise, run backwards. In Malachi and in Luke, turning hearts is the last mercy before the curse; here the Lord turns hearts as the curse. Recover the source and the threat has a shape the verse does not state: what is withdrawn from the Nephites is not merely favour but the specific eleventh-hour reconciliation Malachi ends the Old Testament by promising, and the hearts turned are their brethren's — the Lamanites', the very people Samuel belongs to and chapter 15 will say the Lord has kept.

links.note: 'I will turn the hearts of their brethren against them.' The plural 'turn the hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:17, Gabriel's citation of Malachi's Elijah promise; Malachi 4:6 itself reads 'turn the heart' in the singular. The Book of Mormon has Luke's plural, which is a small mediation result and not a decisive one — the phrase is short and the sense is inverted from reconciliation to estrangement. What carries it is the company: the previous verse borrows Luke 1:19, two verses further on in Gabriel's same speech. Recorded at moderate because the inversion is deliberate enough to be an argument and thin enough to be denied.
links.whyNot: Three words, and the sense is opposed to both Malachi's and Luke's. A reader who takes 'turn the hearts of X against Y' as ordinary English prophetic idiom rather than a citation is not being unreasonable; the case rests on the plural and on 13:7.

pericopes.text: and four hundred years shall not pass away, before I will cause that they shall be smitten; yea, I will visit them with the sword, and with famine, and with pestilence;

links.text: When they fast, I will not hear their cry; and when they offer burnt offering and an oblation, I will not accept them: but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence.

provenance.other: The triad in the order sword–famine–pestilence is Jeremiah's signature; “the sword the famine and the pestilence” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 24:10 and Jeremiah 29:17, both with a single article. Jeremiah 14:12 repeats the preposition — 'by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence' — which is the construction the Book of Mormon has.
provenance.significance: Samuel is preaching in the seventh-century idiom of the prophet whose city fell. Jeremiah 14 is the drought oracle in which the Lord forbids Jeremiah to pray for the people; the Book of Mormon puts its judgment formula in the mouth of a prophet who has just been told to go back and preach to a people he had given up on — the opposite instruction, in the same words.

links.note: 'I will visit them with the sword, and with famine, and with pestilence.' The triad is Jeremiah's and the repeated preposition points at Jeremiah 14:12 ('by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence') rather than the single-article form of Jeremiah 24:10 and 29:17. Ezekiel has the same three judgments but almost always with a fourth, the noisome beast (Ezekiel 14:21), and Leviticus 26 keeps them separate. Moderate because the formula is distributed across a dozen Jeremiah verses and no single one can be isolated — the finding is the idiom, not the verse.

pericopes.text: yea, I will visit them in my fierce anger, and there shall be those of the fourth generation, which shall live, of your enemies, to behold your utter destruction; and this shall surely come, except ye repent, saith the Lord; and those of the fourth generation shall visit your destruction.

links.text: Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;

provenance.other: “Unto the third and fourth generation” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Exodus 20:5, Exodus 34:7 and Deuteronomy 5:9 — and Numbers 14:18 has the same formula with 'unto the third and fourth'. All four pair the span with the verb 'visiting'. The bare phrase 'fourth generation' is commoner, seven verses, the other three being Genesis 15:16, 2 Kings 10:30 and 2 Kings 15:12.
provenance.significance: The second commandment supplies both the verb and the arithmetic, and the Book of Mormon turns the sanction inside out. In Exodus the Lord visits iniquity on the children to the fourth generation; here the fourth generation is the audience rather than the object — they survive to watch, and then 'shall visit your destruction'. The visiting passes from God to the enemy, which is what makes the borrowing worth recording: the commandment's clause is not being quoted, it is being cashed.

links.note: 'I will visit them in my fierce anger, and there shall be those of the fourth generation … to behold your utter destruction … and those of the fourth generation shall visit your destruction.' “Unto the third and fourth generation” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all of them the Decalogue's jealous-God clause. Both terms of that sanction are here — the verb 'visit' and the span 'fourth generation' — and no other KJV context puts them together. Moderate rather than high because the shared wording is two elements rather than a clause, and because 'fourth generation' has three unrelated KJV homes (Genesis 15:16, 2 Kings 10:30, 2 Kings 15:12).

pericopes.text: But if ye will repent and return unto the Lord your God, I will turn away mine anger saith the Lord; yea, thus saith the Lord, Blessed are they who will repent and turn unto me, but wo unto him that repenteth not;

yea, wo unto this great city of Zarahemla; for behold it is because of they which are righteous, that it is saved; yea, wo unto this great city, For I perceive, saith the Lord, that there are many, yea, even the more part of this great city, that will harden their hearts against me, saith the Lord.

But blessed are they who will repent, for them will I spare. But behold if it were not for the righteous which are in this great city, behold I would cause that fire should come down out of heaven, and destroy it.

links.text: And the LORD said, If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes.

provenance.other: “Spare all the place” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 18:26, and it is the only KJV sentence in which a city is spared on account of the righteous inside it. “Fire come down from heaven” occurs in three (2 Kings 1:10, 1:12, Revelation 13:13) and none of those is a city; Genesis 19:24 has the Sodom fire but calls it 'brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven'.
provenance.significance: Abraham's bargain, with the arithmetic dropped and the outcome kept. Genesis 18 works by counting — fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten — and the reader who recovers it knows how the story ends: the number could not be found and the fire fell anyway. Samuel's next sentence supplies exactly that ending in advance ('when ye shall cast out the righteous from among you, then shall ye be ripe for destruction'), so the metalepsis is doing the argument's work. Zarahemla is being told it is Sodom on the night before, and that the count is going down.

links.note: 'If it were not for the righteous which are in this great city, behold I would cause that fire should come down out of heaven, and destroy it.' The proposition is Genesis 18:26's: a city spared for the righteous in it, and burned otherwise. 'Spare all the place' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The fire is Sodom's from the next chapter (Genesis 19:24), and 13:14's 'it is for the righteous' sake, that it is spared' reproduces Genesis 18:26's 'for their sakes'. Note that 2 Kings 1:10, the machine's likelier match on the fire clause alone, has no city and no righteous remnant, and is filed in the register.

pericopes.text: But behold, it is for the righteous’ sake, that it is spared. But behold, the time cometh, saith the Lord, that when ye shall cast out the righteous from among you, then shall ye be ripe for destruction; yea, wo be unto this great city, because of the wickedness and abominations which is in her;
yea, and wo be unto the city of Gideon, for the wickedness and abominations which is in her;
yea, and wo be unto all the cities which are in the land round about, which is possessed by the Nephites, because of the wickedness and abominations which is in them;
and behold, a curse shall come upon the land, saith the Lord of Hosts, because of the people’s sake which is upon the land; yea, because of their wickedness and their abominations.

And it shall come to pass, saith the Lord of Hosts, yea, our great and true God, that whoso shall hide up treasures in the earth, shall find them again no more, because of the great curse of the land, save he be a righteous man, and shall hide it up unto the Lord:

For I will, saith the Lord, that they shall hide up their treasures unto me; and cursed be they who hideth not up their treasures unto me; for none hideth up their treasures unto me save it be the righteous; and he that hideth not up his treasure unto me, cursed is he, and also the treasure, and none shall redeem it because of the curse of the land.

links.text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:

provenance.other: “Treasures upon earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 6:19. The Sermon's antithesis — treasure laid up on earth against treasure laid up with God — has no Old Testament equivalent.
provenance.significance: The Sermon on the Mount's antithesis made literal and local. Matthew's earthly treasure is lost to moth, rust and thieves; Samuel's is lost to the ground itself, which becomes slippery and will not hold it. The metalepsis is in what Matthew's 'treasures in heaven' becomes here: not a heavenly deposit but 'hide up their treasures unto me' — the same act of burying, redirected. The consolation is that the Lord is the only bank in a cursed land.

links.note: 13:18-19 sets 'whoso shall hide up treasures in the earth, shall find them again no more' against 'they shall hide up their treasures unto me', which is the structure of Matthew 6:19-20 with the verb changed from laying up to hiding up. 'Treasures upon earth' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moderate rather than high: the shared material is the antithesis and the noun, not a clause, and the hiding of treasure in the earth is also the servant's act in Matthew 25:18. The heart clause that completes the Sermon's argument arrives one verse later and is adjudicated at 13:20.

pericopes.text: And the day shall come that they shall hide up their treasures, because they have set their hearts upon riches; and because they have set their hearts upon their riches, I will hide up their treasures when they shall flee before their enemies, because they will not hide them up unto me; cursed be they, and also their treasures; and in that day shall they be smitten, saith the Lord.

links.text: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.

provenance.other: “Set not your heart upon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 62:10, and it is the only KJV sentence that attaches the setting of the heart to riches specifically. Matthew 6:21's 'there will your heart be' occurs in exactly two, Matthew 6:21 and Luke 12:34.
provenance.significance: The psalm's prohibition is quoted as an indictment: what Psalm 62 tells the hearer not to do is what Samuel says the hearer has done. Recovering the psalm supplies the reason the Book of Mormon does not give — Psalm 62:9 has just weighed men in the balance and found them 'altogether lighter than vanity', so the riches that are about to become slippery were already weightless.

links.note: 'Because they have set their hearts upon riches … because they have set their hearts upon their riches.' Psalm 62:10's 'if riches increase, set not your heart upon them' is the only KJV verse joining those two ideas, and the phrase 'set not your heart upon' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Matthew 6:21 supplies the treasure-and-heart form the previous verse was already using, so the two sources are working together rather than competing. Moderate: 'set the heart upon' is idiomatic enough that a writer steeped in the KJV could produce it without the psalm in view.

pericopes.text: Behold ye, the people of this great city, and hearken unto my words; yea, hearken unto the words which the Lord saith; for behold, he saith that ye are cursed because of your riches, and also are your riches cursed because ye have set your hearts upon them, and hath not hearkened unto the words of him who gave them unto you.

Ye do not remember the Lord your God in the things which he hath blessed you, but ye do always remember your riches, not to thank the Lord your God for them; yea, your heart is not drawn out unto the Lord, but they do swell with great pride, unto boasting, and unto great swelling, envyings, strifes, malice, persecutions, and murders, and all manner of iniquities:

links.text: For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults:

provenance.other: “Swellings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:20, which also carries 'envyings' (two KJV verses, this and Galatians 5:21) and 'strifes' (four). No other KJV verse has any two of the three together.
provenance.significance: Paul's list is what he fears to find when he arrives; Samuel's is what he says is already there. The suppressed correspondence is that 2 Corinthians 12:20-21 is written by an apostle who expects to be humbled by the congregation he is coming to — and the man on the wall is delivering the same catalogue to a city that has already thrown him over it.

links.note: 'They do swell with great pride, unto boasting, and unto great swelling, envyings, strifes, malice, persecutions, and murders.' Three of the vices — swelling, envyings, strifes — are the distinctive ones, and the single KJV verse that carries all three is 2 Corinthians 12:20; 'swellings' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Great swelling' as a phrase belongs to 2 Peter 2:18 and Jude 16, where it describes the speech of false teachers, which is the subject of 13:27-28 five verses later. Galatians 5:20-21 supplies 'murders' next to 'envyings' but has neither swelling nor strife in the plural.

links.text: But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth, that he may establish his covenant which he sware unto thy fathers, as it is this day.

provenance.other: “Power to get wealth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 8:18, which is also one of only two KJV verses reading “remember the LORD thy God” (the other, 2 Samuel 14:11, is the woman of Tekoah's oath).
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 8 is the chapter that anticipates prosperity and legislates against forgetting; Samuel reports the failure the chapter was written to forestall, in the chapter's own sequence — forget who gave it (8:11-14), heart lifted up (8:14), the wealth was his to give (8:18). What the borrowing adds is the verdict: Moses says 'lest thou forget', and the Book of Mormon says the lest has happened.

links.note: 'Ye do not remember the Lord your God in the things which he hath blessed you … hath not hearkened unto the words of him who gave them unto you' (13:21-22). Deuteronomy 8:18 is the KJV's one verse on God as the giver of the power to get wealth, and Deuteronomy 8:14's 'then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God' is the sentence the Book of Mormon's 'they do swell with great pride' translates into its own idiom. Moderate: the contact is a sustained sequence of ideas with one rare phrase behind it rather than a reproduced clause.

pericopes.text: For this cause hath the Lord God caused that a curse should come upon the land, and also upon your riches; and this because of your iniquities;

yea, wo unto this people, because of this time which has arrriven, that ye do cast out the prophets, and do mock them, and cast stones at them, and do slay them, and do do all manner of iniquity unto them, even as they did of old time.
And now when ye talk, ye say, If our days had been in the days of our fathers of old, ye would not have slain the prophets; ye would not have stoned them, and cast them out.

links.text: And say, If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets.
variants: 1830 'ye would not have slain' → 1920 'we would not have slain'

provenance.other: “In the days of our fathers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 23:30. Luke's version of the same woe (Luke 11:47-48) has no counterfactual at all — it reads 'ye allow the deeds of your fathers' — so Matthew is the only possible source for the sentence's shape as well as its words.
provenance.significance: This is the hinge of the whole sermon, and the metalepsis runs forward rather than back. In Matthew the woe is an argument in three moves: you say you would not have killed the prophets (23:30), therefore you witness against yourselves that you are their children (23:31), and Jerusalem's house is left desolate (23:38). Samuel makes all three moves in the same order across two chapters — the disclaimer here, 'ye are worse than they' at 13:26, and 'your houses shall be left unto you desolate' at 15:1. Recovering Matthew tells the reader what Zarahemla is being cast as before the sermon says it: Jerusalem in the last week.

links.note: 'If our days had been in the days of our fathers of old, ye would not have slain the prophets; ye would not have stoned them, and cast them out.' Matthew 23:30: 'If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets.' The conditional, the phrase 'in the days of our fathers' — a KJV singleton — and the disavowal are all reproduced; what the Book of Mormon substitutes for Matthew's 'partakers … in the blood' is 'slain the prophets … stoned them', which is Matthew 23:37's 'thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them' seven verses further on. So the verse fuses the two ends of the same woe. The 1830 reading is evidence here: the first edition has 'YE would not have slain', which is incoherent inside a speech the people are quoting of themselves, and 1920 changed it to 'we' — that is, the later edition corrected the text back toward the KJV's pronoun (CONVENTIONS §8). Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule.

pericopes.text: Behold ye are worse than they; for as the Lord liveth, if a prophet come among you, and declareth unto you the word of the Lord, which testifieth of your sins and iniquities, ye are angry with him, and cast him out, and seek all manner of ways to destroy him; yea, you will say that he is a false prophet, and that he is a sinner, and of the Devil, because he testifieth that your deeds are evil.

But behold, if a man shall come among you, and shall say, Do this, and there is no iniquity; do that, and ye shall not suffer; yea, he will say, walk after the pride of your own hearts; yea, walk after the pride of your eyes, and do whatsoever your heart desireth; and if a man shall come among you and say this, ye will receive him, and ye will say that he is a prophet;

yea, ye will lift him up, and ye will give unto him of your substance; ye will give unto him of your gold, and of your silver, and ye will clothe him with costly apparel; and because he speaketh flattering words unto you, and he saith that all is well, and then ye will not find fault with him.

links.text: For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness:

provenance.other: “Flattering words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 2:5. The KJV's other flattery language is Psalmic and uses 'lips', 'mouth' or 'tongue' (Psalm 5:9, 12:2-3, Proverbs 26:28, 29:5).
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a denial and Samuel's is an accusation, and they name the same two things in the same order. 1 Thessalonians 2:5 disclaims flattering words and 'a cloke of covetousness'; Helaman 13:28 has the flattering words and then the gold, the silver and the costly apparel that are the covetousness the cloak is for. Recovering Paul gives the verse a control it does not state: this is what a true preacher is on record as not doing, and 13:26 has just said what happens to one who does not do it.

links.note: 'Because he speaketh flattering words unto you, and he saith that all is well.' 'Flattering words' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is Paul distinguishing himself from precisely the paid flatterer Samuel describes. The surrounding detail — substance, gold, silver, costly apparel — matches Paul's 'cloke of covetousness' rather than the psalms' flattering lips. Moderate: two words, and the Book of Mormon uses 'flattering words' as a settled formula elsewhere in its own text, so this may be its idiom rather than a fresh borrowing here.

pericopes.text: O ye wicked and ye perverse generation; ye hardened and ye stiffnecked people, how long will ye suppose that the Lord will suffer you; yea, how long will ye suffer yourselves to be lead by foolish and blind guides; yea, how long will ye choose darkness rather than light;

links.text: Woe unto you, ye blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing; but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor!

provenance.other: “Blind guides” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:16 and Matthew 23:24, both inside the same discourse the sermon has already quoted at 13:25. Luke's parallel woes have 'ye are as graves which appear not' (Luke 11:44) and no guides at all.
provenance.significance: The confirmation of the Matthew 23 reading, four verses after the quotation that established it. A single borrowing from a discourse can be an accident of memory; two, from verses fourteen apart in one chapter, with the epithet reserved to that chapter in the whole King James Bible, is a sustained use. And the epithet is chosen for its object: Matthew's blind guides are the religious leadership, and Samuel is telling a people that the leaders they have chosen over him are that.

links.note: 'How long will ye suffer yourselves to be lead by foolish and blind guides?' 'Blind guides' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and both are Matthew 23, the discourse already quoted at 13:25. The Book of Mormon adds 'foolish', which is not Matthew's, and turns the epithet from an address ('ye blind guides') into a description of the people the audience follows — the same move it makes with the woes themselves. 1830 reads 'lead' where 1920 reads 'led'.

links.text: Then Jesus answered and said, O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? how long shall I suffer you? bring him hither to me.

provenance.other: “Perverse generation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 17:17 and Luke 9:41, and the doubled question “how long shall I suffer you” in exactly two, Matthew 17:17 and Mark 9:19. Luke 9:41 collapses the two questions into one ('how long shall I be with you, and suffer you?'), so the anaphora is Matthew's and Mark's, not Luke's.
provenance.significance: The address is Christ's to his own disciples' generation at the foot of the mount of transfiguration; Samuel gives it to a city. The suppressed half is what follows in Matthew — the failure being rebuked there is a failure of faith to cast out a devil, and Samuel's next chapters are about signs given so that 'there should be no cause for unbelief'.

links.note: 'O ye wicked and ye perverse generation … how long will ye suppose that the Lord will suffer you? Yea, how long will ye suffer yourselves …? Yea, how long will ye choose darkness …?' The epithet and the anaphora both come from one KJV sentence: 'perverse generation' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and 'how long shall I suffer you' in exactly two, with Matthew 17:17 the only verse in both lists. The Book of Mormon extends the doubled 'how long' to three and puts the suffering in the audience's mouth as well as God's, which is a rhetorical development of the source rather than a repetition of it.

links.text: And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.

provenance.other: “Darkness rather than light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 3:19, and the clause that completes it there — 'because their deeds were evil' — has already been used three verses earlier at Helaman 13:26 ('because he testifieth that your deeds are evil').
provenance.significance: Split agreement across three verses, which is exactly what the contiguous-window machine stream cannot see (CONVENTIONS §9). John 3:19 is one sentence with two halves; the Book of Mormon uses the second half at 13:26 and the first half at 13:29, in reverse order, and both halves keep their function — the deeds are why the prophet is hated, and the darkness is what the hearers choose. John 3:20 supplies the missing middle term the Book of Mormon does not state: 'every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved.' That is a description of 13:26's audience.

links.note: 'How long will ye choose darkness rather than light?' 'Darkness rather than light' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. What raises this above a stock antithesis is that 13:26 has already used the other half of the same Johannine sentence — the prophet is cast out 'because he testifieth that your deeds are evil', against John 3:19's 'because their deeds were evil'. The Book of Mormon's one addition is the verb: John's men loved darkness, Samuel's choose it, which is the freedom argument chapter 14 will end on (14:31, 'ye might choose life or death').

pericopes.text: yea, behold the anger of the Lord is already kindled against you; behold, he hath cursed the land, because of your iniquity;
and behold, the time cometh that he curseth your riches, that it becometh slippery, that ye cannot hold them; and in the days of your poverty ye cannot retain them;

links.text: Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction.

provenance.other: “Slippery” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 35:6, Psalm 73:18 and Jeremiah 23:12. Only Psalm 73:18 is about the prosperous, and only it pairs slipperiness with destruction ('thou castedst them down into destruction').
provenance.significance: Psalm 73 is the KJV's sustained complaint about the wealth of the wicked — 'they have more than heart could wish', 'they increase in riches' — answered by the discovery that the Lord had set them in slippery places all along. Samuel's cursing of riches so that 'it becometh slippery, that ye cannot hold them' takes the psalm's metaphor off the people and puts it on the property. Recover the psalm and the answer to Samuel's audience is already there: the security they think they are losing was never footing.

links.note: The Book of Mormon's famous slippery treasures are its own image and are not in the King James Bible; what is there is one psalm in which God sets the rich in slippery places and casts them into destruction. 'Slippery' occurs in exactly three KJV verses and the other two are about the way of the wicked, not their goods. Moderate and offered as an echo: a single adjective, but a rare one used of the same people for the same reason, and the whole complex at 13:31-36 (riches, slipperiness, destruction, and the lament that follows) is Psalm 73's subject in Psalm 73's order.

pericopes.text: and in the days of your poverty, ye shall cry unto the Lord; and in vain shall ye cry, for your desolation is already come upon you, and your destruction is made sure; and then shall ye weep and howl in that day, saith the Lord of Hosts. And then shall ye lament, and say,

links.text: Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you.

provenance.other: “Heaped treasure together” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 5:3; so do 'riches are corrupted' (James 5:2) and 'your gold and silver' (James 5:3). “Weep and howl” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, James 5:1 and Joel 1:5 — but only James has it as a phrase, Joel reading 'and weep; and howl' across a clause break to a different audience.
provenance.significance: Four KJV singletons from three consecutive verses, and the Book of Mormon has kept James's sequence: the summons to weep and howl, then the wealth itself failing. What recovering James adds is the reason — 'ye have heaped treasure together FOR THE LAST DAYS' — which is precisely what Samuel says the Nephites have done and precisely why the treasure is useless: it was stored against a day that has arrived. James's hoard rusts; Samuel's sinks into the ground. Both are unreachable on the morning the owner needs them, and 13:34's 'our swords are taken from us in the day we have sought them for battle' is that image at its most concrete.

links.note: 'And then shall ye weep and howl in that day, saith the Lord of Hosts.' James 5:1 is the KJV's one verse in which the phrase 'weep and howl' stands as a unit, and it is addressed to rich men whose riches are about to fail. The lament Samuel then puts in their mouths at 13:33-35 — 'our riches are gone from us', 'we have hid up our treasures, and they have slipped away' — works through James 5:2-3, each of whose distinctive phrases ('riches are corrupted', 'your gold and silver', 'heaped treasure together') is a KJV singleton. Note that 13:28 has already used James's gold and silver of the false prophet's fee. Joel 1:5 has the summons to weep and to howl in a different construction and to drunkards, and is filed in the register.

pericopes.text: O that I had repented, and had not killed the prophets, and stoned them, and cast them out; yea, in that day shall ye say, O that we had remembered the Lord our God, in the day that he gave us our riches, and then they would not have become slippery, that we should lose them; for behold, our riches are gone from us.
Behold, we layeth a tool here, and on the morrow it is gone; and behold, our swords are taken from us in the day we have sought them for battle.
Yea, we have hid up our treasures, and they have slipped away from us, because of the curse of the land.
O that we had repented in the day that the word of the Lord came unto us; for behold the land is cursed, and all things are become slippery, and we cannot hold them.

Behold we are surrounded by demons, yea, we are encircled about by the angels of him who hath sought to destroy our souls. Behold, our iniquities are great. O Lord, canst thou not turn away thine anger from us? And this shall be your language in them days.

But behold, your days of probation is past; ye have procrastinated the day of your salvation, until it is everlastingly too late, and your destruction is made sure; yea, for ye have sought all the days of your lives for that which ye could not obtain; and ye have sought for happiness in doing iniquity, which thing is contrary to the nature of that righteousness which is in our great and Eternal Head.

links.text: (For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)

provenance.route: Isaiah 49:8 → 2 Corinthians 6:2 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Day of salvation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 49:8 and 2 Corinthians 6:2 — and 2 Corinthians 6:2 is Paul quoting Isaiah 49:8, so the phrase has one home in the KJV and one citation of it. Paul's addition is the urgency: 'behold, NOW is the day of salvation.'
provenance.significance: Samuel's charge is that the day has been let go by, which only makes sense against a text that says the day is now. Recover 2 Corinthians 6:2 and the accusation has a clock in it: Paul's 'now' is what 'procrastinated' negates. Isaiah 49:8 alone would not support the reading, since there the day of salvation is God's and no hearer can miss it by delay.

links.note: 'Ye have procrastinated the day of your salvation, until it is everlastingly too late.' 'Day of salvation' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and only 2 Corinthians 6:2 turns it into a deadline. Echo rather than allusion because the shared material is a three-word phrase that the Book of Mormon uses as a standing formula elsewhere in its own text; what argues for Paul here is the temporal logic rather than the words.

pericopes.text: O ye people of the land, that ye would hear my words. And I pray that the anger of the Lord be turned away from you, and that ye would repent and be saved.
And now it came to pass that Samuel, the Lamanite, did prophesy a great many more things which cannot be written.
And behold, he saith unto them, Behold, I give unto you a sign: for five years more cometh, and behold, then cometh the son of God to redeem all those who shall believe on his name.

And behold, this will I give unto you for a sign at the time of his coming; for behold, there shall be great lights in Heaven, insomuch that in the night before he cometh, there shall be no darkness, insomuch that it shall appear unto man as if it was day;

therefore there shall be one day and a night, and a day, as if it were one day, and there were no night; and this shall be unto you for a sign; for ye shall know of the rising of the sun, and also of its setting; therefore they shall know of a surety that there shall be two days and a night; nevertheless the night shall not be darkened; and it shall be the night before he is born.
And behold there shall a new star arise, such an one as ye never have beheld; and this also shall be a sign unto you.

links.text: I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth.

provenance.other: The Book of Mormon's 'a new star' is in no KJV verse; the King James Bible's messianic star is Balaam's ('there shall come a Star out of Jacob') and the magi's ('we have seen his star in the east').
provenance.significance: The figure, not the wording. The King James Bible has exactly one prophet who is not of Israel, is hired to curse Israel, and prophesies a star at Israel's redemption instead — and Samuel the Lamanite is standing on the wall of a Nephite city in that position. Recovering Balaam gives the sign its shape: the star is announced by the outsider, and the insiders resent the announcement. Matthew 2:2 completes the circuit by having Gentile astrologers, not Jerusalem, see the star when it comes.

links.note: Offered as a typology and not as a borrowing. There is no verbal contact — 'a new star' is not KJV English — and the link is entirely in the speaker's position: the KJV's star prophecies belong to a foreign seer (Numbers 24:17) and to foreign magi (Matthew 2:2), and Samuel is a Lamanite. Recorded at low confidence because the reading is worth having in front of a reader and cannot be argued from the words.
links.whyNot: No shared wording at all. A reader who thinks a nativity star needs no source beyond the nativity is entitled to decline this, and the catalogue is not claiming the writer had Balaam in view.

pericopes.text: And behold this is not all: there shall be many signs and wonders in Heaven.

links.text: He delivereth and rescueth, and he worketh signs and wonders in heaven and in earth, who hath delivered Daniel from the power of the lions.

provenance.other: “Signs and wonders in heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 6:27. The bare phrase 'signs and wonders' occurs in fourteen and is almost always Egypt or the apostles; only Daniel puts the wonders in heaven. Acts 2:19, quoting Joel 2:30, has 'wonders in heaven above, and signs in the earth beneath', which divides the pair between the two realms instead of putting both aloft.
provenance.significance: The one KJV verse that locates signs and wonders in heaven is spoken by Darius the Mede — a foreign king issuing a decree about the God of a captive minority. Samuel is the mirror image: a member of the despised nation telling the ruling one what its God will do in its sky. In Daniel the confession follows the deliverance; here it precedes the sign, which is the whole difficulty the sermon runs into.

links.note: 'There shall be many signs and wonders in Heaven.' 'Signs and wonders in heaven' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moderate rather than high because 'signs and wonders' is one of the KJV's commonest formulas and the Book of Mormon uses it freely elsewhere, so the localisation in heaven is the only distinctive element. Note that the fuller Joel/Acts form, which divides signs and wonders between heaven and earth, is the one the chapter's later verses actually enact (14:21-22 puts the shaking 'both above the earth and beneath'), so it is registered as a composite rather than passed over.

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass that ye shall all be amazed, and wonder, insomuch that ye shall fall to the earth.
And it shall come to pass that whosoever shall believe on the Son of God, the same shall have everlasting life.

links.text: He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him.

provenance.other: “Believeth on the Son” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 3:36 and 1 John 5:10; John 3:36 is the only one that completes it with 'hath everlasting life', and 1 John 5:10 is the only one that reads 'believeth on the Son of God', which is the Book of Mormon's fuller phrase.
provenance.significance: The verse is the Johannine formula assembled from its two KJV halves. Recovering John 3:36 supplies the clause the Book of Mormon leaves out and its whole sermon depends on — 'he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him' — which is what chapters 15 and 16 are about. Samuel gives his audience the promise and lets the threat stand behind it; John states both.

links.note: 'Whosoever shall believe on the Son of God, the same shall have everlasting life.' 'Believeth on the Son' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and the Book of Mormon has 1 John 5:10's fuller subject with John 3:36's predicate. John 3:16's 'whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life' is the better-known verse and reads 'in him' rather than 'on the Son'. Moderate: this is Johannine boilerplate that the Book of Mormon uses continually, so what is being catalogued is the source of the formula rather than a fresh act of borrowing at this verse.

pericopes.text: And behold, thus hath the Lord commanded me, by his angel, that I should come and tell this thing unto you; yea, he hath commanded that I should prophesy these things unto you; yea, he hath said unto me, Cry unto this people, repent and prepare the way of the Lord.

links.text: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.

provenance.route: Isaiah 40:3 → Matthew 3:2-3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Prepare ye the way of the Lord” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Isaiah 40:3 and its three synoptic citations — and the wording is identical in all four, so the phrase alone cannot decide mediation and tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence for this verse. What decides it is the pairing with repentance, which is not in Isaiah: 'Repent ye' is Matthew 3:2, one verse before the citation.
provenance.significance: Samuel is given the Baptist's commission verbatim, and he is given it by an angel. Recover Matthew 3 and the identification is not a flourish but a structure: the herald cries in a wilderness outside the city, preaches repentance, threatens the axe at the root of the tree — and Helaman 14:18 supplies that axe's sentence nine verses later. What the Book of Mormon adds is the audience's reply, which Matthew reports as coming from the Pharisees and Samuel has already received in chapter 13.

links.note: 'He hath said unto me, Cry unto this people, repent and prepare the way of the Lord.' Three elements of Isaiah 40:3 as the gospels use it — the cry, the repentance, the preparing of the way. mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between Isaiah 40:3 and Matthew 3:3, because the KJV renders the quoted clause identically in both; the mediation is argued from elsewhere, as CONVENTIONS §7 allows. Two things carry it. 'Repent' belongs to Matthew 3:2 and not to Isaiah 40, where the crier says 'All flesh is grass'. And the sermon quotes the Baptist's preaching again at 14:18, where 'hewn down, and cast into the fire' is reproduced word for word. One Isaiah 40 citation could be either; a citation plus the Baptist's threat is the gospel setting.

pericopes.text: And now because I am a Lamanite, and hath spoken unto you the words which the Lord hath commanded me, and because it was hard against you, ye are angry with me, and do seek to destroy me, and have cast me out from among you.

And ye shall hear my words, for, for this intent I have come up upon the walls of this city, that ye might hear and know of the judgements of God which doth await you because of your iniquities, and also that ye might know the conditions of repentance;

and also that ye might know of the coming of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Father of Heaven and of earth, the Creator of all things, from the beginning; and that ye might know of the signs of his coming, to the intent that ye might believe on his name.
And if ye believe on his name, ye will repent of all your sins, that thereby ye may have a remission of them through his merits.
And behold, again another sign I give unto you; yea, a sign of his death;

for behold, he surely must die, that salvation may come; yea, it behooveth him, and becometh expedient that he dieth, to bring to pass the resurrection of the dead, that thereby men may be brought into the presence of the Lord;

links.text: And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day:

provenance.other: “Behoved” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 24:46 and Hebrews 2:17, and only Luke's attaches it to Christ suffering and rising. “It is expedient” occurs in exactly two, John 11:50 and John 16:7, and only John 11:50 attaches it to a death.
provenance.significance: Two KJV rarities from two different necessities, fused. Luke 24:46 is the risen Christ on the road telling two disciples what had to happen; John 11:50 is Caiaphas telling a council why a man had to die. The Book of Mormon puts them in one clause — 'it behooveth him, and becometh expedient that he dieth' — so that the divine necessity and the political calculation say the same sentence. That is the same fusion 1 Nephi 4:13 made when Nephi justified killing Laban in Caiaphas's words; here the borrowing has come back to its proper object, and the expediency that was frightening in Nephi's mouth is orthodox in Samuel's.

links.note: 'He surely must die, that salvation may come; yea, it behooveth him, and becometh expedient that he dieth, to bring to pass the resurrection of the dead.' Against Luke 24:46: 'thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day.' 'Behoved' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and Luke's is the only christological one; the resurrection follows in both, and 14:20's 'for the space of three days, to the time that he shall rise again from the dead' supplies Luke's third day. The second rare word is 'expedient', which the KJV joins to a death in exactly one verse, John 11:50 — see the argument at 1 Nephi 4:13, where the same verse is borrowed to justify a killing.

pericopes.text: yea, behold this death bringeth to pass the resurrection, and redeemeth all mankind from the first death; that spiritual death for all mankind, by the fall of Adam, being cut off from the presence of the Lord, are considered as dead, both as to things temporal and to things spiritual.
But behold, the resurrection of Christ redeemeth mankind, yea, even all mankind, and bringeth them back into the presence of the Lord;

yea, and it bringeth to pass the condition of repentance, that whosoever repenteth, the same is not hewn down and cast into the fire; but whosoever repenteth not, is hewn down and cast into the fire, and there cometh upon them again a spiritual death, yea, a second death, for they are cut off again as to things pertaining to righteousness;

links.text: And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

provenance.other: “Hewn down and cast into the fire” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9. The clause is word-identical in all three, so it cannot itself choose between them; Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9 are the Baptist's preaching and Matthew 7:19 is the Sermon on the Mount.
provenance.significance: The Baptist's axe, transplanted from a tree to a person. In all three KJV verses the thing hewn down is a tree that does not bear good fruit — a figure — and the Book of Mormon drops the figure and applies the sentence directly to 'whosoever repenteth not'. Recovering the source restores what the Book of Mormon has taken out: the axe already laid to the root, which is to say the interval before the blow, which is exactly the interval Samuel says his audience is standing in.

links.note: 'Whosoever repenteth, the same is not hewn down and cast into the fire; but whosoever repenteth not, is hewn down and cast into the fire.' A six-word clause reproduced twice in one sentence, occurring in exactly three KJV verses. Which of the three cannot be settled on the wording, since the clause is identical in all; Matthew 3:10 is preferred because 14:9 has already given Samuel the Baptist's commission from Matthew 3:2-3, so the sermon is working in that chapter. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule.

links.text: But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.

provenance.other: “The second death” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, Revelation 2:11, 20:6, 20:14 and 21:8, and nowhere else in the Bible. Revelation 21:8 is the only one that defines it by what precedes — the lake which burneth with fire — which is the image the same Book of Mormon verse has just used.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon takes John's term and gives it a definition John does not: a second cutting off from the presence of the Lord 'as to things pertaining to righteousness'. Recovering Revelation shows what has been changed. There the second death is a place, the lake of fire; here it is a relation, and the fire from the Baptist's axe in the first half of the verse has been left to carry the imagery. The two halves of Helaman 14:18 are two different apocalypses spliced at the word 'fire'.

links.note: 'There cometh upon them again a spiritual death, yea, a second death.' The phrase belongs to Revelation and to no other biblical book — exactly four KJV verses — and the surrounding image of being cast into fire is Revelation 20:14 and 21:8's. Moderate because 'second death' had become a standing term in the Book of Mormon's own theological vocabulary by this point (compare Alma 12-13) and may be arriving from there rather than freshly from John; what argues for the KJV here is the immediate juxtaposition with the fire.

pericopes.text: therefore repent ye, repent ye, lest by knowing these things and not doing them, ye shall suffer yourselves to come under condemnation, and ye are brought down unto this second death.

But behold, as I said unto you concerning another sign, a sign of his death: behold, in that day that he shall suffer death, the sun shall be darkened and refuse to give his light unto you; and also the moon, and the stars; and there shall be no light upon the face of this land, even from the time that he shall suffer death, for the space of three days, to the time that he shall rise again from the dead;

links.text: But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light,

provenance.route: Isaiah 13:10 → Mark 13:24-25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
