provenance.other: “The sun shall be darkened” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 13:10 and Mark 13:24 — the second quoting the first. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points, both for Mark: the Book of Mormon has neither Isaiah's 'in his going forth' nor Isaiah's 'to shine' (backbone of four further shared words — sun, darkened, moon, light).
provenance.significance: The order settles what the tool measures. Isaiah 13:10 runs stars, sun, moon; Mark 13:24-25 runs sun, moon, stars; Helaman 14:20 runs 'the sun shall be darkened … and also the moon, and the stars', which is the gospel sequence. And the setting has moved: Isaiah darkens the sun for the fall of Babylon and Mark for the end of the age, while the Book of Mormon does it for a single execution — the Olivet apocalypse relocated from the last day to Good Friday, which is where Luke 23:44-45 had already put a smaller version of it.

links.note: 'The sun shall be darkened and refuse to give his light unto you; and also the moon, and the stars.' The clause occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and the mediation test is decisive for the New Testament form: mediation-check.py finds the Book of Mormon has dropped both of Isaiah 13:10's distinctive additions ('in his going forth', 'to shine'), and the sun-moon-stars order is Mark's and Matthew's rather than Isaiah's. Matthew 24:29 has the same sequence but reads 'shall the sun be darkened'; the Book of Mormon has Mark's word order exactly. What the Book of Mormon supplies on its own is the duration, three days, and the second-person 'unto you'.

pericopes.text: yea, at the time that he shall yield up the ghost, there shall be thunderings and lightnings for the space of many hours, and the earth shall shake and tremble, and the rocks which is upon the face of this earth, which is both above the earth and beneath, which ye know at this time is solid, or the more part of it is one solid mass, shall be broken up;

links.text: And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;

provenance.other: “The rocks rent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:51. “Rent in twain” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 27:51 and Mark 15:38, both of the temple veil. “Yielded up the ghost” occurs in three, of which Matthew 27:50 is the only one of Christ.
provenance.significance: Everything in Matthew's sentence is transferred to the Book of Mormon's landscape except the veil. Matthew has the veil rent in twain, the earth quaking, the rocks rending; Helaman 14:21-22 has the earth shaking, the rocks broken up, and — the giveaway — the rocks 'rent in twain', which in the KJV is what happens to the veil and not to the rocks. The suppressed correspondence is the temple itself: a land with no temple veil to tear gets the tearing anyway, in the veil's own words, written across its geology. The seams and cracks are said to remain 'ever after', so the sign is permanent where Matthew's was momentary.

links.note: 'At the time that he shall yield up the ghost … the earth shall shake and tremble, and the rocks … shall be broken up; yea, they shall be rent in twain.' Three phrases from two consecutive KJV verses: 'yielded up the ghost' (Matthew 27:50, the only christological one of three), 'the rocks rent' (a KJV singleton at Matthew 27:51) and 'rent in twain' (exactly two verses, both the temple veil). The Book of Mormon has swapped the last of these from the veil onto the rocks, which is the strongest evidence in the passage that Matthew 27:51 is being read rather than merely paralleled.

pericopes.text: yea, they shall be rent in twain, and shall ever after be found in seams, and in cracks, and in broken fragments upon the face of the whole earth; yea, both above the earth and both beneath.

And behold there shall be great tempests, and there shall be many mountains laid low, like unto a valley, and there shall be many places, which are now called valleys, which shall become mountains, whose height thereof is great.

links.text: Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:

provenance.other: tools/mediation-check.py reports one decisive point favouring Isaiah 40:4 over Luke 3:5 — 'places plain' against 'ways shall be made smooth' — but the match is on the word 'places', which in Helaman 14:23 belongs to 'many places, which are now called valleys' and has nothing to do with Isaiah's rough places. The reported backbone (valley, mountain, hill, low, crooked, straight, rough) is shared between the two candidates and not with the Book of Mormon, which has only valley, mountain and low. The tool's verdict is set aside here on inspection; the mediation is recorded as direct-OT on the strength of 14:9, not on this diff.
provenance.significance: Fourteen verses after quoting Isaiah 40:3, the sermon makes Isaiah 40:4 happen. In Isaiah the levelling of the land is a metaphor for clearing a processional road; here mountains are laid low and valleys thrown up as literal seismic damage at the death of the one whose way was being prepared. That is metalepsis running in an unusual direction — the source's figure is recovered and then cashed as an event, so the highway prepared in verse 9 is built by the earthquake in verse 23.

links.note: 'There shall be many mountains laid low, like unto a valley, and there shall be many places, which are now called valleys, which shall become mountains.' Isaiah 40:4's 'every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low' is the only KJV verse that exchanges valleys and mountains, and the sermon has already cited the verse before it at 14:9. Moderate: the wording is a paraphrase ('laid low' is in no KJV verse; “made low” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Isaiah 2:17, Isaiah 40:4 and James 1:10), and an earthquake that flattens hills needs no source. What raises it above coincidence is the pairing with 14:9 in one speech.

pericopes.text: And many highways shall be broken up, and many cities shall become desolate,
and many graves shall be opened, and shall yield up many of their dead; and many saints shall appear unto many.

links.text: And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose,

provenance.other: “The graves were opened” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:52. “Appeared unto many” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:53. They are consecutive verses, and Helaman 14:25 reproduces both in Matthew's order in a single sentence of nineteen words.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons from two consecutive verses is as strong as the evidence in this catalogue gets, and what it discloses is a choice. Matthew 27:52-53 is the strangest half-sentence in the passion narrative — bodies of saints raised, waiting three days, and walking into the holy city — and it is precisely that episode, not the veil, the darkness or the centurion's confession, that the Book of Mormon promises will be repeated in the New World. Recovering Matthew supplies the detail Samuel leaves out and 3 Nephi will need: the saints appear 'after his resurrection', which is why 14:20's darkness has to last three days.

links.note: 'And many graves shall be opened, and shall yield up many of their dead; and many saints shall appear unto many.' Against Matthew 27:52-53: 'And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose, And came out of the graves after his resurrection … and appeared unto many.' Both distinctive phrases are KJV singletons and both belong to this one pair of verses; the shared noun 'saints' and the repeated 'many' do the rest. The Book of Mormon's one addition is 'yield up … their dead', which is Revelation 20:13's idiom for the sea and death. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule.

pericopes.text: And behold thus hath the angel spoken unto me; for he said unto me, That there should be thunderings and lightnings for the space of many hours;

and he said unto me that while the thunder and the lightning lasted, and the tempest, that these things should be, and that darkness should cover the face of the whole earth, for the space of three days.

links.text: And Moses stretched forth his hand toward heaven; and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days:

provenance.other: “Thick darkness” occurs in exactly 9 KJV verses, most of them Sinai theophany. Exodus 10:22 is the only KJV verse that gives a darkness a duration of three days, and the number is the whole of the contact here.
provenance.significance: The ninth plague is the KJV's one three-day darkness, and it is a plague on Egypt from which Israel is exempt — 'all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings' (Exodus 10:23). Helaman 14:27 has darkness covering 'the face of the whole earth' with no exemption stated, and 3 Nephi will report that there was none. Recovering Exodus makes the difference audible: this is the plague without the Goshen.

links.note: 'Darkness should cover the face of the whole earth, for the space of three days.' The synoptic darkness at the crucifixion lasts three hours (Matthew 27:45), not three days; the only three-day darkness in the King James Bible is the ninth plague. Moderate and conceptual: the shared material is a number and a condition rather than wording, and the sign is announced twice in this chapter (14:20, 14:27) in the Book of Mormon's own phrasing. Filed because a reader tracing the three days will otherwise find only the gospels, where they are the days in the tomb, not days of darkness.

pericopes.text: And the angel said unto me that many shall see greater things than these, to the intent that they might believe that these signs and these wonders should come to pass, upon all the face of this land; to the intent that there should be no cause for unbelief among the children of men;

links.text: Jesus answered and said unto him, Because I said unto thee, I saw thee under the fig tree, believest thou? thou shalt see greater things than these.

provenance.other: “Greater things than these” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:50, and in that verse it is a promise made to a man who has just believed on the strength of a smaller sign.
provenance.significance: John 1:50-51 is the KJV's model of the sign that escalates: Nathanael believes because Jesus saw him under a fig tree, and is told he will see greater things — heaven open, the angels ascending and descending. Helaman 14:28 makes the same promise to a crowd that has not believed at all, which reverses the condition. In John the greater things are the reward of faith; here they are given 'to the intent that there should be no cause for unbelief', and chapter 16 records that they produced it anyway.

links.note: 'The angel said unto me that many shall see greater things than these, to the intent that they might believe.' 'Greater things than these' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse joins the phrase to believing, as this one does. Moderate: four words, and they are ordinary enough that a writer could assemble them without John. What argues for the borrowing is that the KJV uses this exact comparative once, and uses it for the same transaction — signs offered as grounds for belief.

pericopes.text: and this to the intent that whosoever will believe, might be saved, and that whosoever will not believe, a righteous judgement might come upon them; and also if they are condemned, they bring upon themselves their own condemnation.

And now remember, remember, my brethren, that whosoever perisheth, perisheth unto himself; and whosoever doeth iniquity, doeth it unto himself; for behold ye are free; ye are permitted to act for yourselves; for behold, God hath given unto you a knowledge, and he hath made you free;

he hath given unto you that ye might know good from evil, and he hath given unto you that ye might choose life or death, and ye can do good and be restored unto that which is good, or have that which is good restored unto you; or ye can do evil, and have that which is evil restored unto you.

links.text: I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live:

provenance.other: “Choose life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 30:19, which is also the KJV's one verse setting life and death before a people as an object of choice. Deuteronomy 30:15 supplies the other pair the Book of Mormon uses: 'life and good, and death and evil'.
provenance.significance: Samuel ends his doctrinal section where Moses ends his covenant, and the two Deuteronomy verses supply both halves of the Book of Mormon's sentence in Moses's own order — good and evil first (30:15), life and death second (30:19). The suppressed clause is the one Moses adds and Samuel does not: 'that both thou and thy seed may live'. The whole sermon is about whether the seed will live, and chapter 15 answers that for the Lamanites and 15:17 for the Nephites.

links.note: 'He hath given unto you that ye might know good from evil, and he hath given unto you that ye might choose life or death.' The two pairs are Deuteronomy 30:15's ('life and good, and death and evil') and 30:19's ('life and death … therefore choose life'), and 'choose life' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. What the Book of Mormon adds is the ground of the choice — 'ye are free; ye are permitted to act for yourselves' at 14:30 — which turns Moses's exhortation into an argument about agency. Compare 13:29's 'how long will ye choose darkness rather than light', where the same verb is already doing this work.

pericopes.text: And now my beloved brethren, behold, I declare unto you that except ye shall repent, your houses shall be left unto you desolate;

links.text: Behold, your house is left unto you desolate.
variants: 1830 and 1920 both read the plural 'your houses'; the KJV has the singular 'your house'

provenance.other: “Left unto you desolate” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:38 and Luke 13:35, which are the same saying in two gospels. The Book of Mormon pluralises the house, which neither has.
provenance.significance: The sermon's Matthew 23 argument closes here, two chapters after it opened. At 13:25 Samuel quotes the woe's counterfactual ('if our days had been in the days of our fathers'), at 13:29 its epithet ('blind guides'), at 13:33 its charge ('killed the prophets, and stoned them'), and here its verdict — and Matthew has them in that order, 23:30, 23:16/24, 23:37, 23:38. Recovering the discourse tells the reader what Zarahemla has been cast as for three chapters: Jerusalem in the week before the temple falls. The pluralised 'houses' is the one adjustment, and it is the right one — Jesus speaks to a city with one house that matters, Samuel to a city with no temple at all.

links.note: 'Except ye shall repent, your houses shall be left unto you desolate.' Against Matthew 23:38: 'Behold, your house is left unto you desolate.' The clause occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both the same dominical saying; Matthew is preferred over Luke 13:35 because the three preceding borrowings in this sermon are all from Matthew 23 and one of them, 'in the days of our fathers' at 13:25, is a KJV singleton that Luke's parallel woes do not contain. The Book of Mormon adds the condition ('except ye shall repent') that Matthew's saying does not offer, and pluralises the house. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule.

pericopes.text: yea, except ye repent, your women shall have great cause to mourn in the day that they shall give suck; for ye shall attempt to flee, and there shall be no place for refuge; yea, and wo unto them which are with child, for they shall be heavy, and cannot flee; therefore they shall be trodden down, and shall be left to perish;

links.text: And woe unto them that are with child, and to them that give suck in those days!

provenance.other: “Them that are with child” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 24:19, Mark 13:17 and Luke 21:23, which are the same saying in the three synoptic apocalypses; the wording is near-identical and cannot be told apart. What can be told apart is the sequence: Matthew 23:38's 'your house is left unto you desolate' is followed, thirteen verses later in the same discourse, by 24:19's woe — and Helaman 15:1 and 15:2 stand in exactly that order.
provenance.significance: The Olivet warning is a warning about speed — the flight will be sudden, so pregnancy and nursing are disabilities. The Book of Mormon states the reason the gospels leave implicit ('they shall be heavy, and cannot flee') and then supplies an outcome none of the three has: 'they shall be trodden down, and shall be left to perish'. Luke 21:24 does say Jerusalem shall be trodden down, but 'trodden down' occurs in ten KJV verses and cannot bear the weight, so the addition is recorded as the Book of Mormon's own hardening of the source rather than as a fourth borrowing.

links.note: 'Your women shall have great cause to mourn in the day that they shall give suck; for ye shall attempt to flee, and there shall be no place for refuge; yea, and wo unto them which are with child.' Three elements of the Olivet discourse — the woe, the child, the suck — plus the flight of Matthew 24:16-20. The phrase occurs in exactly three KJV verses and they are the three synoptic forms of one saying, so no verbal test separates them; Matthew is preferred because 15:1 has just quoted Matthew 23:38 and Matthew alone places the two sayings thirteen verses apart in a single continuous discourse. Recorded at high because the borrowing is not in doubt even though the evangelist is.

pericopes.text: yea, wo unto this people which are called the people of Nephi, except they shall repent when they shall see all those signs and wonders which shall be showed unto them; for behold, they have been a chosen people of the Lord; yea, the people of Nephi hath he loved, and also hath he chastened them; yea, in the days of their iniquities hath he chastened them, because he loveth them.

links.text: For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.

provenance.route: Proverbs 3:11-12 → Hebrews 12:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Whom the Lord loveth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Proverbs 3:12 and Hebrews 12:6 — the second quoting the first — and they differ in one word: Proverbs' Lord correcteth, Hebrews' chasteneth. tools/mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence, because the two candidates differ as whole blocks rather than at a point the Book of Mormon reproduces; the judgment here is made by eye and on that one word.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 12 turns Proverbs' domestic maxim into an argument about who counts as a son: the chastening is the evidence of legitimacy, and 'if ye be without chastisement … then are ye bastards, and not sons' (12:8). Samuel is making exactly that argument about the Nephites — they have been chastened because they are the chosen people — and then reverses it in the next verse for the Lamanites, who have been left alone and are the ones being saved. The suppressed premise cuts against the speaker's own audience harder than anything he says outright.

links.note: 'Yea, in the days of their iniquities hath he chastened them, because he loveth them.' The King James Bible joins these two verbs in two verses, Proverbs 3:12 and Hebrews 12:6, the second quoting the first, and they differ in exactly one word: Proverbs' Lord CORRECTETH whom he loveth, Hebrews' CHASTENETH. The Book of Mormon has chasten. mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence at this verse because its alignment treats the two clauses as blocks, so the result is argued rather than measured — but the single word the two candidates disagree about is the single word the Book of Mormon supplies, which is the whole of the test. Moderate: it is one word, and 'chasten' is common KJV vocabulary outside this pair.

pericopes.text: But behold my brethren, the Lamanites hath he hated, because their deeds have been evil continually; and this because of the iniquity of the tradition of their fathers. But behold, salvation hath come unto them, through the preaching of the Nephites; and for this intent hath the Lord prolonged their days.

links.text: As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.

provenance.route: Malachi 1:2-3 → Romans 9:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The loved/hated pair has two KJV homes, Malachi 1:2-3 and Romans 9:13 quoting it; “have I hated” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which Romans 9:13 is the only one about Esau. They differ in word order: Malachi reads 'yet I loved Jacob. And I hated Esau' — verb before object — while Romans inverts to 'Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated'. The Book of Mormon has the inversion: 'the people of Nephi hath he loved … the Lamanites hath he hated'. mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for Romans, but on a thin backbone of a single shared word, so the word order rather than the tool's count is what carries this.
provenance.significance: Samuel takes the harshest election text in the Bible and assigns the roles against his hearers' expectation — and then unsays it. Paul uses Jacob and Esau to argue that God's choice is not earned; Samuel reports that the Nephites are Jacob and the Lamanites are Esau, and immediately adds that the hated brother is the one being saved, keeping the commandments, and adding to his numbers daily. The metalepsis is Romans 9's whole argument, which ends by transferring the promise to those 'which were not my people' (9:25). The verse quotes the premise and lets the conclusion arrive over the next thirteen verses.

links.note: 'The Lamanites hath he hated, because their deeds have been evil continually', following 15:3's 'the people of Nephi hath he loved'. The distinctive thing is the syntax, not the vocabulary: Malachi puts the verb first and Romans fronts the object, and the Book of Mormon fronts the object twice. Hardy's apparatus cross-references both Malachi 1:2-3 and Romans 9:13 at this verse, which is right about the pair and does not choose between them; the choice is what this row records. Note also that 'their deeds have been evil continually' fuses Genesis 6:5's 'only evil continually' into Paul's clause, which neither source has.

pericopes.text: And I would that ye should behold that the more part of them are in the path of their duty, and they do walk circumspectly before God, and they do observe to keep his commandments, and his statutes, and his judgements, according to the law of Moses.

links.text: See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,

provenance.other: “Walk circumspectly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:15. The adjective appears once more, at Exodus 23:13 ('in all things that I have said unto you be circumspect'), and the adverb nowhere else. The rest of the verse — 'keep his commandments, and his statutes, and his judgements' — is the Deuteronomic triad, closest to Deuteronomy 26:17, which also has the walking.
provenance.significance: A Pauline adverb inside a Mosaic sentence, describing Lamanites keeping the law of Moses. Recover Ephesians 5:15-16 and the reason for circumspection is the times: 'redeeming the time, because the days are evil' — which is the situation Samuel has spent two chapters describing, and the reason his audience has run out of. The Lamanites are walking carefully because the days are evil; the Nephites are told at 13:38 that they have procrastinated.

links.note: 'The more part of them are in the path of their duty, and they do walk circumspectly before God, and they do observe to keep his commandments, and his statutes, and his judgements, according to the law of Moses.' 'Walk circumspectly' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The second half of the sentence is Deuteronomy's standing formula for covenant obedience and Deuteronomy 26:17 is its closest form, joining the walking to the statutes, commandments and judgments in one verse. 1830 spells 'judgements'; 1920 modernises to 'judgments'.

pericopes.text: Yea, I say unto you, that the more part of them are doing this, and they are striving, with unwearied diligence, that they may bring the remainder of their brethren to the knowledge of the truth; therefore there are many which do add to their numbers daily.

links.text: Praising God, and having favour with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved.

provenance.other: “Added to the church daily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:47. The King James Bible has no other verse in which converts are added to anything on a daily basis; Acts 16:5 has churches 'increased in number daily', which is congregations rather than persons.
provenance.significance: Samuel describes the Lamanite mission in the vocabulary of Pentecost. Recovering Acts 2:47 supplies the clause the Book of Mormon leaves off — 'such as should be saved' — and the picture the whole chapter is drawing: a community with all things common, praising God, growing daily, which is what Acts 2:44-47 describes and what 15:5-9 says the Lamanites have become while the Nephites were setting their hearts on riches.

links.note: 'There are many which do add to their numbers daily.' 'Added to the church daily' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moderate rather than high because the Book of Mormon substitutes 'their numbers' for Luke's 'the church' and reverses the voice — Luke's converts are added by the Lord, Samuel's missionaries do the adding — so the shared material is the idiom of daily accession rather than a clause. Its force comes from the paragraph around it, which reproduces the rest of Acts 2:44-47's picture.

pericopes.text: And behold ye do know of yourselves, for ye have witnessed it, that as many of them as are brought to the knowledge of the truth, and to know of the wicked and abominable traditions of their fathers, and are lead to believe the Holy Scriptures, yea, the prophecies of the holy prophets, which are written, which leadeth them to faith on the Lord, and unto repentance, which faith and repentance bringeth a change of heart unto them;

links.text: Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.

provenance.other: “Knowledge of the truth” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Timothy 2:4, 2 Timothy 3:7 and Hebrews 10:26; all three are late epistles and the phrase has no Old Testament existence. The Book of Mormon uses it three times in this chapter alone (15:7, 15:11, 15:13).
provenance.significance: The phrase carries a soteriology with it. 1 Timothy 2:4's God 'will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth' is the universalist half of the Pastorals, and Samuel is arguing precisely that the despised nation is being brought to it. 2 Timothy 3:7's 'ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth' is the mirror image and is what 15:15 says of the Nephites.

links.note: 'As many of them as are brought to the knowledge of the truth … are lead to believe the Holy Scriptures.' The phrase occurs in exactly three KJV verses and belongs entirely to the Pastorals and Hebrews. Echo rather than allusion: no single one of the three can be isolated, and the Book of Mormon has made the expression a standing formula of its own. Registered because the chapter's argument turns on it three times and because a reader should know the phrase is Pauline rather than prophetic.

pericopes.text: therefore as many as have come to this, ye know of yourselves, are firm and steadfast in the faith, and in the thing wherewith they have been made free.—

links.text: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.

provenance.other: “Hath made us free” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 5:1, and the fuller relative construction 'wherewith Christ hath made us free' likewise occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reproduces the relative clause with the pronoun changed: 'the thing wherewith they have been made free'.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is an exhortation to stand fast; Samuel reports that the Lamanites already are. Recovering Galatians supplies the warning attached — 'be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage' — and the Book of Mormon has been telling the reader for two chapters what that yoke is here: not the law, but riches, which at 13:31 have been cursed so they cannot be held. And 15:9 immediately shows what the Lamanites do with their freedom, which is to bury their weapons and let themselves be trodden down. That is Galatians 5:13's 'by love serve one another' rather than 5:1's standing fast.

links.note: 'As many as have come to this … are firm and steadfast in the faith, and in the thing wherewith they have been made free.' 'Wherewith Christ hath made us free' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the Book of Mormon reproduces its unusual relative construction — a freedom identified by the thing it was won with — while replacing 'liberty' with the vague 'thing'. Note that 'stand fast' at the head of Paul's sentence has become 'firm and steadfast' at the head of the Book of Mormon's, which is 1 Peter 5:9's phrase and is adjudicated separately at this verse. Compare 14:30, 'he hath made you free', where the same Pauline verb is already in the sermon.

links.text: Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world.

provenance.other: “Stedfast in the faith” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 5:9. Colossians 1:23's 'continue in the faith grounded and settled' and 1 Corinthians 16:13's 'stand fast in the faith' are the near neighbours and neither uses the adjective.
provenance.significance: Peter's steadfastness is resistance to a devouring adversary, and the reason given is that the same afflictions are being borne by the brethren elsewhere in the world. Samuel's Lamanites are steadfast in the faith and are being trodden down and slain for it two verses later. What the source supplies is the comparative frame: they are not the only ones, which is the argument Samuel is making to a Nephite audience that thinks it is.

links.note: 'Are firm and steadfast in the faith.' 'Stedfast in the faith' occurs in exactly one KJV verse; 1830 spells it 'steadfast', which is the modern form, so the orthographic evidence runs the other way here and is worth saying. Moderate: three words, and 'steadfast' is one of the Book of Mormon's own favourite words (compare the 'steadfast and immovable' formula), so the phrase may be arriving from its own usage rather than freshly from Peter. It is recorded separately from the Galatians link because the two halves of this verse borrow from two different epistles.

pericopes.text: And ye know also that they have buried their weapons of war, and they fear to take them up, lest by any means they shall sin; yea, ye can see that they fear to sin; for behold, they will suffer themselves that they be trodden down and slain by their enemies, and will not lift their swords against them; and this because of their faith in Christ.

And now because of their steadfastness when they do believe in that thing which they do believe; for because of their firmness when they are once enlightened, behold the Lord shall bless them and prolong their days, notwithstanding their iniquity;

yea, even if they should dwindle in unbelief, the Lord shall prolong their days until the time shall come which hath been spoken of by our fathers, and also by the prophet Zenos, and many other prophets, concerning the restoration of our brethren, the Lamanites again, to the knowledge of the truth;

yea, I say unto you, That in the latter times, the promises of the Lord hath been extended to our brethren, the Lamanites; and notwithstanding the many afflictions which they shall have, and notwithstanding they shall be driven to and fro upon the face of the earth, and be hunted, and shall be smitten and scattered abroad, having no place for refuge, the Lord shall be merciful unto them;

links.text: Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;

provenance.other: “In the latter times” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 4:1. The commoner KJV expression is 'in the last days' (Isaiah 2:2, Acts 2:17, 2 Timothy 3:1 and others) or 'in the latter days' (Jeremiah 23:20, Daniel 2:28), and the Book of Mormon uses those elsewhere; 'latter times' is Paul's alone.
provenance.significance: Paul's latter times are when 'some shall depart from the faith'. Samuel's sentence puts the departure and the latter times in the same order across two verses — 15:11's 'even if they should dwindle in unbelief' and then 15:12's 'in the latter times, the promises of the Lord hath been extended' — and then reverses the outcome. Where 1 Timothy 4:1 makes the latter times the era of apostasy, Helaman 15:12 makes them the era in which the apostates are reclaimed. Recovering Paul is what shows the reversal is deliberate rather than accidental.

links.note: 'In the latter times, the promises of the Lord hath been extended to our brethren, the Lamanites.' 'In the latter times' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse pairs the period with a falling away from the faith, which is what 15:11 has just described. Moderate: three words, and the sense is inverted from the source's. What argues for the borrowing is that the KJV offers three commoner ways of saying this and the text has chosen the singleton.
links.whyNot: A short temporal formula, and the Book of Mormon's eschatological vocabulary is already saturated with 'latter day' language of its own. A reader who takes this as the text's own idiom rather than a citation of Paul has a fair case; the reversal of sense is the argument, and reversal is easier to assert than to prove.

links.text: Wilt thou break a leaf driven to and fro? and wilt thou pursue the dry stubble?

provenance.other: “Driven to and fro” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 13:25, where it describes a leaf. The KJV's other 'to and fro' phrases are running (2 Chronicles 16:9, Zechariah 4:10), reeling (Isaiah 24:20) and being tossed (Ephesians 4:14).
provenance.significance: Job's line is a question — 'Wilt thou break a leaf driven to and fro? and wilt thou pursue the dry stubble?' — put to a God who seems to be doing exactly that. Helaman 15:12 says the Lamanites will be driven to and fro, hunted, smitten and scattered, and then answers Job's question in the affirmative's opposite: 'the Lord shall be merciful unto them'. If the echo is real the verse is a reply to Job, which is more than the words alone can establish.

links.note: 'Notwithstanding they shall be driven to and fro upon the face of the earth, and be hunted, and shall be smitten and scattered abroad.' 'Driven to and fro' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Recorded at low because a KJV singleton this ordinary is weak evidence — the phrase is natural English and the Book of Mormon could reach it without Job — and because the surrounding verbs (hunted, smitten, scattered) belong to the deuteronomic curse vocabulary rather than to Job.
links.whyNot: Four common words, a singleton only because the KJV had little occasion to use them. Nothing else in the verse points at Job, and the mercy that answers the driving is the Book of Mormon's own promise to the Lamanites, made repeatedly elsewhere without Joban language.

pericopes.text: and this is according to the prophecy, that they shall again be brought to the true knowledge, which is the knowledge of their Redeemer, and their great and their true Shepherd, and be numbered among his sheep.

links.text: Now the God of peace, that brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant,

provenance.other: “Great shepherd” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 13:20 ('that great shepherd of the sheep'). John 10:11's is the 'good shepherd' and 1 Peter 5:4's the 'chief Shepherd'; the KJV keeps the three adjectives distinct.
provenance.significance: Two shepherd texts fused, and the join is the point. Hebrews 13:20 supplies the epithet and the resurrection frame ('brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus'), which is what the chapter has been about since 14:15; John 10:16 supplies the other sheep who are not of this fold and must also be brought — the verse the Book of Mormon will make its own at 3 Nephi 15:21. So Samuel's promise that the Lamanites will be 'numbered among his sheep' is stated in the vocabulary of the one KJV passage about sheep outside the fold, three books before the Book of Mormon makes that identification explicit.

links.note: 'Their great and their true Shepherd, and be numbered among his sheep.' 'Great shepherd' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The being numbered among the sheep is John 10:16's other fold rather than Hebrews', so the verse is composite. Moderate: 'great shepherd' is two words and the epithet 'true Shepherd' is the Book of Mormon's own (Alma 5:38-39, 1 Nephi 22:25), so what is being caught here is the KJV colouring of a formula the text had already made its own.

pericopes.text: Therefore I say unto you, It shall be better for them than for you, except ye repent.

links.text: But I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you.

provenance.other: “Than for you” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 11:22 and Luke 10:14, which are the same saying about Tyre and Sidon. 'More tolerable' occurs in six, always in this comparative-judgment formula. The Book of Mormon substitutes 'better' for 'more tolerable' and drops the day of judgment.
provenance.significance: The formula's whole force is that the comparison is with the outsiders — the Gentile cities, the proverbially wicked ones — and the Book of Mormon takes it over exactly: the people who will fare better are the Lamanites, and the audience being told so is the covenant nation. Recovering the source supplies what Samuel does not say, which is when the comparison will be made: 'in the day of judgment'.

links.note: 'It shall be better for them than for you, except ye repent.' 'Than for you' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both the Tyre and Sidon saying, and this is the sentence that introduces the counterfactual at 15:15. Moderate on its own — the shared string is three common words — and it should be read with 15:15, where the mighty works and the counterfactual repentance make the identification of the source secure.

pericopes.text: For behold, had the mighty works been shewn unto them which have been shewn unto you; yea, unto them which have dwindled in unbelief because of the traditions of their fathers, ye can see of yourselves, that they never would again have dwindled in unbelief;

links.text: And thou, Capernaum, which art exalted unto heaven, shalt be brought down to hell: for if the mighty works, which have been done in thee, had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day.

provenance.route: Matthew 11:21-23 (or Luke 10:13) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “The mighty works” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, Matthew 11:21, Matthew 11:23, Matthew 13:54 and Luke 10:13. The construction is a counterfactual with three parts — mighty works, done in one city rather than another, and a repentance that would have followed — and it exists in the KJV only at Matthew 11:21, Matthew 11:23 and Luke 10:13. The evangelist cannot be settled here, and the catalogue records that rather than hiding it. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Matthew 11:23, but both rest on material Helaman 15:15 does not reproduce (Sodom; sackcloth and ashes), so they are artifacts of the alignment and are set aside. Against Matthew, the clause order matches Luke: Luke 10:13 has 'had been done in Tyre and Sidon, WHICH HAVE BEEN DONE IN YOU' — them before you — and Helaman 15:15 has 'been shewn unto them WHICH HAVE BEEN SHEWN UNTO YOU'. Matthew 11:21 and 11:23 both put the hearers first. On the other hand the sermon's other borrowings in these two chapters are all Matthaean.
provenance.significance: Jesus' saying is an indictment of privilege: the cities that saw the miracles did not repent, and the ones that never saw them would have. Samuel applies it to a nation that has just been given a list of miracles to expect. The suppressed clause in Matthew is the one that follows — 'thou, Capernaum, which art exalted unto heaven, shalt be brought down to hell' — and the Book of Mormon's audience has been told the same thing in chapter 13 in Sodom's terms. The counterfactual is a rebuke that cannot be answered, because the condition can never be tested; that is exactly why 15:15 ends 'ye can see of yourselves'.

links.note: 'Had the mighty works been shewn unto them which have been shewn unto you … they never would again have dwindled in unbelief.' The three-part counterfactual is the synoptic saying about Tyre and Sidon, and the Book of Mormon has substituted 'shewn' for 'done' and 'dwindled in unbelief' for 'repented'. Which evangelist cannot be decided: the mediation tool's two decisive points both fall on words the Book of Mormon does not have, while the clause order — the others before the hearers — is Luke's rather than Matthew's, and the sermon's other borrowings are Matthew's. Recorded as Matthew with Luke 10:13 as a composite and the disagreement stated. The 1830 'shewn', modernised to 'shown' in 1920, preserves the KJV's orthography (CONVENTIONS §8), though the KJV's own verb here is 'done'.

pericopes.text: therefore, saith the Lord, I will not utterly destroy them, but I will cause that in the day of my wisdom, they shall return again unto me, saith the Lord.

links.text: Behold, the eyes of the Lord GOD are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from off the face of the earth; saving that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, saith the LORD.

provenance.other: “I will not utterly destroy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Amos 9:8, and it is the KJV's one sentence in which God announces destruction and then withholds it from a remnant in the same breath. 'Utterly destroy' by itself occurs in twelve, almost all of them commands to exterminate Canaanites or Amalekites.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon splits Amos's sentence between two peoples. Amos 9:8 destroys the sinful kingdom from off the face of the earth 'saving that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob'; Helaman 15:16 gives the Lamanites the saving clause and 15:17 gives the Nephites the destruction, in the same words, one verse apart. Recovering Amos supplies the mechanism the Book of Mormon leaves out and then spends a thousand years enacting — 9:9's sifting of the house of Israel among all nations, 'yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth', which is what 'in the day of my wisdom, they shall return again unto me' means.

links.note: 'I will not utterly destroy them, but I will cause that in the day of my wisdom, they shall return again unto me' (15:16), against 'if they will not repent … I will utterly destroy them' (15:17). 'I will not utterly destroy' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Amos 9:8 is also the only KJV verse that puts the two verdicts in one sentence, which is what the Book of Mormon does across two. The machine stream returned the verse independently. Note that 1 Samuel 15:9 and 2 Chronicles 12:7 are the near matches and both are filed in the register.

pericopes.text: And now behold, saith the Lord, concerning the people of the Nephites, if they will not repent, and observe to do my will, I will utterly destroy them, saith the Lord, because of their unbelief, notwithstanding the many mighty works which I have done among them; and as surely as the Lord liveth, shall these things be, saith the Lord.

links.text: And that thou mayest tell in the ears of thy son, and of thy son’s son, what things I have wrought in Egypt, and my signs which I have done among them; that ye may know how that I am the LORD.

provenance.other: “Which I have done among them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 10:2, where the antecedent is 'my signs'. The 'mighty works' the Book of Mormon attaches to it are the synoptic saying's, ten KJV verses, all in the gospels.
provenance.significance: Two economies of sign fused in one clause. Exodus 10:2 is spoken in the middle of the plagues and gives their purpose — that a father may tell his son, and that they may know the Lord — and the sign that follows it three verses later is the darkness Helaman 14:27 has already borrowed. The gospels' 'mighty works' come with the opposite outcome: the cities that saw them did not repent. Samuel's sentence has Exodus's grammar and Matthew's verdict, and the result is a threat: the signs were given, the knowing did not follow, and 'I will utterly destroy them'.

links.note: 'I will utterly destroy them … because of their unbelief, notwithstanding the many mighty works which I have done among them.' 'Which I have done among them' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and in Exodus 10:2 the works so described are the plagues — which is what chapter 14 has been promising, three days of darkness included. The pairing with 'mighty works' brings Matthew 11:20's unrepentant cities into the same clause. Moderate: a five-word run of ordinary words, and it may be coincidence; what raises it is that the Book of Mormon has just spent a chapter promising a plague and now describes it in the plague narrative's own phrase.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that there were many which heard the words of Samuel, the Lamanite, which he spake upon the walls of the city. And as many as believed on his words, went forth and sought for Nephi; and when they had came forth and found him, they confessed unto him their sins and denied not, desiring that they might be baptized unto the Lord.

provenance.other: “denied not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:20, and that verse is also the only place in the King James Bible where it follows 'confessed'. “confessing their sins” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 3:6 and Mark 1:5, both of them John's baptism in Jordan.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowed words are the Baptist's disclaimer of messiahship: 'he confessed, and denied not; but confessed, I am not the Christ.' Helaman 16 is the chapter in which a whole city argues about whether the Christ will come, and it opens by putting John 1:20's formula in the mouths of the converts and Nephi in the Baptist's place — baptizing, in the same sentence, those who confess and deny not. What John denies is exactly what the sceptics of 16:18 will deny: that such a being as a Christ shall come. The chapter's first clause and its central quarrel are held together by one verb pair.

links.note: 'They confessed unto him their sins and denied not, desiring that they might be baptized unto the Lord.' Strip the four inserted words and the sentence is John 1:20 verbatim — 'confessed ... and denied not' — which is a KJV singleton, and the remainder ('confessing their sins', at 16:5) is the Baptist's baptism in Matthew 3:6 and Mark 1:5. The Book of Mormon has fused the two Johannine baptism passages into one act, and given the Baptist's own vocabulary to the crowd rather than the baptizer. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his 36; the case rests on the singleton, not on length.
links.text: And he confessed, and denied not; but confessed, I am not the Christ.

pericopes.text: But as many as there were which did not believe in the words of Samuel, were angry with him; and they cast stones at him upon the wall, and also many shot arrows at him, as he stood upon the wall; but the spirit of the Lord was with him, insomuch that they could not hit him with their stones, neither with their arrows.

provenance.other: “stonest them” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:37 and its Lukan parallel 13:34, and in both the object is the prophets sent to the city. The Book of Mormon's own wording here — 'they cast stones at him upon the wall' — matches no KJV verse but 2 Samuel 16:6, where Shimei stones the fleeing David; see the exclusion at this verse.
provenance.significance: The scene executes the accusation. Helaman 13:25 has Samuel put the Matthew 23 charge to the city in its own form — 'if we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have slain the prophets' — and three verses into the next chapter the city is throwing stones at him on the wall. Matthew 23:37 is the verse where that indictment turns into lament over Jerusalem, and the Book of Mormon has separated the two halves of it across a chapter break: the accusation in Samuel's mouth, the stoning in the reader's sight.

links.note: No verbal borrowing; the link is the shape of the episode. What makes it worth recording rather than passing over is that Samuel has just made the Matthew 23 argument himself at 13:25 — the fathers' murder of the prophets, denied by sons who would have done the same — and 16:2 is the narrative answering it. Recorded as figural because the KJV wording ('stonest them which are sent unto thee') is nowhere reproduced.
links.whyNot: A crowd stoning an unwelcome prophet needs no literary source; the practice is in Numbers, Chronicles and Acts alike, and the only distinctive KJV wording near this verse points at Shimei, not at Matthew. A reader who takes 13:25 as the chapter's only Matthew 23 contact is entitled to decline this one.
links.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!

pericopes.text: Now when they saw this, that they could not hit him, there were many more which did believe on his words, insomuch that they went away unto Nephi to be baptized.

For behold, Nephi was baptizing, and prophesying, and preaching, crying repentance unto the people; shewing signs and wonders; working miracles among the people, that they might know that the Christ must shortly come;

telling them of things which must shortly come, that they might know and remember at the time of their coming, that they had been made known unto them beforehand, to the intent that they might believe; therefore as many as believed on the words of Samuel, went forth unto him to be baptized, for they came repenting and confessing their sins.

provenance.other: “things which must shortly come” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 1:1 ('things which must shortly come to pass'); Revelation 22:6 has the near-twin 'things which must shortly be done'. No other KJV verse joins 'shortly' to 'come'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 1:1 describes the mechanics of prophecy, not its content: God gives the revelation to Jesus Christ, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass, and signifies it by his angel to his servant John. Helaman 16:4-5 describes exactly the same chain in its own terms — Nephi telling them of things which must shortly come, that they might know and remember at the time of their coming that they had been made known beforehand — and 16:14 will supply the angel. The Book of Mormon has taken the Apocalypse's self-description of how a prophecy is delivered and applied it to Samuel's.

links.note: The unusual word is 'shortly'. 16:4 has 'the Christ must shortly come' and 16:5 'things which must shortly come', and the KJV joins those two words in one verse only, at the head of Revelation. The borrowing is functional rather than decorative: the surrounding sentence is an argument about *why* prophecy is given in advance ('that they might know and remember at the time of their coming'), which is the argument of Revelation 1:1-3.
links.text: The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:

pericopes.text: But the more part of them did not believe in the words of Samuel; therefore when they saw that they could not hit him with their stones and their arrows, they cried out unto their captains, saying, Take this fellow and bind him, for behold, he hath a Devil; and because of the power of the Devil which is in him, we cannot hit him with our stones and our arrows; therefore take him and bind him, and away with him.

provenance.route: Matthew 12:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon; with John 10:20 and John 19:15
provenance.other: “he hath a devil” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Matthew 11:18, Luke 7:33, John 10:20); “away with him” occurs in exactly two KJV verses (John 19:15, Acts 21:36); “this fellow” occurs in exactly 12 KJV verses, of which Matthew 12:24 is the one that joins it to the charge of working by the devil's power.
provenance.significance: Every clause of the accusation is a Gospel accusation, and they are drawn from the three occasions on which one is made. Matthew 12:24 supplies the reasoning — the works are real, therefore the power is Beelzebub's; John 10:20 supplies the formula 'he hath a devil'; John 19:15 and Acts 21:36 supply the mob's cry. Recovering them puts the crowd of Zarahemla in the position of the Pharisees at the Beelzebub controversy and of the crowd before Pilate at once, and makes the logic explicit: an inexplicable preservation is evidence of demonic power precisely because it cannot be denied.

links.note: Three separate KJV accusations in one sentence. 'Take this fellow' with 'because of the power of the Devil which is in him' is the Beelzebub charge of Matthew 12:24, where 'this fellow' works by the prince of the devils; 'he hath a Devil' is John 10:20 word for word; 'away with him' is the cry of John 19:15 and Acts 21:36. The composite is the point — the writer is not quoting a verse but assembling the standard KJV vocabulary of a crowd turning on a preacher, and the assembly is dense enough that no single source explains it.
links.text: But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, This fellow doth not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub the prince of the devils.

pericopes.text: And as they went forth to lay their hands on him, behold, he did cast himself down from the wall, and did flee out of their lands, yea, even unto his own country, and began to preach and to prophesy among his own people.

provenance.other: “cast thyself down” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 4:6 and Luke 4:9, both the pinnacle temptation; Luke's alone adds 'from hence', the preposition the Book of Mormon has ('down from the wall'). The reflexive third-person “cast himself down” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 18:42, where Elijah prostrates himself to pray — a different act, and excluded at this verse.
provenance.significance: The temptation is to prove divine protection by jumping from a height, and the proof offered is Psalm 91's promise of angelic rescue. Samuel jumps from the wall and is not hurt, having already been shielded from stones and arrows — the demonstration Jesus refuses to give. The unstated correspondence is that the sign the sceptics of 16:18 will demand ('why will he not shew himself unto us') is the sign the Gospels have Christ decline, and the Book of Mormon has just let a prophet give it.

links.note: Samuel escapes by throwing himself off the city wall, which in KJV English is the devil's proposal at the pinnacle: 'If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down from hence.' Two words of Luke 4:9 are reversed into the third person and the preposition survives. Thin on its own — but 16:18 puts 'if so, and he be the Son of God' into the mouths of the same crowd eleven verses later, which is the other half of Luke 4:9's sentence, and the coincidence of both halves in one chapter is what lifts this above an exclusion.
links.whyNot: Jumping off a wall to escape a mob is a thing that happens, and the phrase the Book of Mormon actually uses matches Elijah at Carmel rather than the temptation. If the 'Son of God' clause at 16:18 is judged to be ordinary christological vocabulary rather than an echo of the same verse, this row loses most of its support.
links.text: And he brought him to Jerusalem, and set him on a pinnacle of the temple, and said unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down from hence:

pericopes.text: And behold, he was never heard of more among the Nephites; and thus were the affairs of the people.
And thus ended the eighty and sixth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.

And thus ended, also, the eighty and seventh year of the reign of the Judges, the more part of the people remaining in their pride and wickedness, and the lesser part walking more circumspectly before God.

provenance.other: “circumspectly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:15, and “walk circumspectly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse likewise; the adjective 'circumspect' occurs once more, at Exodus 23:13. The word is otherwise absent from the King James Bible.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:15 finishes the sentence the Book of Mormon breaks off: 'See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise.' Helaman 16 then spends ten verses on precisely that antithesis. The lesser part walk circumspectly at 16:10; the more part begin at 16:15 to depend 'upon their own wisdom', reason as the wise at 16:17-21, and are described at 16:22 as imagining things 'foolish and vain'. Recovering Paul's clause supplies the chapter's own verdict on the argument it is about to report — the wise men of 16:16 are the fools of Ephesians 5:15.

links.note: A one-word borrowing that carries a chapter. 'Circumspectly' is a KJV singleton and the Book of Mormon uses it in Paul's exact construction, walking circumspectly, at the hinge where the people divide into a lesser believing part and a more part in pride. The strength of the link is not the word alone but the argument the rest of Ephesians 5:15 supplies and Helaman 16:15-22 then runs.
links.text: See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,

pericopes.text: And these were the conditions also, in the eighty and eighth year of the reign of the Judges.

And there were but little alteration in the affairs of the people, save it were the people began to be more hardened in iniquity, and do more and more of that which was contrary to the commandments of God, in the eighty and ninth year of the reign of the Judges.
But it came to pass in the ninetieth year of the reign of the Judges, there were great signs given unto the people, and wonders; and the words of the prophets began to be fulfilled;
and angels did appear unto men, wise men, and did declare unto them glad tidings of great joy; thus in this year the Scriptures began to be fulfilled.

provenance.route: Luke 2:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon; 'glad' from Luke 1:19
provenance.other: “tidings of great joy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 2:10, where the adjective is 'good'. “glad tidings” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Luke 1:19, Luke 8:1, Acts 13:32, Romans 10:15), the first of them Gabriel's word to Zacharias. Matthew 2:10 is the only other nativity verse with 'great joy', and it belongs to the wise men.
provenance.significance: The single clause holds both nativity narratives at once. From Luke comes the angelic annunciation — angels appearing, tidings of great joy — and from Matthew come the wise men, who in the KJV rejoice with exceeding great joy when they see the star. The Book of Mormon's sign of the nativity is a star (14:5), and here the shepherds' angels and Matthew's star-following magi are collapsed into one sentence, on the other side of the world, in the same year. The two Gospel infancy accounts share almost nothing; this verse makes them share an audience.

links.note: 'Angels did appear unto men, wise men, and did declare unto them glad tidings of great joy.' 'Tidings of great joy' is a KJV singleton at Luke 2:10, with 'glad' substituted for 'good' from Gabriel's 'glad tidings' at Luke 1:19 — and Luke 1:19 is already the source adjudicated at Helaman 13:7, where an angel brings Samuel his message. The recipients, though, are Matthew's: wise men, whose response to the star at Matthew 2:10 is 'exceeding great joy'. Luke supplies the announcement, Matthew the audience.
links.text: And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless, the people began to harden their hearts, all save it were the most believing part of them, both of the Nephites, and also of the Lamanites, and began to depend upon their own strength, and upon their own wisdom, saying:
Some things they may have guessed right, among so many; but behold, we know that all these great and marvellous works cannot come to pass, of which hath been spoken.

provenance.other: “great and marvellous” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3, and nowhere else in the King James Bible. The 1830 text preserves the KJV spelling 'marvellous'; the 1920 edition changed it to 'marvelous', so the borrowing is plainer in the first edition than in the current one (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: The two verses the phrase comes from are the two things the sceptics deny. Revelation 15:1 is 'another sign in heaven, great and marvellous' — and 16:13-14 has just reported great signs and angels; Revelation 15:3 is 'Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty', and 16:16 denies that 'all these great and marvellous works' can come to pass. So the unbelievers are refusing, in the Apocalypse's own words, both the sign and the works the Apocalypse ascribes to God. The same six words of Revelation 15:3 are the source adjudicated at 1 Nephi 1:14, where Lehi sings them; here they are quoted to be denied, which puts the first and last speeches of the Nephite record on opposite sides of one sentence.

links.note: 'All these great and marvellous works cannot come to pass.' The adjectival pair is confined in the KJV to Revelation 15, where 15:3 attaches it to God's works — the noun the Book of Mormon keeps — and 15:1 to a sign in heaven, which is what the chapter has just described. The phrase returns at 16:20 in its 15:1 form ('some great and marvellous thing which should come to pass'), so the objectors use both halves of the source in five verses. 1830's 'marvellous' is KJV orthography; the modern text's 'marvelous' is not.
links.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

pericopes.text: And they began to reason and to contend among themselves, saying,

provenance.other: “began to reason” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 5:21, where the scribes and Pharisees begin to reason at the forgiveness of the palsied man's sins. “reasoned among themselves” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Matthew 16:7, Mark 8:16, Luke 20:14), of which Luke 20:14 is the wicked husbandmen agreeing to kill the heir.
provenance.significance: Both Lukan reasoning scenes are refusals of a christological claim, and both are answered by a demonstration rather than an argument. In Luke 5 the question the scribes begin to reason is 'Who is this which speaketh blasphemies?', and Jesus answers by healing; in Luke 20 the reasoning ends 'This is the heir: come, let us kill him'. Helaman 16:17-18 sets its own reasoning between those two — it begins from the Christ's identity and ends, in the chapter following, in the reader's knowledge that the heir will be killed.

links.note: 'They began to reason and to contend among themselves, saying' — and what follows is a denial that a Christ will come. 'Began to reason' is a KJV singleton and its one occurrence is the scribes reasoning against Christ's authority to forgive sins, the same objection in the same posture; the fuller construction 'reasoned among themselves, saying' introduces the husbandmen's plot at Luke 20:14. Moderate rather than high because 'reason' is common English and the argument that follows is the writer's own, not Luke's.
links.text: And the scribes and the Pharisees began to reason, saying, Who is this which speaketh blasphemies? Who can forgive sins, but God alone?

pericopes.text: That it is not reasonable that such a being as a Christ shall come; if so, and he be the Son of God, the Father of Heaven and of earth, as it hath been spoken, why will he not shew himself unto us, as well as unto they which shall be at Jerusalem?

provenance.other: “shew thyself” occurs in exactly 12 KJV verses; John 7:4 is the one where it is a taunt from unbelievers demanding a public appearance, and John 7:5 supplies the reason — 'for neither did his brethren believe in him'. The 1830 text keeps the KJV spelling 'shew' at 16:18 and 16:19, modernized to 'show' in 1920.
provenance.significance: John 7:3-5 is the KJV's one scene of unbelievers challenging Christ to relocate his signs: leave here, go to Judaea, do it where it will be seen, shew thyself to the world. Helaman 16:18-19 makes the identical demand with the geography reversed — why Jerusalem and not this land — so the Nephite objection is the Johannine objection read from the far end of the map. Recovering John 7:5 supplies what the Book of Mormon leaves unsaid about the speakers, which is that they are relatives of the person they are challenging.

links.note: 'Why will he not shew himself unto us, as well as unto they which shall be at Jerusalem?' The demand that Christ shew himself where the sceptic is standing is John 7:4, and the KJV's verb, in 1830's spelling, is the one the Book of Mormon uses twice. The verbal contact is two words and 'shew thyself' is not rare; what carries the row is that no other KJV passage puts this demand in unbelieving mouths, and that the Book of Mormon inverts its geography exactly.
links.whyNot: Two words, one of them a KJV spelling the Book of Mormon uses everywhere. The objection 'why not here' is an obvious one for a New World record to script for its sceptics and needs no source. Recorded as an echo, not an allusion, for that reason.
links.text: For there is no man that doeth any thing in secret, and he himself seeketh to be known openly. If thou do these things, shew thyself to the world.

pericopes.text: Yea, why will he not shew himself in this land, as well as in the land of Jerusalem?

But behold, we know that this is a wicked tradition, which has been handed down unto us by our fathers, to cause us that we should believe in some great and marvellous thing which should come to pass, but not among us, but in a land which is far distant, a land which we know not; therefore they can keep us in ignorance, for we cannot witness with our own eyes that they are true.

And they will, by the cunning and the mysterious arts of the evil one, work some great mystery, which we cannot understand, which will keep us down to be servants to their words, and also servants unto them, for we depend upon them for to teach us the word; and thus will they keep us in ignorance, if we will yield ourselves unto them all the days of our lives.

And many more things did the people imagine up in their hearts, which were foolish and vain; and they were much disturbed, for satan did stir them up to do iniquity continually; yea, he did go about, spreading rumors and contentions upon all the face of the land, that he might harden the hearts of the people against that which was good, and against that which should come;

provenance.route: Psalm 2:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon, or Psalm 2:1 via Acts 4:25; mediation-check.py finds no divergence the Book of Mormon reproduces
provenance.other: “the people imagine” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 2:1 ('a vain thing') and Acts 4:25, which quotes it ('vain things'). The two differ only at 'do/did', the article, and the plural, and Helaman 16:22 reproduces none of those points: it has 'many more things did the people imagine up in their hearts, which were foolish and vain'. The plural leans to Acts; the tool declines to call it.
provenance.significance: Psalm 2 is the psalm of the nations conspiring against the Lord and against his Anointed, and Acts 4 applies it to the coalition that put Christ to death. Helaman 16:22 describes a population being stirred up against a Christ who has not yet come. Recovering the psalm supplies the verse's missing subject: what the people are imagining is not a private folly but the standing biblical conspiracy against the Messiah, and the Book of Mormon has placed it thirty years before the crucifixion Acts 4 is looking back at.

links.note: 'Many more things did the people imagine up in their hearts, which were foolish and vain.' The collocation of 'the people imagine' with vanity is confined in the KJV to Psalm 2:1 and its quotation at Acts 4:25, and the context is exact — a populace stirred up against the Anointed. Moderate rather than high because the wording is redistributed across the sentence rather than reproduced, and because 'imagine' plus 'vain' is the kind of pairing a writer steeped in the psalms would produce without quoting.
links.text: Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?

pericopes.text: and notwithstanding the signs and the wonders which was wrought among the people of the Lord, and the many miracles which they did, satan did get great hold upon the hearts of the people, upon all the face of the land.

provenance.other: “wrought among the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:12, and “signs and wonders wrought among the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse likewise. “signs and wonders” alone occurs in exactly 14 KJV verses and identifies nothing; the machine's best match here was Deuteronomy 34:11, which shares only the formula and is excluded at this verse.
provenance.significance: Acts 5:12 is the summary verse of the apostolic church at its height — signs and wonders wrought among the people, the believers with one accord in Solomon's porch — and the verses on either side of it report that the people magnified them and that multitudes were added. Helaman 16:23 takes the same clause and gives it the opposite outcome: the signs and wonders are wrought, the miracles are done, and Satan gets great hold upon the hearts of the people notwithstanding. The borrowing is an inversion, and its force depends on the reader knowing what the sentence normally reports.

links.note: The chapter's clearest single borrowing, and the one the n-gram stream nearly missed: it ranked Deuteronomy 34:11 first on the shared formula 'the signs and the wonders' and put Acts 5:12 last, but 'wrought among the people' is a KJV singleton and Acts 5:12 is the only verse that has the whole clause. The Book of Mormon keeps the clause and reverses its result — the same apostolic summary, ending in Satan's hold rather than the church's increase.
links.text: And by the hands of the apostles were many signs and wonders wrought among the people; (and they were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch.

pericopes.text: And thus ended the ninetieth year of the reign of the Judges over the people of Nephi.
And thus ended the book of Helaman, according to the record of Helaman and his sons.
